docs.t: What is the regulatory classification of the FOM?
docs.x: What is the regulatory classification of the FOM? It is classified as an FAA-accepted manual with approved content. FOM 1.1.6 — Regulatory Classification The FOM is classified as an FAA-accepted manual with approved content. The FOM is an accepted manual, but portions of its content are FAA-approved. Publication follows the FAA Approval/Acceptance Request Process defined in the Company Administrative Manual.

docs.t: Per the FOM, who has the authority and responsibility to deviate from published guidance in the interest of safety, and under which regulations?
docs.x: Per the FOM, who has the authority and responsibility to deviate from published guidance in the interest of safety, and under which regulations? The PIC, as set forth in CFR 91.3 and 121.557. FOM 1.1 — Manual Overview and Usage As set forth in CFR 91.3 and 121.557, the PIC has the authority and responsibility to deviate from published guidance to the extent required in the interest of safety. The manual cannot anticipate every situation, so the PIC retains deviation authority scoped to what safety requires.

docs.t: If a conflict exists between Company manuals, what hierarchy applies?
docs.x: If a conflict exists between Company manuals, what hierarchy applies? F&F/Company NOTAMs, then Required Operational Memos, then 10-7 information. FOM 1.1.1 — Manual Hierarchy If a conflict exists between Company manuals, the following hierarchy applies: The listed order ranks the sources: F&F/Company NOTAMs are highest, followed by Required Operational Memos, then 10-7 information.

docs.t: When manual guidance conflicts, which guidance governs?
docs.x: When manual guidance conflicts, which guidance governs? The more restrictive guidance will apply. FOM 1.1.1 — Manual Hierarchy In the event of conflicting manual guidance, the more restrictive guidance will apply. This 'most restrictive wins' rule also reappears in 1.5 for conflicting directives across the Company Manual System.

docs.t: How are incremental revisions to the FOM numbered?
docs.x: How are incremental revisions to the FOM numbered? They are numbered subsequent to the current revision (e.g., 123.1, 123.2) until the next full revision (e.g., 124, 125). FOM 1.1.3 — Incremental Revisions An incremental revision will be numbered subsequent to the current revision (e.g., 123.1, 123.2) until the next full revision (e.g., 124, 125), and will retain the change bars from the current full revision. Incremental revisions push out information earlier than a full revision allows, or for content with a specific effective date, and keep the current full revision's change bars.

docs.t: By what means are changes to regulatory information conveyed to crews?
docs.x: By what means are changes to regulatory information conveyed to crews? By Required Operational Memo, Field & Facility (F&F)/Company NOTAMs, and Manual Revision or Incremental Revision. FOM 1.1.2 — Information Management Alaska Airlines is responsible for timely dissemination of all regulatory information required for safe, compliant flight operations. Regulatory changes use those three channels; administrative information instead goes out by Informational Memo and Company email.

docs.t: In the FOM's conventions, what do the words 'Shall' or 'Must' indicate?
docs.x: In the FOM's conventions, what do the words 'Shall' or 'Must' indicate? That a procedure, practice, or condition is mandatory. FOM 1.6 — Manual Conventions “Shall” or “Must” indicates that a procedure, practice, or condition is mandatory. By contrast 'Should' means recommended, and 'May' or 'Need not' means optional.

docs.t: What does the word 'Should' indicate in this manual, versus 'May' or 'Need not'?
docs.x: What does the word 'Should' indicate in this manual, versus 'May' or 'Need not'? 'Should' indicates a procedure, practice, or condition is recommended; 'May' or 'Need not' indicates it is optional. FOM 1.6 — Manual Conventions “Should” indicates that a procedure, practice, or condition is recommended. Three tiers: mandatory (Shall/Must), recommended (Should), optional (May/Need not).

docs.t: What is the difference between a WARNING and a CAUTION in the FOM?
docs.x: What is the difference between a WARNING and a CAUTION in the FOM? A WARNING flags a procedure, practice, or condition that may result in injury or death; a CAUTION flags one that may result in damage to equipment. FOM 1.6 — Manual Conventions An operating procedure, practice, or condition that may result in injury or death if not carefully observed or followed. WARNING is about people (injury or death); CAUTION is about equipment damage; a Note simply adds emphasis or explanation.

docs.t: What are the three phases of the 'Ready, SAFE, Go' model?
docs.x: What are the three phases of the 'Ready, SAFE, Go' model? Am I Ready?, Is Everything SAFE?, and Can I Go? FOM 1.2.4 — Ready, SAFE, Go This phase focuses on your preparation. Before you act, ensure you are ready and have the right resources. Ready = preparation and resources; SAFE = self-assess for hazards and act to prevent adverse outcomes; Go = proceed with a safety focus without rushing.

docs.t: What are the four pillars of Alaska's SMS?
docs.x: What are the four pillars of Alaska's SMS? Safety Policy, Safety Risk Management, Safety Assurance, and Safety Promotion. FOM 1.2.3 — SMS Pillars A process within our SMS that describes a system, identifies any associated hazards, and analyzes, assesses, and controls risk to as low as reasonably practicable. Safety Risk Management controls risk to as low as reasonably practicable; the four pillars together form the SMS framework.

docs.t: Who owns the SMS at AAG, and who are the named Accountable Executives?
docs.x: Who owns the SMS at AAG, and who are the named Accountable Executives? The AAG Accountable Executives own the SMS: Jason Berry (AS, COO) for Alaska Airlines and Andy Schneider (QX, CEO/President) for Horizon Air. FOM 1.2.2 — SMS Ownership The AAG Accountable Executives own the SMS and are responsible for ensuring its design and performance. Ownership formally rests with the Accountable Executives, but the manual stresses each teammate OWNS SAFETY.

docs.t: Who is responsible for the overall content and quality of the FOM, and who may modify its policies and procedures?
docs.x: Who is responsible for the overall content and quality of the FOM, and who may modify its policies and procedures? The Managing Director, Standards, Fleet, and Operational Control is responsible for overall content and quality; the Director, Flight Standards, or their designee, has authority to establish and modify policies and procedures. FOM 1.3 — Responsibility and Authority The Managing Director, Standards, Fleet, and Operational Control is responsible for the overall content and quality of this manual. Two distinct roles: one owns content and quality, the other holds authority to change policies and procedures.

docs.t: Where can questions about this manual's content or suggested improvements be sent?
docs.x: Where can questions about this manual's content or suggested improvements be sent? To flightstandards@alaskaair.com. FOM 1.1.7 — Comments, Questions, Suggestions Questions about the content of this manual or suggested improvements should be sent to flightstandards@alaskaair.com. This is the single feedback channel for FOM content questions and improvement suggestions.

docs.t: What is the purpose of airline identifiers such as (AS) and (HA) in the manual?
docs.x: What is the purpose of airline identifiers such as (AS) and (HA) in the manual? They distinguish differences in policies and procedures between Alaska Airlines and Hawaiian Airlines. FOM 1.6.1 — Airline Identifiers Airline identifiers are used to distinguish the differences in policies and procedures for Alaska Airlines and Hawaiian Airlines. Placed after a heading when the whole topic is airline-specific, or before content in a paragraph when only that portion applies; a color-filled end box (AS or HA) may be used.

docs.t: Where are terms and definitions used in this manual found?
docs.x: Where are terms and definitions used in this manual found? In the Pilot/Controller Glossary of the AIM, the Introduction of the Jeppesen General Airway Manual, and 14 CFR Part 1; unique terms and acronyms are in Chapter 26 Abbreviations and Acronyms. FOM 1.7 — Terms, Definitions, and Acronyms Terms and definitions used within this manual can be found in the Pilot/Controller Glossary of the AIM, the Introduction of the Jeppesen General Airway Manual, and 14 CFR Part 1. General definitions live in those three external sources; manual-specific terms and acronyms are consolidated in Chapter 26.

docs.t: What does Green Policy guidance support, and what constraint always overrides it?
docs.x: What does Green Policy guidance support, and what constraint always overrides it? It supports Flight Crews in making operational decisions aligned with AAG's commitment to fuel efficiency, but safety is always the top priority and fuel-saving measures must never compromise safety. FOM 1.6.3 — Green Policy Fuel saving measures must never compromise safety under any circumstances. Green guidance is marked with a symbol and targets fleet-wide fuel savings, but never at the expense of safety.

docs.t: Under Compliance with Regulations, what happens in the event of conflicting directives?
docs.x: Under Compliance with Regulations, what happens in the event of conflicting directives? The more restrictive directive will apply. FOM 1.5 — Compliance with Regulations In the event of conflicting directives, the more restrictive directive will apply. Operations must comply with all applicable Laws, Regulations, Operations Specifications, and the CMS; no regulation or policy replaces sound judgment and a commitment to safety.

docs.t: Where can teammates file safety reports?
docs.x: Where can teammates file safety reports? The Virtual Safety Center, safety reporting apps on company-issued mobile devices, Alaska's World Vendor Portal, and the Safety Hotline (on the back of all teammate badges). FOM 1.2.6 — Safety Reporting AAG has provided a non-punitive safety reporting system for all teammates and business partners. The system is non-punitive so long as the teammate was not engaged in unacceptable behaviors, and offers four filing channels.

docs.t: What behaviors are defined as 'unacceptable' and therefore outside safety-reporting protection?
docs.x: What behaviors are defined as 'unacceptable' and therefore outside safety-reporting protection? Illegal activities, intentional disregard for safety/regulations/policies/procedures, drug and alcohol use, workplace violence, reckless conduct and/or willful misconduct, and falsification of records. FOM 1.2.6 — Safety Reporting Unacceptable behaviors are defined as illegal activities, intentional disregard for safety, regulations, policies, or procedures, drug and alcohol use, workplace violence, reckless conduct and/or willful misconduct, and falsification of records. These are established in the AAG Code of Conduct and Ethics; filing a report otherwise will not result in discipline.

docs.t: SCENARIO: You are the Captain on a 787 during a line trip. A situation develops that is not covered anywhere in the FOM, and following the nearest published procedure would clearly be unsafe given the conditions. What does the FOM authorize you to do?
docs.x: SCENARIO: You are the Captain on a 787 during a line trip. A situation develops that is not covered anywhere in the FOM, and following the nearest published procedure would clearly be unsafe given the conditions. What does the FOM authorize you to do? Exercise your PIC authority to deviate from published guidance to the extent required in the interest of safety. Per the FOM, it is not possible to develop detailed procedures for all conceivable situations, and as set forth in CFR 91.3 and 121.557 the PIC has the authority and responsibility to deviate — scoped to what safety requires, using decision-making that serves the intent of providing the highest level of operational safety. FOM 1.1 — Manual Overview and Usage As set forth in CFR 91.3 and 121.557, the PIC has the authority and responsibility to deviate from published guidance to the extent required in the interest of safety. Deviation authority is not a blank check; it is bounded by 'to the extent required in the interest of safety,' and the FOM's philosophy supports decisions that serve the intent of the highest level of operational safety when published guidance is inadequate or inappropriate.

docs.t: SCENARIO: On IOE, your check airman points out that two Company manuals give conflicting guidance for the same task — one is more permissive, one is more restrictive. Which do you apply, and what FOM rule governs?
docs.x: SCENARIO: On IOE, your check airman points out that two Company manuals give conflicting guidance for the same task — one is more permissive, one is more restrictive. Which do you apply, and what FOM rule governs? Apply the more restrictive guidance. Per FOM 1.1.1, in the event of conflicting manual guidance the more restrictive guidance will apply, and FOM 1.5 repeats the same principle for conflicting directives across the Company Manual System. FOM 1.1.1 — Manual Hierarchy In the event of conflicting manual guidance, the more restrictive guidance will apply. The 'most restrictive wins' rule appears twice — 1.1.1 for conflicting manual guidance and 1.5 for conflicting directives — so conflict always resolves toward the stricter standard.

docs.t: SCENARIO: After a line flight you realize you and the other pilot had a procedural non-compliance — nothing was damaged and no one was hurt, but a step was missed. It feels awkward to write it up. What does the FOM say you should do?
docs.x: SCENARIO: After a line flight you realize you and the other pilot had a procedural non-compliance — nothing was damaged and no one was hurt, but a step was missed. It feels awkward to write it up. What does the FOM say you should do? File a safety report. The FOM states that reporting close calls and procedural non-compliance is critical because they are early warning signs, and AAG provides a non-punitive safety reporting system. File via the Virtual Safety Center, the safety reporting apps on company-issued devices, Alaska's World Vendor Portal, or the Safety Hotline on the back of your badge; if your division participates in ASAP, you may submit an ASAP report. FOM 1.2.6 — Safety Reporting Reporting close calls and procedural non-compliance is also critical. Protection is non-punitive as long as you were not engaged in unacceptable behaviors; close calls and non-compliance are early warning signs that let the Company fix problems before something worse happens.

docs.t: How does the FOM define "operational control" with respect to a flight?
docs.x: How does the FOM define "operational control" with respect to a flight? The exercise of authority over initiating, conducting, or terminating a flight. FOM 2.1 — Operational Control Operational control with respect to a flight means the exercise of authority over initiating, conducting, or terminating a flight. This is the core definition, repeated verbatim in 2.2.1. Remember the three verbs: initiating, conducting, terminating.

docs.t: Who has the authority for the supervision and control of all Alaska Airlines flights?
docs.x: Who has the authority for the supervision and control of all Alaska Airlines flights? The 14 CFR Part 119 designated Director of Operations (DO). FOM 2.1 — Operational Control The 14 CFR Part 119 designated Director of Operations (DO) has the authority for the supervision and control of all Alaska Airlines flights. The DO sits at the top of the operational-control structure under Part 119.

docs.t: To whom has the DO delegated the authority to conduct certain operational-control functions?
docs.x: To whom has the DO delegated the authority to conduct certain operational-control functions? The Flight Operations Duty Officer (FODO). FOM 2.1 — Operational Control The DO has delegated the authority to conduct certain functions to the Flight Operations Duty Officer (FODO). The FODO acts on delegated DO authority for daily oversight of line flying operations.

docs.t: For what three items are the PIC and Aircraft Dispatcher jointly responsible under Joint Responsibility?
docs.x: For what three items are the PIC and Aircraft Dispatcher jointly responsible under Joint Responsibility? The preflight planning, delay, and Dispatch Release of a flight. FOM 2.1.1 — Joint Responsibility The PIC and Aircraft Dispatcher are jointly responsible for the preflight planning, delay, and Dispatch Release of a flight in compliance with Federal Aviation Regulations Both must agree the flight can be accomplished safely; agreement is shown by their signatures on the Dispatch Release.

docs.t: If the flight cannot be completed safely due to hazardous conditions but the PIC believes there is no safer procedure than continuing toward the airport, what does that continuation become?
docs.x: If the flight cannot be completed safely due to hazardous conditions but the PIC believes there is no safer procedure than continuing toward the airport, what does that continuation become? An emergency. FOM 2.1.1 — Joint Responsibility unless, in the opinion of the PIC, there is no safer procedure. In that event, continuation toward that airport is an emergency. The PIC may not otherwise allow a flight to continue toward a dispatched airport if it cannot be completed safely due to hazardous conditions.

docs.t: How is the PIC's and Dispatcher's agreement that the flight can be accomplished safely indicated?
docs.x: How is the PIC's and Dispatcher's agreement that the flight can be accomplished safely indicated? By the signatures of the PIC and Dispatcher on the Dispatch Release. FOM 2.1.1 — Joint Responsibility Agreement is indicated by the signatures of the PIC and Dispatcher on the Dispatch Release. Both must agree the flight as planned can be accomplished safely and in accordance with 14 CFR and Company policy.

docs.t: When conditions change enroute so the flight cannot be conducted in accordance with the Dispatch Release, who is required to contact whom?
docs.x: When conditions change enroute so the flight cannot be conducted in accordance with the Dispatch Release, who is required to contact whom? The person encountering or learning of the changed conditions must contact the other to institute the necessary amendment to the Dispatch Release. FOM 2.1.1 — Joint Responsibility it is required that the person encountering or learning of the changed conditions contact the other to institute the necessary amendment to the Dispatch Release. The duty to initiate an amendment falls on whoever learns of the change first, PIC or Dispatcher.

docs.t: What is the scope of the PIC's control and authority over other crewmembers during flight time?
docs.x: What is the scope of the PIC's control and authority over other crewmembers during flight time? Full control and authority in the operation of the aircraft, without limitation, over other crewmembers and their duties during flight time, whether or not they hold valid certificates authorizing those duties. FOM 2.1.2 — PIC's Responsibility and Authority The PIC has full control and authority in the operation of the aircraft, without limitation, over other crewmembers and their duties during flight time, whether or not they hold valid certificates authorizing them to perform the duties of those crewmembers. This mirrors 14 CFR 91.3 PIC authority; crewmembers shall comply with the PIC's orders.

docs.t: What must happen if the PIC is not sure that any aspect of flight operations can be safely executed and in compliance with regulations?
docs.x: What must happen if the PIC is not sure that any aspect of flight operations can be safely executed and in compliance with regulations? The operation will be stopped. FOM 2.1.2 — PIC's Responsibility and Authority If the PIC is not sure that any aspect of flight operations can be safely executed and in compliance with regulations, then the operation will be stopped. When in doubt about safety or compliance, the default is to stop, not to press on.

docs.t: During a training or evaluation event conducted by a Check Pilot from a pilot seat, who is the designated PIC?
docs.x: During a training or evaluation event conducted by a Check Pilot from a pilot seat, who is the designated PIC? The Check Pilot is the designated PIC. FOM 2.1.2 — PIC's Responsibility and Authority (Note) Any time a training/evaluation event is being conducted by a Check Pilot from a pilot seat, the Check Pilot is the designated PIC. This shifts designated PIC status to the Check Pilot whenever they run the event from a pilot seat.

docs.t: For what period is the PIC's control and authority in effect (Duration of Command)?
docs.x: For what period is the PIC's control and authority in effect (Duration of Command)? From the time they report for duty until the termination of the flight. FOM 2.1.2.1 — Duration of Command The PIC's control and authority is in effect from the time they report for duty until the termination of the flight. Command authority begins at report-for-duty, not at pushback, and runs through flight termination.

docs.t: What is the sequence of command listed in the Chain of Command?
docs.x: What is the sequence of command listed in the Chain of Command? Captain (PIC); International Relief Officer (IRO)/Second in Command (SIC); PIC-qualified First Officer; First Officer; "A" Flight Attendant/FFA; Flight Attendants in descending order. FOM 2.1.3 — Chain of Command The sequence of command is as follows: The list runs Captain, IRO/SIC, PIC-qualified FO, FO, then the A Flight Attendant/FFA and remaining Flight Attendants.

docs.t: On a flight with an augmented Flight Crew, who becomes the acting Captain when the assigned Captain begins their rest period?
docs.x: On a flight with an augmented Flight Crew, who becomes the acting Captain when the assigned Captain begins their rest period? The IRO becomes the acting Captain. FOM 2.1.3 — Chain of Command when the assigned Captain begins their rest period, the IRO will become the acting Captain. The IRO steps up to acting Captain for the duration of the Captain's rest on an augmented crew.

docs.t: In the Flight Operations Structure, what role does the FODO serve relative to the Director of Operations?
docs.x: In the Flight Operations Structure, what role does the FODO serve relative to the Director of Operations? The FODO serves as a direct representative of the Director of Operations. FOM 2.2.1 — Operational Control The FODO serves as a direct representative of the Director of Operations. Operational-control decisions are made under the DO's authority by the Dispatcher, the PIC, and, when required, the FODO.

docs.t: When does the Operational Control Window (OCW) start and end for a normal flight?
docs.x: When does the Operational Control Window (OCW) start and end for a normal flight? It starts two and a half hours (D-150) prior to the scheduled departure time and ends when the aircraft is blocked in at the destination airport. FOM 2.2.2.1 — Operational Control Window (OCW) OCW starts two and a half hours (D-150) prior to the scheduled departure time and ends when the aircraft is blocked in at the destination airport. D-150 means 150 minutes (two and a half hours) before scheduled departure; the window closes at block-in.

docs.t: Which flights get a D-180 Operational Control Window instead of D-150, and where is that list?
docs.x: Which flights get a D-180 Operational Control Window instead of D-150, and where is that list? Flights requiring the Dispatch Release and ATS Flight Plan 180 minutes prior to scheduled departure, listed in 8.5.2.1: South Korea departures, Amazon Cargo, and (787/A330) Europe departures. All others are D-150. FOM 2.2.2.1 — Operational Control Window (OCW) For flights which require the Dispatch Release and ATS Flight Plan to be produced 180 minutes prior to scheduled departure, the OCW starts three hours (D-180), see 8.5.2.1 - Dispatch Release - Preparation. South Korea flights get a longer, three-hour (D-180) window versus the standard D-150 (two and a half hours) — relevant to your 787 transpacific departures.

docs.t: Within the OCW, a decision to cancel or modify a flight is an operational control action requiring coordination and endorsement from whom, and who is ultimately responsible?
docs.x: Within the OCW, a decision to cancel or modify a flight is an operational control action requiring coordination and endorsement from whom, and who is ultimately responsible? It requires coordination and endorsement from the Dispatcher and the PIC; the Director of Operations is ultimately responsible. FOM 2.2.2.3 — Cancel or Modify Flights any decision to cancel or modify the flight is an operational control action which requires coordination and endorsement from the Dispatcher and the PIC. The FODO and Pilot Crew Scheduling provide guidance when required, but the DO is ultimately responsible.

docs.t: May a Flight Crewmember holding a restricted ATP certificate act as PIC or IRO?
docs.x: May a Flight Crewmember holding a restricted ATP certificate act as PIC or IRO? No. A Flight Crewmember holding a restricted ATP certificate must not act as PIC or IRO. FOM 2.2.8.3 — International Relief Officer (IRO) A Flight Crewmember holding a restricted ATP certificate must not act as PIC or IRO. The IRO is SIC of the aircraft and assumes command if the Captain is incapacitated, so a restricted ATP is disqualifying for that seat.

docs.t: What phases of flight constitute a Sterile Flight Deck (critical phases of flight)?
docs.x: What phases of flight constitute a Sterile Flight Deck (critical phases of flight)? Ground operations involving pushback, towing, taxi, takeoff, and landing; and all other flight operations conducted below 10,000 ft MSL, except cruise flight. FOM 2.3.12 — Sterile Flight Deck All other flight operations conducted below 10,000 ft MSL, except cruise flight. The deck is not considered sterile during lengthy ground holds when the parking brake is set.

docs.t: What bank angle and nose-up pitch attitude should normal flying not require to be exceeded?
docs.x: What bank angle and nose-up pitch attitude should normal flying not require to be exceeded? Bank angles greater than 30 degrees or pitch attitude greater than 20 degrees nose up. FOM 2.3.14 — Style of Flying/Bank and Pitch Angles Normal flying should not require bank angles greater than 30 or airspeeds higher than the normal limit speed or pitch attitude greater than 20 nose up. Aircraft may exceed 20 nose up under certain flight conditions or departure/climb profiles.

docs.t: Check-airman scenario: airborne, an event requires the PIC to deviate from a Company procedure and from an ATC clearance to keep the aircraft safe. What authority lets the PIC do this on their own?
docs.x: Check-airman scenario: airborne, an event requires the PIC to deviate from a Company procedure and from an ATC clearance to keep the aircraft safe. What authority lets the PIC do this on their own? The PIC may unilaterally exercise emergency authority. FOM 2.2.8.1 — Pilot-In-Command May unilaterally exercise emergency authority. Listed among the PIC's responsibilities in the job description; echoes 14 CFR 91.3 emergency authority. "Unilaterally" means no prior coordination is required to act.

docs.t: Check-airman scenario: enroute, the PIC is unsure whether a reroute still allows the flight to be conducted per the Dispatch Release. Per the FOM, who is the PIC's contact and the primary source of flight-status information?
docs.x: Check-airman scenario: enroute, the PIC is unsure whether a reroute still allows the flight to be conducted per the Dispatch Release. Per the FOM, who is the PIC's contact and the primary source of flight-status information? The Dispatcher. FOM 2.1.1 — Joint Responsibility When the PIC has an issue related to operational control of a flight, the PIC should contact the Dispatcher. The Dispatcher is the primary source of information related to the status of a flight Under joint responsibility the Dispatcher — not crew scheduling or the gate — is the PIC's operational-control contact for delay, reroute, or cancellation.

docs.t: Check-airman scenario: on an augmented crew, the Captain becomes incapacitated during cruise. Per the chain of command, who assumes command?
docs.x: Check-airman scenario: on an augmented crew, the Captain becomes incapacitated during cruise. Per the chain of command, who assumes command? The IRO assumes command, performs the Captain's duties, and assumes the Captain's responsibilities. FOM 2.2.8.3 — International Relief Officer (IRO) If the Captain becomes incapacitated, the IRO will assume command, perform the Captain's duties, and assume the Captain's responsibilities. This is why a Flight Crewmember holding a restricted ATP certificate must not act as PIC or IRO — the IRO can inherit command.

docs.t: Check-airman scenario: inside the Operational Control Window, the NOC business group wants to cancel your flight for commercial reasons. What does the FOM require, and who is ultimately responsible?
docs.x: Check-airman scenario: inside the Operational Control Window, the NOC business group wants to cancel your flight for commercial reasons. What does the FOM require, and who is ultimately responsible? Inside the OCW, canceling or modifying is an operational control action requiring coordination and endorsement from the Dispatcher and the PIC; the Director of Operations is ultimately responsible. FOM 2.2.2.3 — Cancel or Modify Flights Within the OCW, any decision to cancel or modify the flight is an operational control action which requires coordination and endorsement from the Dispatcher and the PIC. Contrast 2.2.2.2: before the OCW the same decision is a business decision that does not require operational-control endorsement.

docs.t: For AS operations, what is the maximum number of Flight Crewmembers on a pairing who may have less than 150 hours line operating flight time in type and crew position?
docs.x: For AS operations, what is the maximum number of Flight Crewmembers on a pairing who may have less than 150 hours line operating flight time in type and crew position? Only one Flight Crewmember (CA, F/O, IRO) may have less than 150 hours line operating flight time (including OE) at the Company in type and crew position (seat). FOM 3.2 — Crew Pairing only one Flight Crewmember (CA, F/O, IRO) may have less than: (AS) 150 hours line operating flight time at the Company (including Operating Experience, "OE") in type and crew position (seat). Applies to all operations under 14 CFR 121.438. The HA equivalent threshold is 100 hours line operating flight time in type.

docs.t: How many hours in type must a qualified Check Pilot have to be exempt from the crew pairing requirement while performing Check Pilot duties?
docs.x: How many hours in type must a qualified Check Pilot have to be exempt from the crew pairing requirement while performing Check Pilot duties? At least 75 hours in type. FOM 3.2 — Crew Pairing A qualified Check Pilot with at least 75 hours in type is not subject to this pairing requirement while performing Check Pilot duties. The exemption applies only while the Check Pilot is actually performing Check Pilot duties.

docs.t: First Officers with less than how many hours in aircraft type at Alaska Airlines may not make takeoffs or landings at special airports?
docs.x: First Officers with less than how many hours in aircraft type at Alaska Airlines may not make takeoffs or landings at special airports? First Officers with less than 100 hours in aircraft type at Alaska Airlines shall not make takeoffs or landings at special airports. FOM 3.3 — Special Airports – Qualification/Currency First Officers with less than 100 hours in aircraft type at Alaska Airlines shall not make takeoffs or landings at special airports FAA Special Airports are marked "Airport Qualification" on the Jeppesen 19-XX chart; "Airport Familiarization" charts carry no qualification/currency requirement.

docs.t: To satisfy PIC Special Airport currency by making a takeoff or landing to that airport, what ceiling and visibility conditions must exist?
docs.x: To satisfy PIC Special Airport currency by making a takeoff or landing to that airport, what ceiling and visibility conditions must exist? The ceiling must be at least 1000 ft above the lowest MEA or MOCA, or initial approach altitude prescribed for the instrument approach for that airport, and visibility at least 3 miles. FOM 3.3 — Special Airports – Qualification/Currency Make a takeoff or landing to that airport if the ceiling at that airport is at least 1000 ft above the lowest MEA or MOCA, or initial approach altitude prescribed for the instrument approach for that airport and the visibility is at least 3 miles. Alternatively, currency may be re-established within the preceding 12 calendar months by an aircraft/level-D sim entry or by reviewing the FAA-accepted Jeppesen FD Pro airport pictorials.

docs.t: How often must a pilot accomplish a NAT HLA segment as a required Flight Crewmember to maintain North Atlantic High-Level Airspace currency on the 787?
docs.x: How often must a pilot accomplish a NAT HLA segment as a required Flight Crewmember to maintain North Atlantic High-Level Airspace currency on the 787? At least one NAT HLA segment every 24 months. FOM 3.3.4 — North Atlantic High-Level Airspace (NAT HLA) Qualification (787) Pilots are required to accomplish at least one NAT HLA segment as a required Flight Crewmember every 24 months. NAT HLA qualification applies to qualified PICs and SICs; see the applicable FOTM for the requirements to re-establish currency once it lapses.

docs.t: For Consolidation, how many hours of line operating flight time must Captains and First Officers acquire, and within what period of their Qual LOE in type?
docs.x: For Consolidation, how many hours of line operating flight time must Captains and First Officers acquire, and within what period of their Qual LOE in type? 100 hours of line operating flight time at Alaska Airlines within 120 days of their Qual LOE in type (flight time includes OE). FOM 3.4 — Consolidation Captains and First Officers must acquire 100 hours of line operating flight time at Alaska Airlines within 120 days of their Qual LOE in type. Prior consolidation in type as PIC or SIC satisfies the requirement for all seats in that aircraft type. Resting time on augmented flights cannot be counted toward consolidation.

docs.t: For consolidation on augmented flights, how much of the flight segment's total hours is subtracted for double augment versus single augment?
docs.x: For consolidation on augmented flights, how much of the flight segment's total hours is subtracted for double augment versus single augment? 50% is subtracted for double augment and 33% for single augment. FOM 3.4 — Consolidation For augmented crews, the total hours of the flight segment will be subtracted as follows: 50% for double augment 33% for single augment Time spent resting, while not seated at the controls, cannot count toward OE or consolidation requirements.

docs.t: To qualify for Captain Upgrade, how many hours SIC at the Company must a pilot have?
docs.x: To qualify for Captain Upgrade, how many hours SIC at the Company must a pilot have? 1000 hours SIC at the Company, or the pilot must meet the requirements listed in 14 CFR 121.436. FOM 3.5 — Captain Upgrade To qualify for Captain Upgrade, a pilot must have 1000 hours SIC at the Company or meet the requirements listed in 14 CFR 121.436. The upgrade requirement is governed by 14 CFR 121.436.

docs.t: Under the Initial First Officer takeoff/landing restrictions, at what crosswind component must the Captain make all takeoffs and landings (unless the FO is paired with a Check Pilot)?
docs.x: Under the Initial First Officer takeoff/landing restrictions, at what crosswind component must the Captain make all takeoffs and landings (unless the FO is paired with a Check Pilot)? When the crosswind component is greater than 15 kts (for a First Officer with less than 100 hours in aircraft type). FOM 3.6 — Initial First Officer Restrictions – Takeoff and Landing The crosswind component is greater than 15 kts The Captain must also make all takeoffs and landings at special airports, on contaminated runways, when braking action is less than GOOD, when windshear is reported nearby, or when visibility is at or below 3/4 sm or RVR at or below 4000.

docs.t: A High Minimums Captain is any Captain with less than how many hours as PIC in type at the Company?
docs.x: A High Minimums Captain is any Captain with less than how many hours as PIC in type at the Company? Less than 100 hours as a PIC in type at the Company. FOM 3.7 — High Minimums Captain High minimums apply to any Captain who has less than 100 hours as a PIC in type at the Company. The Captain must advise Dispatch of high minimums status prior to each flight segment when weather is reported or forecast below 1000 ft ceiling and 3 miles visibility at or near time of landing.

docs.t: For military charter operations, what combined minimum total flight hours in the aircraft type must the Captain and First Officer have?
docs.x: For military charter operations, what combined minimum total flight hours in the aircraft type must the Captain and First Officer have? A combined minimum of 250 total flight hours in the aircraft type (except for aircraft new to the Company). FOM 3.8 — High Minimums Crewmembers – Military Charters The Captain and First Officer must have a combined minimum of 250 total flight hours in the aircraft type except for aircraft new to the Company, to operate any military charter operations. This requirement stems from 32 CFR 861 governing military charter operations.

docs.t: How many hours as PIC in type at the Company must a Captain have to perform CAT III operations, and is it reducible?
docs.x: How many hours as PIC in type at the Company must a Captain have to perform CAT III operations, and is it reducible? A minimum of 100 hours as PIC in type at the Company, and it is not reducible. FOM 3.15 — Category III Operations – Captain Hours Required Captain must have minimum of 100 hours as PIC in type at the Company (not reducible) to perform CAT III operations. During Captain OE, CAT III is not authorized for the qualifying Captain unless they had previously met this hours requirement.

docs.t: For SA CAT I / CAT II operations under Exemption 5549, how many hours as a pilot in a turbojet aircraft must the Captain have?
docs.x: For SA CAT I / CAT II operations under Exemption 5549, how many hours as a pilot in a turbojet aircraft must the Captain have? A minimum of 300 hours as a pilot (PIC or SIC) in a turbojet aircraft. FOM 3.16.2 — SA CAT I/CAT II Operations at Destination or Alternate The Captain has a minimum of 300 hours as a pilot (PIC or SIC) in a turbojet aircraft For AS the Captain must also comply with the SA CAT I/II Approach Briefing Card; HGS Experience Card completion is not required.

docs.t: During Captain/First Officer OE takeoffs, at what RVR must the left seat occupant conduct all takeoffs?
docs.x: During Captain/First Officer OE takeoffs, at what RVR must the left seat occupant conduct all takeoffs? The left seat occupant will conduct all takeoffs when the RVR is 1600 ft or less. FOM 3.18.2 — Takeoff The left seat occupant will conduct all takeoffs when the RVR is 1600 ft or less. During OE the Check Pilot is the Company-designated PIC and must occupy a pilot seat.

docs.t: What is the Takeoff and Landing Currency requirement, including the currency interval and any limit on Autolands?
docs.x: What is the Takeoff and Landing Currency requirement, including the currency interval and any limit on Autolands? At least 3 takeoffs and landings within 90 days, in the specific aircraft type or an AS-approved simulator, in either seat; only one of the required landings may be an Autoland. Documented by ACARS entry. FOM 3.19 — Operational Currency and Training Requirements At least 3 takeoffs and landings in: Specific aircraft type or an AS-approved simulator supervised by an AS Instructor or Check Pilot Either seat Only one of the required landings may be an Autoland. The currency interval is 90 days; credit for an Autoland landing may go to both the Captain and First Officer.

docs.t: Under Exemption 5549, if the crosswind component exceeds 15 kts combined with a braking action report of less than 'good,' what minimum visibility is required?
docs.x: Under Exemption 5549, if the crosswind component exceeds 15 kts combined with a braking action report of less than 'good,' what minimum visibility is required? Visibility must be at least 4000 RVR (3/4 mile visibility). FOM 3.16.1 — CAT I Precision Approach at Destination or Alternate If the crosswind component exceeds 15 kts combined with a braking action report of less than "good," visibility must be at least 4000 RVR (3/4 mile visibility). For AS the approach is flown by the Captain with autopilot coupled (dual channel on a CAT II/III runway only) or following HGS AIII guidance to DA/DH.

docs.t: CHECK-AIRMAN SCENARIO: You're a 787 First Officer and monthly bid closure is tomorrow. A check airman notices your last takeoff and landing was 91 days ago, so your Takeoff and Landing Currency has lapsed. Under FOM 3.19, what happens to next month's bid and how do you correct the deficiency?
docs.x: CHECK-AIRMAN SCENARIO: You're a 787 First Officer and monthly bid closure is tomorrow. A check airman notices your last takeoff and landing was 91 days ago, so your Takeoff and Landing Currency has lapsed. Under FOM 3.19, what happens to next month's bid and how do you correct the deficiency? Because the currency requirement was not maintained, the following month's bid will not be honored and you will be removed from flight duty and payroll until the deficiency is corrected. Currency deficiencies are corrected by submission of appropriate Training Certification Forms, simulator requalification, or supervised line flying. FOM 3.19 — Operational Currency and Training Requirements Failure to initially accomplish and/or maintain currency requirements will result in the following month's bid not being honored and will result in removal from flight duty and payroll until any deficiencies are corrected. Operational currency and training requirements must be accomplished prior to monthly bid closure; Takeoff and Landing Currency is documented by ACARS entry.

docs.t: CHECK-AIRMAN SCENARIO: A check airman reviews your last 90 days and finds 3 takeoffs and landings in the 787 — but 2 of the 3 landings were Autolands. Are you legally current for Takeoff and Landing Currency under FOM 3.19, and why or why not?
docs.x: CHECK-AIRMAN SCENARIO: A check airman reviews your last 90 days and finds 3 takeoffs and landings in the 787 — but 2 of the 3 landings were Autolands. Are you legally current for Takeoff and Landing Currency under FOM 3.19, and why or why not? No. Only one of the three required landings may be an Autoland, so at least two must be hand-flown landings. With two Autolands you are one manual landing short and are not current. FOM 3.19 — Operational Currency and Training Requirements At least 3 takeoffs and landings in: Specific aircraft type or an AS-approved simulator supervised by an AS Instructor or Check Pilot Either seat Only one of the required landings may be an Autoland. Landings may be in the specific aircraft type or an AS-approved simulator, in either seat; credit for an Autoland landing may go to both the Captain and First Officer.

docs.t: CHECK-AIRMAN SCENARIO: Scheduling wants to assign you as a required Flight Crewmember on a 787 segment through North Atlantic High-Level Airspace, but your last NAT HLA segment was 25 months ago. Under FOM 3.3.4, are you current for NAT HLA, and what governs re-establishing it?
docs.x: CHECK-AIRMAN SCENARIO: Scheduling wants to assign you as a required Flight Crewmember on a 787 segment through North Atlantic High-Level Airspace, but your last NAT HLA segment was 25 months ago. Under FOM 3.3.4, are you current for NAT HLA, and what governs re-establishing it? No. NAT HLA currency requires accomplishing at least one NAT HLA segment as a required Flight Crewmember every 24 months; at 25 months your currency has lapsed. Re-establishing currency is governed by the applicable FOTM. FOM 3.3.4 — North Atlantic High-Level Airspace (NAT HLA) Qualification (787) Pilots are required to accomplish at least one NAT HLA segment as a required Flight Crewmember every 24 months. NAT HLA qualification applies to qualified PICs and SICs on the 787; see the applicable FOTM for the requirements to re-establish currency once it lapses.

docs.t: How far in advance of scheduled departure must a pilot check in with Pilot Crew Scheduling for the originating flight of a pairing, and what is the deadheading check-in time?
docs.x: How far in advance of scheduled departure must a pilot check in with Pilot Crew Scheduling for the originating flight of a pairing, and what is the deadheading check-in time? One hour prior to scheduled departure, or 45 minutes prior for deadheading. FOM 4.2.2 — Crew Check-In – Scheduling Pilots shall check in one hour prior (45 minutes for deadheading) to the scheduled departure of the originating flight of a pairing. Missing the one-hour check-in can trigger assignment of a reserve pilot and a possible 'No Show' pending Base Chief Pilot review.

docs.t: A pilot may voluntarily check in earlier than one hour before departure, but no earlier than what limit?
docs.x: A pilot may voluntarily check in earlier than one hour before departure, but no earlier than what limit? No earlier than four hours prior to the scheduled departure. FOM 4.2.2 — Crew Check-In – Scheduling a pilot may voluntarily check-in prior to one hour, but in no case earlier than four hours prior to the scheduled departure. Early check-in is at the individual pilot's discretion but is bounded at four hours before scheduled departure.

docs.t: What is the minimum pilot crew for a flight, and how are the two positions designated?
docs.x: What is the minimum pilot crew for a flight, and how are the two positions designated? Two pilots: one designated as Pilot-In-Command and one as Second-In-Command. FOM 4.2.1 — Composition of Flight Crew The minimum pilot crew is two pilots; one pilot designated as Pilot-In-Command and one as Second-In-Command. Each pilot is designated no more than one Flight Crew function per flight segment.

docs.t: Under Part 117 Table A (unaugmented), what maximum flight time applies for a report time of 0500-1959 versus 0000-0459 or 2000-2359?
docs.x: Under Part 117 Table A (unaugmented), what maximum flight time applies for a report time of 0500-1959 versus 0000-0459 or 2000-2359? 9 hours for a report time of 0500-1959; 8 hours for report times of 0000-0459 or 2000-2359. FOM 4.3.2.2 — Flight Time Limitation the flight time limits in Table A of Part 117 (unaugmented operations) restrict a Flight Crewmember's time on task (flight time) to either 8 or 9 hours. Table A is entered using the report time at local domicile or the acclimated local time in theater; 0500-1959 gives 9 hours, the two night bands give 8.

docs.t: For augmented operations, the Part 117 flight time limits restrict time on task to what values for a 3-pilot crew versus a 4-pilot crew?
docs.x: For augmented operations, the Part 117 flight time limits restrict time on task to what values for a 3-pilot crew versus a 4-pilot crew? 13 hours for a 3-pilot crew and 17 hours for a 4-pilot crew. FOM 4.3.2.2 — Flight Time Limitation Flight time limits (augmented operations) restrict a Flight Crewmember's time on task (flight time) to either 13 hours (3-pilot crew) or 17 hours (4-pilot crew). These are flight-time (time-on-task) limits, distinct from the Flight Duty Period limits in Tables B and C.

docs.t: What are the cumulative flight time limitations a Flight Crewmember may not exceed under Part 117?
docs.x: What are the cumulative flight time limitations a Flight Crewmember may not exceed under Part 117? 100 hours in any 672 consecutive hours, or 1000 hours in any 365 consecutive calendar-day period. FOM 4.3.2.3 — Cumulative Flight Time Limitations 100 hours in any 672 consecutive hours, or 1000 hours in any 365 consecutive calendar-day period. Cumulative FTL uses rolling windows of 672 consecutive hours and 365 consecutive calendar days and includes all Part 91 and 121 flying.

docs.t: What are the cumulative Flight Duty Period (FDP) limits under Part 117?
docs.x: What are the cumulative Flight Duty Period (FDP) limits under Part 117? 60 FDP hours in any 168 consecutive hours, or 190 FDP hours in any 672 consecutive hours. FOM 4.3.2.6 — Cumulative Flight Duty Limitations 60 FDP hours in any 168 consecutive hours, or 190 FDP hours in any 672 consecutive hours. A post-takeoff FDP extension may exceed these cumulative limits only to the extent necessary to complete the flight; it expires once the aircraft lands.

docs.t: What is the minimum rest period Part 117 prescribes before a RAP or between FDPs, and what sleep opportunity must it provide?
docs.x: What is the minimum rest period Part 117 prescribes before a RAP or between FDPs, and what sleep opportunity must it provide? 10 consecutive hours measured from release from duty, providing a minimum of 8 uninterrupted hours of sleep opportunity. FOM 4.3.2.7 — Rest Period the minimum rest period (prior to beginning a Reserve Availability Period (RAP) or between FDPs) as 10 consecutive hours measured from the time the Flight Crewmember is released from duty. This 10-hour rest period must provide the Flight Crewmember with a minimum of 8 uninterrupted hours of sleep opportunity. If the pilot determines the rest will not provide 10 hours or the 8 uninterrupted sleep hours, they must notify Pilot Crew Scheduling.

docs.t: What is the maximum FDP extension permitted under 14 CFR 117.19, and what is the prior-extension gate?
docs.x: What is the maximum FDP extension permitted under 14 CFR 117.19, and what is the prior-extension gate? Up to 2 hours, provided neither Flight Crewmember has had an extension greater than 30 minutes since their last period of 30 consecutive hours free from all duty. FOM 4.3.2.5 — Flight Duty Period Extensions Flight Duty Period (FDP) extensions of up to 2 hours are permitted provided: Other conditions: the extension addresses unforeseen operational circumstances, CBA/PWA limits are not exceeded, and the PIC and certificate holder agree on the length.

docs.t: How does a Flight Crewmember become acclimated to a new theater under Part 117?
docs.x: How does a Flight Crewmember become acclimated to a new theater under Part 117? By receiving 36 consecutive hours of rest in the new theater, or by having been in the new theater for 72 hours. FOM 4.3.2.4.6 — Acclimation A Flight Crewmember operating in a new theater that has received 36 consecutive hours of rest, or who has been in a new theater for 72 hours, is considered to be acclimated to that new theater. If a crewmember transitions theaters and is not acclimated, the Table B or Table C maximum FDP limit must be reduced by 30 minutes.

docs.t: How does Part 117 define a 'theater' for acclimation purposes?
docs.x: How does Part 117 define a 'theater' for acclimation purposes? A geographical area where the FDP departure and arrival points differ by no more than 60 degrees of longitude. FOM 4.3.2.4.6 — Acclimation Theater means a geographical area in which the distance between the Flight Crewmember's flight duty period departure point and arrival point differs by no more than 60 degrees of longitude. The same 60-degree-longitude threshold drives theater-change compensatory rest in 4.3.2.11.

docs.t: What is the minimum recline requirement that defines a Class 3 rest facility?
docs.x: What is the minimum recline requirement that defines a Class 3 rest facility? A seat in an aircraft cabin or Flight Deck that reclines at least 40 degrees and provides leg and foot support. FOM 4.3.2.4.1 — Classification of Rest Facilities Class 3 rest facility means a seat in an aircraft cabin or Flight Deck that reclines at least 40 degrees and provides leg and foot support. Class 1 (flat bunk, isolated) yields the longest FDP limit; Class 3 provides the least quality and the shortest augmented FDP limit.

docs.t: How many consecutive nighttime FDPs infringing on the WOCL are Flight Crewmembers limited to, and what are the WOCL hours?
docs.x: How many consecutive nighttime FDPs infringing on the WOCL are Flight Crewmembers limited to, and what are the WOCL hours? A maximum of three consecutive nighttime FDPs scheduled to infringe on the WOCL, which is 0200-0559. FOM 4.3.2.14 — Consecutive Nighttime Operations Flight Crewmembers are limited to a maximum of three consecutive nighttime FDPs that are scheduled to infringe on WOCL (0200-0559). This applies whenever an FDP infringes on any part of the crewmember's Window of Circadian Low.

docs.t: For a short-call reserve pilot, what is the maximum length of a Reserve Availability Period (RAP)?
docs.x: For a short-call reserve pilot, what is the maximum length of a Reserve Availability Period (RAP)? The RAP may not exceed 14 hours. FOM 4.3.2.12 — Reserve Status The Flight Crewmember's RAP may not exceed 14 hours. The combined RAP plus FDP may not exceed the lesser of the applicable Table B FDP limit plus 4 hours, or 16 hours, measured from the start of the RAP.

docs.t: Within what time must a Fatigue Report be submitted for a fatigue call in order for pay protection to be considered?
docs.x: Within what time must a Fatigue Report be submitted for a fatigue call in order for pay protection to be considered? Within 3 days of the fatigue event, in a timely manner. FOM 4.3.1.4 — Fatigue Call Review A Fatigue Report must be submitted for a fatigue call in a timely manner (within 3 days of the fatigue event) in order for pay protection to be considered. If the FRP finds extenuating circumstances precluded timely submission, it may still accept the report for a pay evaluation.

docs.t: By no later than what time prior to departure should the Captain be on board the aircraft?
docs.x: By no later than what time prior to departure should the Captain be on board the aircraft? On board prior to passenger boarding if possible, but no later than 25 minutes prior to departure. FOM 4.2.3.2 — Arrival at Aircraft Captain – Be on board prior to passenger boarding, if possible, but no later than 25 minutes prior to departure. The First Officer arrives at the aircraft at least 45 minutes prior for preflight and should be on board 20 minutes prior to departure.

docs.t: CHECK AIRMAN SCENARIO: You're the PIC on a long Pacific pairing. An unforeseen gate hold has pushed you toward your Flight Duty Period limit and Pilot Crew Scheduling asks for an extension so you can complete the flight. What is the maximum FDP extension, and what prior-extension condition must be satisfied before you can accept it?
docs.x: CHECK AIRMAN SCENARIO: You're the PIC on a long Pacific pairing. An unforeseen gate hold has pushed you toward your Flight Duty Period limit and Pilot Crew Scheduling asks for an extension so you can complete the flight. What is the maximum FDP extension, and what prior-extension condition must be satisfied before you can accept it? Up to 2 hours, provided neither Flight Crewmember has experienced an extension greater than 30 minutes since their last period of 30 consecutive hours free from all duty (and the extension addresses unforeseen operational circumstances, CBA/PWA limits are not exceeded, and the PIC and certificate holder agree on the length). FOM 4.3.2.5 — Flight Duty Period Extensions Flight Duty Period (FDP) extensions of up to 2 hours are permitted provided: Extension is required to address unforeseen operational circumstances. Neither Flight Crewmember has experienced an extension greater than 30 minutes since the crewmember's last period of 30 consecutive hours free from all duty. Pilot Crew Scheduling and/or the Flight Operations Duty Officer are authorized to act on behalf of the certificate holder in agreeing upon the length of the extension.

docs.t: CHECK AIRMAN SCENARIO: After a red-eye Pacific crossing you determine you are too fatigued to safely fly the next leg. What action does the FOM require of you to be removed from the assignment, and what is the disciplinary consequence of removing yourself for fatigue on the Alaska side?
docs.x: CHECK AIRMAN SCENARIO: After a red-eye Pacific crossing you determine you are too fatigued to safely fly the next leg. What action does the FOM require of you to be removed from the assignment, and what is the disciplinary consequence of removing yourself for fatigue on the Alaska side? You must contact and advise Pilot Crew Scheduling in order to be removed from the flight assignment (and should complete a Fatigue Report). Removal from assignments for flight time due to fatigue will not be cause for disciplinary action. FOM 4.3.1.2 — Procedure If a Flight Crewmember feels they are too fatigued to fly, the Flight Crewmember shall contact and advise Pilot Crew Scheduling in order to be removed from the flight assignment. A Fatigue Report should be completed to identify and address any systemic conditions that caused the fatigue. Removal from assignments for flight time due to fatigue will not be cause for disciplinary action. To be considered for pay protection, the Fatigue Report must be submitted within 3 days of the event (FOM 4.3.1.4).

docs.t: CHECK AIRMAN SCENARIO: On a long Pacific pairing your scheduled outstation layover looks like it will not give you a full 10 hours of rest or the 8 uninterrupted hours of sleep opportunity. What does Part 117 prescribe for minimum rest, and what is your obligation when you spot the shortfall?
docs.x: CHECK AIRMAN SCENARIO: On a long Pacific pairing your scheduled outstation layover looks like it will not give you a full 10 hours of rest or the 8 uninterrupted hours of sleep opportunity. What does Part 117 prescribe for minimum rest, and what is your obligation when you spot the shortfall? Minimum rest is 10 consecutive hours measured from release from duty, and that period must provide at least 8 uninterrupted hours of sleep opportunity. If you determine your scheduled rest will not provide the 10 hours or the 8 uninterrupted sleep hours, you must notify Pilot Crew Scheduling. FOM 4.3.2.7 — Rest Period Part 117 prescribes the minimum rest period (prior to beginning a Reserve Availability Period (RAP) or between FDPs) as 10 consecutive hours measured from the time the Flight Crewmember is released from duty. This 10-hour rest period must provide the Flight Crewmember with a minimum of 8 uninterrupted hours of sleep opportunity. The assignment must be scheduled in advance so the crewmember can plan to maximize sleep opportunity within the rest period.

docs.t: CHECK AIRMAN SCENARIO: You're airborne on a long over-water leg when an unforeseen circumstance means finishing the flight will push you past your cumulative FDP limits. Is exceeding those cumulative limits permitted, and what is the catch?
docs.x: CHECK AIRMAN SCENARIO: You're airborne on a long over-water leg when an unforeseen circumstance means finishing the flight will push you past your cumulative FDP limits. Is exceeding those cumulative limits permitted, and what is the catch? Yes. Under 14 CFR 117.19 a post-takeoff FDP extension allows a Flight Crewmember to exceed the cumulative FDP limits, but only to the extent necessary to complete that flight, and the extension expires once the aircraft lands. FOM 4.3.2.6 — Cumulative Flight Duty Limitations Under 14 CFR 117.19, a post-takeoff FDP extension allows a Flight Crewmember to exceed the cumulative FDP limits. However, a post-takeoff FDP extension is limited in that it expires once the aircraft lands. Once the flight on which the post-takeoff extension was used has been completed, the Flight Crewmember would again be bound by the cumulative FDP limitations. Cumulative FDP limits are 60 hours in any 168 consecutive hours and 190 hours in any 672 consecutive hours.

docs.t: On the 787, what takeoff and landing operations are authorized on a narrow runway, and how is a narrow runway defined?
docs.x: On the 787, what takeoff and landing operations are authorized on a narrow runway, and how is a narrow runway defined? None. On the 787, takeoff and landing are not authorized on any narrow runway. A narrow runway is one whose nominal paved width is less than 100 ft (30 m). FOM 5.1.3 — Narrow Runway Operations the nominal paved runway width is less than 100 ft (30 m) The 100 ft / 30 m threshold defines a narrow runway; the 787 is flatly prohibited from takeoff and landing on one.

docs.t: When must the cabin doors be armed relative to aircraft movement?
docs.x: When must the cabin doors be armed relative to aircraft movement? Doors shall be armed for any surface movement, including all pushbacks, taxi, and towing. Pilots must give Flight Attendants adequate time and notice to secure the cabin for movement. FOM 5.1.7 — Door Arming with Passengers on Board Doors shall be armed for any surface movement, including all pushbacks, taxi, and towing Applies to every ground movement with passengers aboard, not just pushback.

docs.t: How many start attempts constitute a successful APU start, and when is the APU considered to have failed to start?
docs.x: How many start attempts constitute a successful APU start, and when is the APU considered to have failed to start? The APU is considered to have started successfully on any one of three start attempts. It is considered to have failed to start after three consecutive start attempt failures, or when fleet-specific procedures preclude subsequent attempts. FOM 5.1.8.1 — APU Start/Failed to Start an APU is considered to have started successfully on any one of three start attempts Three consecutive failures equals a failed start and drives a required Maintenance Logbook entry.

docs.t: During which phases of flight may the crew rest facility not be occupied?
docs.x: During which phases of flight may the crew rest facility not be occupied? It must not be occupied from pushback to 10,000 ft AFE, and from 45 minutes prior to landing to aircraft block-in. FOM 5.1.23.1 — Limitations and Restrictions The crew rest facility must not be occupied from pushback to 10,000 ft AFE and from 45 minutes prior to landing to aircraft block-in Brackets the rest facility to the cruise/enroute window; the 787 Overhead Flight Crew Rest seat, bunks, and common area likewise may not be occupied during taxi, takeoff, or landing.

docs.t: Under what braking-action report is taxi prohibited?
docs.x: Under what braking-action report is taxi prohibited? Taxi operations are prohibited when braking action is reported as NIL by the airport or other aircraft. FOM 5.3.1 — Taxi Prohibited Taxi operations are prohibited when braking action is reported as NIL by airport or other aircraft A NIL braking action report is an absolute bar to taxi.

docs.t: For which taxi clearances is dual acknowledgment between both pilots required?
docs.x: For which taxi clearances is dual acknowledgment between both pilots required? Runway Crossing, Hold Short, Line Up and Wait, Cleared for Takeoff, and Cleared to Land. FOM 5.3.4.1 — Runway Awareness Dual acknowledgment should be used for all taxi instructions between both pilots and is required for the following clearances The listed five clearances require the transmitting pilot's readback plus a verbal confirmation from the other pilot.

docs.t: Who must taxi the aircraft during low visibility operations?
docs.x: Who must taxi the aircraft during low visibility operations? The Captain must taxi the aircraft during low visibility operations. Restricted visibility includes any time the RVR is less than 1200. FOM 5.3.11 — Taxi Operations – Low Visibility During low visibility operations, the Captain must taxi the aircraft Restricted visibility includes dense fog, heavy precipitation, or any time RVR is less than 1200; checklists are done stopped with the parking brake set.

docs.t: What are the standard takeoff minimums for an aircraft with two engines or less?
docs.x: What are the standard takeoff minimums for an aircraft with two engines or less? 1 sm visibility or RVR 5000. FOM 5.4.1.1 — Standard Takeoff Minimums Defined as 1 sm visibility or RVR 5000 for aircraft having 2 engines or less The 787, having two engines, uses this standard; when published minimums are higher and no special procedure exists, takeoff below published minimums is prohibited.

docs.t: What is the maximum takeoff-alternate distance for the 787?
docs.x: What is the maximum takeoff-alternate distance for the 787? 393 nm. FOM 5.4.2 — Takeoff Alternate 787 393 nm The 787's takeoff-alternate limit is 393 nm, and takeoff-alternate weather must meet destination-alternate requirements.

docs.t: At what visibility must the Captain make the takeoff?
docs.x: At what visibility must the Captain make the takeoff? Any time the visibility is less than or equal to 1/4 sm or 1600 RVR, the Captain will make the takeoff. FOM 5.4.3 — Captain Required Takeoff the visibility is less than or equal to 1/4 sm or 1600 RVR, the Captain will make the takeoff The same 1600 RVR / 1/4 sm threshold appears in the lower-than-standard takeoff table as the Captain-required trigger.

docs.t: On the 787, above what speed does a rejected takeoff require a return to the gate and a Maintenance Logbook entry regardless of the reason?
docs.x: On the 787, above what speed does a rejected takeoff require a return to the gate and a Maintenance Logbook entry regardless of the reason? Above 80 kts (Boeing). An RTO initiated above 80 kts requires that the flight return to the gate and a Maintenance Logbook entry be made regardless of the reason. FOM 5.4.10 — Rejected Takeoff (RTO) requires that the flight returns to the gate and a Maintenance Logbook entry be made regardless of the reason for the RTO At or below the Boeing 80 kt threshold for correctable issues, no gate return is required, but brake temperature limits must still be considered; a safety report is required after any RTO.

docs.t: At what minimum height is an initial turn after takeoff normally commenced when no turn point is procedurally defined, and what turn is exempt?
docs.x: At what minimum height is an initial turn after takeoff normally commenced when no turn point is procedurally defined, and what turn is exempt? Normally at a minimum of 400 ft AFE, to comply with TERPS ODP criteria. A required course or heading change of less than 15 degrees initially is a non-maneuvering turn and may be commenced below 400 ft. FOM 5.5.1 — Turns After Takeoff an initial turn after takeoff is normally commenced at a minimum of 400 ft AFE Applies to departure procedures lacking a defined turn point; a fleet manual or DP-specified altitude overrides the 400 ft default.

docs.t: Within what tolerance must the two primary altimeters agree during RVSM operations, and how often are crosschecks made?
docs.x: Within what tolerance must the two primary altimeters agree during RVSM operations, and how often are crosschecks made? The two primary altimeters should agree within 200 ft (or a lesser value if specified in the FH/FCOM). Crosschecks between the primary altimeters and the standby are made at intervals of approximately one hour. FOM 5.5.6.5 — Enroute RVSM Altitude Monitoring Requirements The two primary altimeters should agree within 200 ft RVSM airspace is FL290 to FL410 inclusive with 1000 ft vertical separation; at level-off all altimeters are set to 29.92, and use of the standby as a primary is prohibited.

docs.t: What assigned-altitude deviation requires a Flight Crew safety report, and within what time?
docs.x: What assigned-altitude deviation requires a Flight Crew safety report, and within what time? An assigned altitude deviation of 300 ft or more (also an altimeter system error of 245 ft or more, or a total vertical error of 300 ft or more) requires a safety report within 24 hours. The Company must separately report altitude-keeping errors to the FAA within 72 hours. FOM 5.5.7 — Altitude Deviation Reporting Assigned altitude deviation of 300 ft or more 24-hour crew safety report thresholds are 300 ft assigned deviation, 245 ft altimeter system error, and 300 ft total vertical error; Company FAA reporting is within 72 hours.

docs.t: If a pilot leaves their duty station above FL410, what is required of the remaining crewmember?
docs.x: If a pilot leaves their duty station above FL410, what is required of the remaining crewmember? The remaining crewmember must put on and use their oxygen mask before the other pilot leaves the seat and continue using it until the other crewmember has returned. FOM 5.5.12 — Oxygen Use above FL410, the remaining crewmember must put on and utilize their oxygen mask The trigger is the aircraft being above FL410 while one pilot is away from the controls.

docs.t: For what enroute navigation performance is the 787 approved?
docs.x: For what enroute navigation performance is the 787 approved? The 787 is approved for RNP-4 operations, the enroute oceanic/remote navigation capability. FOM 5.5.13 — Enroute Navigation All Company aircraft are approved for RNP-4 operations RNP-4 is the enroute oceanic/remote navigation capability the 787 carries.

docs.t: On what maximum airspeed is holding pattern protection based?
docs.x: On what maximum airspeed is holding pattern protection based? A maximum of 280 KIAS / Mach 0.8, whichever is lower. Standard holding patterns are right-hand turns, and a speed reduction is begun no earlier than three minutes prior to reaching the fix. FOM 5.5.15 — Holding Holding pattern protection is based on a maximum of 280 KIAS/Mach 0.8, whichever is lower US holding max airspeeds by altitude are 200 KIAS at/below 6000, 230 KIAS above 6000 through 14,000, and 265 KIAS above 14,000; holding fuel is calculated every 15 minutes.

docs.t: By what height must the 787 normally be aligned with the runway for an approach to be stabilized?
docs.x: By what height must the 787 normally be aligned with the runway for an approach to be stabilized? Normally the aircraft must be aligned with the runway by 500 ft AFE. Approaches that include a 300 ft AFE runway alignment exception are indicated in the relevant airport 10-7. FOM 5.6.5 — Stabilized Approach the aircraft must be aligned with the runway by 500 ft AFE For the 787 an approach is stabilized only if all criteria are met; either crewmember may call a no-fault go-around, and do not land from an unstable approach.

docs.t: What are the circling approach minimums?
docs.x: What are the circling approach minimums? 1000 ft ceiling and 3 sm visibility, or the charted circling minimums, whichever is greater. FOM 5.6.10 — Circling Approach Circling minimums are 1000 ft and 3 sm visibility or charted circling minimums whichever is greater After reaching MDA the PF keeps an identifiable portion of the runway environment in sight and maintains MDA until in a position to descend to land.

docs.t: With only the approach lighting system in sight, below what height is descent not allowed, and what would then permit continuing?
docs.x: With only the approach lighting system in sight, below what height is descent not allowed, and what would then permit continuing? With only the approach lights in sight, a descent below 100 ft is not allowed unless the red side row bars or the red terminating bars are in sight. FOM 5.6.15 — Descent Below Minimums a descent below 100 ft is not allowed unless the red side row bars or the red terminating bars are in sight One of the 14 CFR 91.175 visual references must be distinctly visible to continue below DH/MDA; the approach light system alone is limited to 100 ft above TDZE without the red bars.

docs.t: Within what limits must touchdown be planned, and what is the earliest allowable touchdown point from the threshold?
docs.x: Within what limits must touchdown be planned, and what is the earliest allowable touchdown point from the threshold? Touchdown shall be planned within the first 3000 ft beyond the threshold, the first third of the runway, or (AS) the Latest Touchdown Point, whichever is less. The earliest planned touchdown point shall never be less than 500 ft from the runway threshold. FOM 5.6.22.1 — Landing Policy Touchdown shall be planned within the first 3000 ft beyond the threshold, the first third of the runway A safety report is required for any touchdown less than 500 ft from the threshold or beyond the applicable distance policy.

docs.t: What are the LAHSO weather minimums, and how do they change with a PAPI or VASI installed and operational?
docs.x: What are the LAHSO weather minimums, and how do they change with a PAPI or VASI installed and operational? Ceiling no less than 1500 ft and visibility no less than 5 sm. If a PAPI or VASI is installed and operational, conditions may be lowered to a ceiling no less than 1000 ft and visibility no less than 3 sm. LAHSO is prohibited on wet runways, and the tailwind on the hold short runway shall be calm (less than 3 kts). FOM 5.6.32.2 — Operational Information – LAHSO Ceiling of no less than 1500 ft and a visibility of no less than 5 sm. Prohibited on wet runways. The tailwind on the hold short runway shall be calm (less than 3 kts). LAHSO also requires the aircraft not to have descended below 1000 ft AGL on final, no windshear within the previous 20 minutes, and vertical guidance (PLASI is not acceptable).

docs.t: SCENARIO (check airman): You're the PM on a 787 visual to a wet runway. At 400 ft AFE the aircraft is fast and still drifting back toward centerline, not yet aligned. The PF says he'll 'have it by the numbers.' By 300 ft AFE it's still not aligned and airspeed is above target. What is the required action and who may take it?
docs.x: SCENARIO (check airman): You're the PM on a 787 visual to a wet runway. At 400 ft AFE the aircraft is fast and still drifting back toward centerline, not yet aligned. The PF says he'll 'have it by the numbers.' By 300 ft AFE it's still not aligned and airspeed is above target. What is the required action and who may take it? The approach is unstable. On the 787 the aircraft must normally be aligned with the runway by 500 ft AFE; it is not aligned by 500 ft, so the stabilized-approach gate is busted. Do not land from an unstable approach. Either crewmember may call for a go-around under the no-fault go-around policy, so the PM calls and the crew goes around. FOM 5.6.5 — Stabilized Approach Do not land from an unstable approach. ... Either crewmember may call for a go-around under Alaska Airlines "no-fault" go-around policy. ... Normally, the aircraft must be aligned with the runway by 500 ft AFE. 500 ft AFE runway alignment is the 787 gate (300 ft AFE only where an exception is published in the 10-7); an unaligned, fast approach past the gate requires a go-around, and either pilot may call it.

docs.t: SCENARIO (check airman): On an ILS in fog you reach DH with only the approach lighting system in sight, no red side row or terminating bars, and no other listed visual reference. The PF continues descending below 100 ft looking for the runway. What is the correct action?
docs.x: SCENARIO (check airman): On an ILS in fog you reach DH with only the approach lighting system in sight, no red side row or terminating bars, and no other listed visual reference. The PF continues descending below 100 ft looking for the runway. What is the correct action? This is a violation. With only the approach lighting system in sight, a descent below 100 ft is not allowed unless the red side row bars or the red terminating bars are in sight. With no other 14 CFR 91.175 visual reference distinctly visible, a missed approach must be immediately executed when operating below the DH/MDA. The PF must go around, not continue. FOM 5.6.15 — Descent Below Minimums A missed approach must be immediately executed if any of the 14 CFR 91.175 requirements are not met when operating below the DH/MDA. The approach light system alone permits descent only to 100 ft above TDZE; below that the red side row bars or red terminating bars, or another listed reference, must be distinctly visible or a missed approach is mandatory.

docs.t: SCENARIO (check airman): Level at FL360 in RVSM airspace, you lose one primary altimeter and the autopilot altitude-control system flags a fault, so required RVSM equipment is no longer operating normally. Can you reset and press on, and what does the FOM require?
docs.x: SCENARIO (check airman): Level at FL360 in RVSM airspace, you lose one primary altimeter and the autopilot altitude-control system flags a fault, so required RVSM equipment is no longer operating normally. Can you reset and press on, and what does the FOM require? No. In the event of required RVSM equipment failure prior to or within RVSM airspace, notify ATC and Dispatch to coordinate a prudent course of action. ATC may not require any action, but a reroute or diversion may be required. Both primary altimeters and one autopilot altitude-control system must be operating normally for RVSM; the standby altimeter may not be used as a primary. FOM 5.5.6.4 — System Failure Enroute In the event of required RVSM equipment failure prior to or within RVSM airspace, notify ATC and Dispatch to coordinate a prudent course of action. ATC may not require any action; however, a reroute or diversion may be required. Required RVSM equipment includes both primary altimeters, one autopilot altitude-control system, and the altitude alerting system; loss of any of these drives the ATC/Dispatch coordination, and the standby altimeter is prohibited as a primary.

docs.t: SCENARIO (check airman): Landing rollout complete, the RVR is 900 and dropping in dense fog. The First Officer offers to taxi to the gate while the Captain runs the after-landing flow. Is that acceptable, and how are checklists handled?
docs.x: SCENARIO (check airman): Landing rollout complete, the RVR is 900 and dropping in dense fog. The First Officer offers to taxi to the gate while the Captain runs the after-landing flow. Is that acceptable, and how are checklists handled? No. RVR 900 is below 1200, so this is restricted/low visibility. During low visibility operations, the Captain must taxi the aircraft, not the First Officer. Checklists are performed with the aircraft stopped and the parking brake set, all exterior lights except landing lights are on, and maximum attention is devoted to scanning outside while taxiing. FOM 5.3.11 — Taxi Operations – Low Visibility During low visibility operations, the Captain must taxi the aircraft. ... Perform checklists with the aircraft stopped and the parking brake set. Restricted visibility includes any time RVR is less than 1200; the Captain taxis, checklists are done stopped with the parking brake set, and no taxiing-unrelated duties are performed until stopped.

docs.t: Rev 125: how is 787 operational/in-flight landing distance now calculated, and what safety margin applies?
docs.x: Rev 125: how is 787 operational/in-flight landing distance now calculated, and what safety margin applies? On TALPA guidance, using a 7-second air/flare distance from 50 ft above the runway threshold to touchdown.
