A 15% safety margin is applied to TOTAL landing distance, including the air distance, for both maximum manual braking and autobrake. The touchdown point is not a fixed distance; it is calculated and varies with weight, pressure altitude, temperature, approach speed, and wind. FOM 5.6.22.3 - Landing Performance (717/787/A321/A330) Operational/In-flight landing distance calculations are based on TALPA guidance, using a 7-second air/flare distance (from 50 ft above runway threshold to touchdown). A 15% safety margin is applied to total landing distance, including the air distance, for both maximum manual braking and autobrake configurations. The touchdown point is not a fixed distance but rather a calculated value that varies with landing conditions such as aircraft weight, pressure altitude, temperature, approach speed, and wind. NEW in Rev 125. The old fixed 'touchdown 1000 ft past the threshold' model is now banner-tagged (737) and no longer applies to the 787.

docs.t: Rev 125: you are planning a 787 takeoff below RVR 500 (150 m). What governs, and what changed?
docs.x: Rev 125: you are planning a 787 takeoff below RVR 500 (150 m). What governs, and what changed? Use the Takeoff Low Visibility Card in the PRC, and the HGS/HUD Takeoff Briefing Card. Rev 125 extended this from 737-only to (737/787), so it now applies to you. FOM 5.4.4 - IFR Lower than Standard Takeoff Minimum Requirements (737/787) For takeoffs less than 500 RVR (150 m), see Takeoff Low Visibility Card in PRC. Table row: (737/787) <500 (150 m) - SEE HGS/HUD TAKEOFF BRIEFING CARD. Rev 125 change. Through 124.2 this read (737) and referenced the HGS card only.

docs.t: Rev 125: after 'Cabin Secure' and Flight Deck Door closure, what must the Flight Crew confirm before the aircraft moves?
docs.x: Rev 125: after 'Cabin Secure' and Flight Deck Door closure, what must the Flight Crew confirm before the aircraft moves? All door indications closed, verbal confirmation from the Ground Crew that the Walkaround Check is complete, and, if installed, the Installed Physical Secondary Barrier (IPSB) verified stowed and latched. FOM 5.2.20 - Cabin Safety Check Prior to Taxi or Pushback The Flight Crew must check all door indications to confirm they are closed and receive a verbal confirmation from the Ground Crew that the Walkaround Check is complete. If installed, the Installed Physical Secondary Barrier (IPSB) must be verified stowed and latched. The IPSB sentence is NEW in Rev 125.

docs.t: How does the FOM define an ETOPS operation in terms of distance from an adequate airport?
docs.x: How does the FOM define an ETOPS operation in terms of distance from an adequate airport? A flight that operates over a route containing a point farther than 60 minutes of flying time from an adequate airport, at an approved one-engine-inoperative cruise speed under standard conditions in still air. FOM 6.1.1 — Applicability flights that operate over a route that contains a point farther than 60 minutes of flying time from an adequate airport, at an approved one-engine inoperative cruise speed under standard conditions in still air This 60-minute threshold is the trigger for ETOPS. On the 787 fleet, the ICAO-equivalent term is EDTO. The one-engine-inoperative cruise speed used to measure the 60 minutes is the 787's .84M/290 KIAS.

docs.t: What distance defines an Extended Over-Water Operation?
docs.x: What distance defines an Extended Over-Water Operation? An operation over water at a horizontal distance of more than 50 nautical miles from the nearest shoreline. FOM 6.1.2 — Definitions An operation over water at a horizontal distance of more than 50 nautical miles from the nearest shoreline. Do not confuse the 50 NM over-water trigger with the 60-minute ETOPS trigger; they are separate concepts.

docs.t: What is the two-part premise of ETOPS philosophy?
docs.x: What is the two-part premise of ETOPS philosophy? To preclude a diversion and, if one were to occur, to have programs in place to protect the diversion. FOM 6.1.3 — ETOPS Philosophy: Preclude and Protect The premise of ETOPS is to preclude a diversion and, if it were to occur, to have programs in place to protect the diversion. Preclude layers include design, testing, maintenance, and flight ops procedures; protect layers include monitored alternates, enhanced comms, and enhanced dispatch fuel.

docs.t: For an adequate airport, within what portion of runway length must a turbojet be able to stop, and from what height?
docs.x: For an adequate airport, within what portion of runway length must a turbojet be able to stop, and from what height? Within 60 percent of the effective length of a runway, measured from a point 50 ft above the intersection of the obstruction clearance plane and the runway. FOM 6.2.1 — Adequate Airport Turbojet aircraft must be able to be stopped within 60 percent of the effective length of a runway from a point 50 ft above the intersection of the obstruction clearance plane and the runway. An adequate airport must also meet 14 CFR 121.197 landing limitations and Part 139 Subpart D (excluding ARFF), or be an active military airport.

docs.t: What minimum rescue and firefighting (RFFS) category must each designated ETOPS alternate airport have?
docs.x: What minimum rescue and firefighting (RFFS) category must each designated ETOPS alternate airport have? RFFS equivalent to that specified by ICAO as Category 4, or higher. FOM 6.2.1 - Adequate Airport rescue and firefighting service (RFFS) equivalent to that specified by ICAO as Category 4, or higher Note the distinction: an adequate airport does not require ARFF, but a designated ETOPS alternate must have at least ICAO Category 4 RFFS.

docs.t: What firefighting response time must an FAA-approved ETOPS alternate meet, and what does it actually require?
docs.x: What firefighting response time must an FAA-approved ETOPS alternate meet, and what does it actually require? A 30-minute response time. It does not require equipment to be pre-positioned; it means firefighting equipment must be available on arrival of the diverting airplane and remain on station as long as needed. FOM 6.2.2 — ETOPS Alternate Airport firefighting assistance within a 30-minute response time The FOM clarifies the 30-minute response time means equipment available on arrival of the diverting airplane, not standing by for 30 minutes beforehand.

docs.t: What is Alaska Airlines' authorized Maximum Diversion Time (MDT), and where does the ETOPS area of operation begin?
docs.x: What is Alaska Airlines' authorized Maximum Diversion Time (MDT), and where does the ETOPS area of operation begin? The authorized MDT is 180 minutes. The ETOPS area of operation begins beyond 60 minutes from the adequate airport and extends to the planned MDT from the planned ETOPS alternates. FOM 6.2.3 — ETOPS Area of Operation The Alaska Airlines' authorized MDT is 180 minutes. MDT is computed at one-engine-inoperative cruise speed under standard conditions in still air, and the MDT the flight was planned on must be listed in the Dispatch Release.

docs.t: For ETOPS up to and including 180 minutes, the time to an ETOPS alternate may not exceed what limit?
docs.x: For ETOPS up to and including 180 minutes, the time to an ETOPS alternate may not exceed what limit? It may not exceed the approved time for the aircraft's most limiting ETOPS-significant system (including the most limiting fire-suppression system time for compartments required to have fire suppression) minus 15 minutes. FOM 6.2.3 — ETOPS Area of Operation would exceed the approved time for the aircraft's most limiting ETOPS-significant system (including the aircraft's most limiting fire-suppression system time for those cargo and baggage compartments required by regulation to have fire-suppression systems) minus 15 minutes This 'minus 15 minutes' buffer also appears in 6.2.5 as the ceiling on actual diversion time per 14 CFR 121.633.

docs.t: What can occasionally reduce the MDT to 120 minutes, and what is the maximum diversion time to an ETOPS alternate from any point along the route?
docs.x: What can occasionally reduce the MDT to 120 minutes, and what is the maximum diversion time to an ETOPS alternate from any point along the route? MEL-deferred items may occasionally limit the MDT to 120 minutes. The diversion time from any point along the route must be no more than 120 or 180 minutes (as dispatched) to the ETOPS alternate. FOM 6.2.3 — ETOPS Area of Operation Occasionally, MEL-deferred items may limit the MDT to 120 minutes. This diversion time is measured at one-engine-inoperative cruise speed under standard conditions in still air and yields a fixed Maximum Diversion Distance (MDD) per aircraft.

docs.t: For the 787, what single-engine speed and what flying distances correspond to the 60-, 120-, and 180-minute rings?
docs.x: For the 787, what single-engine speed and what flying distances correspond to the 60-, 120-, and 180-minute rings? 787: .84M/290 KIAS, giving 410 nm at 60 minutes, 806 nm at 120 minutes, and 1207 nm at 180 minutes. FOM 6.2.3 — Table 6.2.3(1): ETOPS Area of Operations 787 .84M/290 KIAS 410 nm 806 nm 1207 nm These are the fixed 787 distances that define the range rings; the 60-minute ring (410 nm) marks the EEP/EXP distance.

docs.t: What are the three critical fuel scenarios used to compute fuel to fly to an ETOPS alternate?
docs.x: What are the three critical fuel scenarios used to compute fuel to fly to an ETOPS alternate? (1) Immediate descent from cruise to 10,000 ft with both engines operating (pressurization loss); (2) descent to best single-engine altitude with one engine operating (engine failure); (3) immediate descent to 10,000 ft with one engine operating (simultaneous pressurization loss and engine failure). FOM 6.2.5 — Critical Fuel Planning An immediate descent to 10,000 ft with one engine operating (pressurization loss and simultaneous engine-failure scenario) The fuel calculation uses the most critical of these scenarios from the critical point (CP/ETP) to the diversion airport.

docs.t: Upon reaching the ETOPS alternate, what fuel allowance does the critical fuel calculation include?
docs.x: Upon reaching the ETOPS alternate, what fuel allowance does the critical fuel calculation include? Fuel to descend to 1500 ft above the airport, hold for 15 minutes, and then conduct an instrument approach and landing. FOM 6.2.5 — Critical Fuel Planning Fuel to descend to 1500 ft above the airport, hold for 15 minutes, and then conduct an instrument approach and landing. This arrival allowance is one element added on top of the fuel to fly to the alternate under the critical scenario.

docs.t: How is forecast wind adjusted in the ETOPS critical fuel calculation?
docs.x: How is forecast wind adjusted in the ETOPS critical fuel calculation? Forecast wind speeds are increased by 5%, resulting in an increase in headwind or a decrease in tailwind. FOM 6.2.5 — Critical Fuel Planning forecast wind speeds which have been increased by 5% (resulting in an increase in headwind or a decrease in tailwind) This is one of several conservative adjustments, alongside icing, engine deterioration, APU use, and MEL/CDL penalties.

docs.t: What does the '(AS) ER or ETOPS' designation mean in the MEL, and how is it typically used?
docs.x: What does the '(AS) ER or ETOPS' designation mean in the MEL, and how is it typically used? It refers to Extended Operations of a two-engine aircraft with a type design approval for ETOPS. The designation is used primarily as an exception to a normally allowed MEL deferred item. FOM 6.2.8 — MEL Policy The ER or ETOPS designation is used primarily as an exception to a normally allowed MEL deferred item. MEL ETOPS-critical items may limit the ETOPS area of operations or preclude ETOPS entirely; compliance with the MEL is a critical factor in ETOPS.

docs.t: For the 787, what one-engine-inoperative reference speed, reference weight, and reference flight level are used to derive ETOPS speeds?
docs.x: For the 787, what one-engine-inoperative reference speed, reference weight, and reference flight level are used to derive ETOPS speeds? 787: .84M/290 KIAS, a reference weight of 515,000 lb, and reference FL350. FOM 6.2.9 — One-Engine-Inoperative Cruise Speed 787 .84M/290 KIAS 515,000 350 Reference weights and OEI flight levels derive the ring distances; for dispatch planning, actual planned weights are used.

docs.t: How long does the ETOPS Dispatch Release / Pre-Departure Check remain valid, and what is required after that?
docs.x: How long does the ETOPS Dispatch Release / Pre-Departure Check remain valid, and what is required after that? It remains valid for four hours after the scheduled departure time. After the release expiration, a new Pre-Departure Check and an amended Dispatch Release are required. FOM 6.3.2 — Flight Crew Duties / ETOPS Dispatch Release A new Pre-Departure Check and amended Dispatch Release are required after the valid time (release expiration), which is four hours after the scheduled departure time. 'ETOPS NA' on the release indicates the aircraft is not ETOPS capable; the 'EQUIP ETOPS' line is not an indication of ETOPS status.

docs.t: When does the aircraft reach the ETOPS Entry Point (EEP), and how is the EXP distance related?
docs.x: When does the aircraft reach the ETOPS Entry Point (EEP), and how is the EXP distance related? The EEP is reached when the aircraft is 60 minutes from the adequate airport (at OEI cruise speed, standard conditions, still air). The EXP represents the same 60-minute distance and results in the same fixed distance as the EEP. FOM 6.3.3 — ETOPS Entry/Exit Point/Equal Time Point reaches the ETOPS Entry Point (EEP) when it is 60 minutes from the adequate airport Flight Crew and Dispatch must use the same adequate airports to define EEP and EXP, and those airports must be listed on the Dispatch Release.

docs.t: Do ETOPS regulations add fuel requirements once in flight, and what does arriving at the CP/ETP below critical fuel actually require?
docs.x: Do ETOPS regulations add fuel requirements once in flight, and what does arriving at the CP/ETP below critical fuel actually require? No; ETOPS regulations do not add any additional fuel requirements once in flight. Arriving at the CP/ETP at or above critical fuel is only a dispatch requirement, so there is no requirement to divert prior to the CP for that reason alone, provided estimated fuel at destination is above arrival requirements. FOM 6.3.6 — ETOPS Fuel Monitoring ETOPS regulations do not add any additional fuel requirements once in flight. Fuel monitoring remains critical given the potential for a long diversion; the Dispatcher may adjust altitude, speed, enroute alternate, and routing to meet the critical fuel requirement.

docs.t: At what altitude and winds does Alaska calculate Equal-Time Points (ETPs), and what is an ETP?
docs.x: At what altitude and winds does Alaska calculate Equal-Time Points (ETPs), and what is an ETP? ETPs are calculated using flight performance and winds at 10,000 ft. An ETP is a point where the flight time, considering wind, to each of two selected diversion destinations is equal. FOM 6.3.7 — Equal-Time Point (ETP) ETPs are calculated using flight performance and winds at 10,000 ft. Because ETPs are wind-affected, a different ETP exists for each altitude; crews should also stay aware of the airport that takes the least time to reach near cruise altitude.

docs.t: Within what timeframe must ETOPS discrepancies such as IFSDs and diversions be reported?
docs.x: Within what timeframe must ETOPS discrepancies such as IFSDs and diversions be reported? Within 96 hours. FOM 6.5.2 — Discrepancy Reporting Within 96 hours, the certificate holder must report IFSDs, diversions/turnbacks for failures/malfunctions/defects Reportable events include uncommanded thrust changes, inability to control thrust, fuel loss/imbalance, and any event jeopardizing safe flight and landing; prompt crew reporting helps meet this requirement.

docs.t: Alaska/Hawaiian's 787 is approved for a maximum ETOPS operation of how many minutes?
docs.x: Alaska/Hawaiian's 787 is approved for a maximum ETOPS operation of how many minutes? 180 minutes. (Options were 60, 120, 180, 240 — the authorized Maximum Diversion Time is 180.) FOM 6.2.3 — ETOPS Area of Operation The Alaska Airlines' authorized MDT is 180 minutes. VERIFIED in ch6.txt. MEL-deferred items can occasionally cut the MDT to 120 minutes; the release states the MDT the flight was planned on.

docs.t: ETOPS philosophy is 'Preclude and Protect.' Which is true — that Preclude means avoiding a diversion through maintenance/dispatch/pilot planning, that Protect means the analysis of airports, weather, firefighting, passenger handling, landing performance and fuel to the alternate, or all of the above?
docs.x: ETOPS philosophy is 'Preclude and Protect.' Which is true — that Preclude means avoiding a diversion through maintenance/dispatch/pilot planning, that Protect means the analysis of airports, weather, firefighting, passenger handling, landing performance and fuel to the alternate, or all of the above? All of the above. Preclude = keep the diversion from happening (design, testing, maintenance, dispatch and pilot planning); Protect = if it happens anyway, programs (monitored alternates, enhanced comms, enhanced dispatch fuel) carry it out safely. FOM 6.1.3 — ETOPS Philosophy: Preclude and Protect The premise of ETOPS is to preclude a diversion and, if it were to occur, to have programs in place to protect the diversion. VERIFIED in ch6.txt 6.1.3. Preclude layers: aircraft/propulsion design and testing, maintenance procedures, flight ops procedures. Protect layers: designated alternates monitored throughout the flight, increased communication requirements, enhanced dispatch fuel.

docs.t: True or false: PACOTS are tracks established WEEKLY via a Track Definition Message and NOTAM, with dispatch providing a copy.
docs.x: True or false: PACOTS are tracks established WEEKLY via a Track Definition Message and NOTAM, with dispatch providing a copy. FALSE. Organized Pacific tracks (PACOTS) are built and published on a DAILY cycle via the Track Definition Message, not weekly. The 'weekly' claim is what makes the statement false. PACOTS Track Definition Message (TDM) PACOTS tracks are issued on a daily Track Definition Message cycle, not weekly. Not covered in FOM ch6 (oceanic track systems live in the oceanic/international chapters). Marked FALSE per the pop quiz key and consistent with eq04 (Central East Pacific tracks change daily). The specific daily-cycle detail is not in the provided ch6.txt; answer FALSE is the load-bearing point.
docs.r: 6 ETOPS PACOTS Track Definition Message / AIP

docs.t: True or false: the tracks between the US West Coast and Hawaii lie within the Central East Pacific (CEP) track system and change daily.
docs.x: True or false: the tracks between the US West Coast and Hawaii lie within the Central East Pacific (CEP) track system and change daily. FALSE. Per FOM 6.2.1, any regular, provisional, refueling, or alternate airport may be used as an adequate airport provided it is listed in 8.1.3 - Authorized Airports. Rev 125 removed the HA OpSpec B342/C070 sourcing from the definition. West Coast–Hawaii routings use the Central East Pacific (CEP) organized track system, which is republished daily. Central East Pacific (CEP) track system West Coast to Hawaii routes lie in the Central East Pacific (CEP) track system and change daily. Not in ch6.txt; oceanic-track knowledge. Supports eq03 (organized Pacific tracks are daily, not weekly).
docs.r: 6 ETOPS Central East Pacific (CEP) track system / AIP

docs.t: Which is true — that over-water operations begin more than 50 NM from the nearest shoreline and require survival equipment under FAR 121.339, that a flag operation is a scheduled flight from a point in the 48 states/AK/HI/territory to a point outside (or between two points both outside), or all of the above?
docs.x: Which is true — that over-water operations begin more than 50 NM from the nearest shoreline and require survival equipment under FAR 121.339, that a flag operation is a scheduled flight from a point in the 48 states/AK/HI/territory to a point outside (or between two points both outside), or all of the above? All of the above. Extended over-water begins beyond 50 NM from the nearest shoreline (survival gear per FAR 121.339); a flag operation is the scheduled international/overseas operation described. FOM 6.1.2 — Definitions An operation over water at a horizontal distance of more than 50 nautical miles from the nearest shoreline. The 50 NM over-water definition is VERIFIED in ch6.txt 6.1.2. FAR 121.339 (over-water survival equipment) and the flag-operation definition (FAR 1.1) are cited from the question; they are not restated in ch6.txt.

docs.t: True or false: RVSM provides 1,000 ft vertical separation from FL290 up to and including FL410, and with failure of any required RVSM equipment the crew must exit RVSM airspace.
docs.x: True or false: RVSM provides 1,000 ft vertical separation from FL290 up to and including FL410, and with failure of any required RVSM equipment the crew must exit RVSM airspace. TRUE. RVSM gives 1,000 ft separation FL290 through FL410; loss of required altimetry/altitude-control equipment must be reported to ATC and the aircraft must leave RVSM airspace. NAT Doc 007 — RVSM / altimetry failure reporting Loss of one or more primary altimetry systems, or failure of all automatic altitude-control systems, must be reported to ATC as soon as practicable. Not in ch6.txt (RVSM lives in the oceanic/international chapters). The equipment-failure reporting requirement is supported by NAT Doc 007 as reflected in the NAT HLA reference.

docs.t: Class I navigation — which is true: that it is operation within the service volume of ground-based facilities (VOR/VORTAC/DME/NDB), that it includes flying through MEA gaps using pilotage/DR or GPS, that VOR service range is about 130 NM and NDB about 75 NM, or all of the above?
docs.x: Class I navigation — which is true: that it is operation within the service volume of ground-based facilities (VOR/VORTAC/DME/NDB), that it includes flying through MEA gaps using pilotage/DR or GPS, that VOR service range is about 130 NM and NDB about 75 NM, or all of the above? All of the above. Class I navigation definition (AIM) Class I navigation is conducted within the operational service volume of ICAO-standard ground-based navaids, including short gaps flown by pilotage/DR or GPS. Not in ch6.txt. The VOR ~130 NM / NDB ~75 NM service ranges are navigation-reference values cited from the question, not from ch6.txt.

docs.t: True or false: Class II (ORCN) navigation is operation outside the service volume of ground-based navaids for more than one hour and requires one Long Range Navigation System (GPS or self-contained IRS) and one Long Range Communication System (HF or SATCOM).
docs.x: True or false: Class II (ORCN) navigation is operation outside the service volume of ground-based navaids for more than one hour and requires one Long Range Navigation System (GPS or self-contained IRS) and one Long Range Communication System (HF or SATCOM). TRUE. Class II navigation / LRCS requirement Class II navigation outside ground-navaid service volume requires a Long Range Navigation System (GPS or IRS) and a Long Range Communication System (HF or SATCOM). Not in ch6.txt; ch6.txt 6.2.6 points to '7.1.8 – Long Range Communication System (LRCS) Requirements' for LRCS. Supported by the NAT HLA reference (LRCS = HF/SATCOM).
docs.r: 6 ETOPS FOM 7.1.8 — LRCS Requirements; OpSpec B036

docs.t: To enter ETOPS airspace where PBCS is used you need Communication, Navigation and Surveillance performance. Which is true — NAV = PBN/RNP, Comm = Performance-Based Communication (RCP), Surveillance = Performance-Based Surveillance (RSP), or all of the above?
docs.x: To enter ETOPS airspace where PBCS is used you need Communication, Navigation and Surveillance performance. Which is true — NAV = PBN/RNP, Comm = Performance-Based Communication (RCP), Surveillance = Performance-Based Surveillance (RSP), or all of the above? All of the above. PBCS is built on Performance-Based Navigation (RNP), Required Communication Performance (RCP) and Required Surveillance Performance (RSP). PBCS — Communication/Navigation/Surveillance PBCS tracks require Performance-Based Navigation (RNP), Required Communication Performance (RCP) and Required Surveillance Performance (RSP). Not in ch6.txt. Supported by the ETOPS review material (PBCS tracks: CPDLC/FANS 1/A+, RNP-4, RCP240, ADS-C, RSP180).

docs.t: True or false: RNP operations carry time limits per OpSpec B036, with specific requirements for specific aircraft types, and MEL issues can affect those time limits.
docs.x: True or false: RNP operations carry time limits per OpSpec B036, with specific requirements for specific aircraft types, and MEL issues can affect those time limits. TRUE. OpSpec B036 — RNP time limits OpSpec B036: unlimited with GPS updating, 18 hours with inertial position updating. Not in ch6.txt. VERIFIED against the NAT HLA reference, which cites OpSpec B036 (unlimited with GPS updating, 18 hours on inertial).

docs.t: True or false: RNP 10 is the minimum navigation requirement for operation in the Central East Pacific.
docs.x: True or false: RNP 10 is the minimum navigation requirement for operation in the Central East Pacific. TRUE. RNP 10 (RNAV 10) is the minimum navigation specification for the Central East Pacific. Central East Pacific — RNP 10 minimum RNP 10 is the minimum navigation requirement for the Central East Pacific. Not in ch6.txt. Consistent with the NAT HLA reference, which shows RNP 10 as the reduced-capability floor for oceanic entry; RNP 10 is the recognized CEP minimum.

docs.t: True or false: RCP means Required Communication Performance, with time requirements of 400 seconds or 240 seconds depending on the airspace, CPDLC as the application and VHF or SATCOM datalink as the equipment.
docs.x: True or false: RCP means Required Communication Performance, with time requirements of 400 seconds or 240 seconds depending on the airspace, CPDLC as the application and VHF or SATCOM datalink as the equipment. TRUE (RCP 400 / RCP 240, CPDLC via VHF or SATCOM datalink). RCP — Required Communication Performance Required Communication Performance: RCP 400 or RCP 240 depending on airspace; CPDLC is the application over VHF or SATCOM datalink. Not in ch6.txt. RCP 240 is the PBCS-track value in the ETOPS review material.

docs.t: True or false: RSP means Required Surveillance Performance, with time requirements of 400 seconds or 180 seconds depending on the airspace, ADS-C as the application and VHF or SATCOM datalink as the equipment.
docs.x: True or false: RSP means Required Surveillance Performance, with time requirements of 400 seconds or 180 seconds depending on the airspace, ADS-C as the application and VHF or SATCOM datalink as the equipment. TRUE (RSP 400 / RSP 180, ADS-C via VHF or SATCOM datalink). RSP — Required Surveillance Performance Required Surveillance Performance: RSP 400 or RSP 180 depending on airspace; ADS-C is the application over VHF or SATCOM datalink. Not in ch6.txt. RSP 180 is the PBCS-track value in the ETOPS review material.

docs.t: Operational control — which is true: that the Director of Operations has authority and responsibility for supervision and control of all flight operations, that the FODO can act as DO and authority is delegated to the Controlling Dispatcher and PIC, that the Controlling Dispatcher maintains control through SOCC, or all of the above?
docs.x: Operational control — which is true: that the Director of Operations has authority and responsibility for supervision and control of all flight operations, that the FODO can act as DO and authority is delegated to the Controlling Dispatcher and PIC, that the Controlling Dispatcher maintains control through SOCC, or all of the above? All of the above. Operational control / joint responsibility The Director of Operations holds authority for control of all flight operations; that authority is exercised jointly by the Controlling Dispatcher (through SOCC) and the PIC. Not in ch6.txt (operational control is defined in the general/administrative FOM chapters). ch6.txt 6.3.1 does assign the Dispatcher specific ETOPS duties and 6.4.x pairs the PIC and Dispatcher on diversion decisions.

docs.t: True or false: the Dispatcher is the primary resource in every phase of flight, assists in emergency situations, may declare or initiate emergency procedures, and disseminates emergency information to company personnel and outside agencies.
docs.x: True or false: the Dispatcher is the primary resource in every phase of flight, assists in emergency situations, may declare or initiate emergency procedures, and disseminates emergency information to company personnel and outside agencies. TRUE. Dispatcher as primary in-flight resource The Dispatcher is the primary resource in every phase of flight and shares responsibility with the PIC, including relaying critical information during an ETOPS diversion. Not fully in ch6.txt, but ch6.txt 6.3.1 lists the Dispatcher's ETOPS duties (relay weather/NOTAM/field changes, revised ETP and critical fuel) and 6.4.1 pairs the crew 'in concert with Dispatch.'

docs.t: Dispatcher ETOPS duties — which is true: (A) before the EEP the Dispatcher sends current weather/NOTAMs for the ETOPS alternates and requires crew acknowledgement; (B) enroute the Dispatcher monitors the ETOPS alternates for weather/NOTAM/field conditions; (C) enroute the Dispatcher follows fuel consumption and relays significant info and release changes requiring Dispatcher/Captain concurrence; or (D) B and C only?
docs.x: Dispatcher ETOPS duties — which is true: (A) before the EEP the Dispatcher sends current weather/NOTAMs for the ETOPS alternates and requires crew acknowledgement; (B) enroute the Dispatcher monitors the ETOPS alternates for weather/NOTAM/field conditions; (C) enroute the Dispatcher follows fuel consumption and relays significant info and release changes requiring Dispatcher/Captain concurrence; or (D) B and C only? B and C only. The FOM's before-EEP duty is to PROVIDE relevant weather/NOTAM updates for the ETOPS alternates via ACARS/SATCOM/HF — it does not state a crew-acknowledgement requirement — so option A overstates it; the enroute duties in B and C match the FOM. FOM 6.3.1 — Dispatcher Duties Before EEP: Provide via ACARS, SATCOM, or HF any relevant updates to weather and/or safety of flight NOTAMs for ETOPS alternate airports. Enroute: Evaluate the weather, NOTAMs, and field conditions ... Be aware of any variance in fuel consumption. Relay ... any significant changes ... VERIFIED against ch6.txt 6.3.1. The answer excludes A because the FOM before-EEP duty is to 'provide' updates, not to require crew acknowledgement (acknowledgement is tied to verification-flight results and specific message receipts elsewhere).

docs.t: ETOPS 'Preclude'/maintenance — which is true: (A) ETOPS-significant systems are detailed in the manufacturer's configuration/maintenance program; (B) servicing two separate systems, or two of the same ETOPS-significant items, requires an ETOPS-qualified mechanic to sign off (dual-maintenance limitation); (C) ETOPS-significant parts require a specific ETOPS part number; or all of the above?
docs.x: ETOPS 'Preclude'/maintenance — which is true: (A) ETOPS-significant systems are detailed in the manufacturer's configuration/maintenance program; (B) servicing two separate systems, or two of the same ETOPS-significant items, requires an ETOPS-qualified mechanic to sign off (dual-maintenance limitation); (C) ETOPS-significant parts require a specific ETOPS part number; or all of the above? All of the above. FOM 6.5.1 — Maintenance / Dual Maintenance Limitations Dual Maintenance Limitations: Restrictions are placed on performing dual maintenance on ETOPS Significant Systems to prevent failures. Dual-maintenance limitations and ETOPS-qualified sign-off are VERIFIED in ch6.txt 6.5.1; the ETOPS-significant-systems list (6.5.3) sits in the manufacturer-supplemented ETOPS maintenance program. The specific-ETOPS-part-number detail comes from the ETOPS maintenance program cited in the question and is not spelled out in ch6.txt.

docs.t: True or false: ETOPS in-flight shutdown (IFSD) rate targets come from AC 120-42B, and for a two-engine aircraft operating beyond 120 up to 180 minutes the target IFSD rate must not exceed 0.03 per 1,000 engine-hours.
docs.x: True or false: ETOPS in-flight shutdown (IFSD) rate targets come from AC 120-42B, and for a two-engine aircraft operating beyond 120 up to 180 minutes the target IFSD rate must not exceed 0.03 per 1,000 engine-hours. TRUE — per AC 120-42B. For the beyond-120-to-180-minute band the two-engine IFSD rate target is 0.03/1,000 engine-hours. AC 120-42B — IFSD rate targets Beyond 120 up to 180 minutes ETOPS: target IFSD rate not to exceed 0.03 per 1,000 engine-hours (per AC 120-42B). Per AC 120-42B, the target IFSD rate for the 120-to-180-minute band must not exceed 0.03 per 1000 engine-hours. This is an Advisory Circular figure and is not restated in the FOM chapter text.

docs.t: The ETOPS Pre-Departure Service Check (PDSC) verifies airworthiness by checking which — (A) the condition of the ETOPS-significant systems; (B) overall aircraft status via maintenance records; (C) an interior/exterior inspection including engine and APU oil levels and consumption; or all of the above?
docs.x: The ETOPS Pre-Departure Service Check (PDSC) verifies airworthiness by checking which — (A) the condition of the ETOPS-significant systems; (B) overall aircraft status via maintenance records; (C) an interior/exterior inspection including engine and APU oil levels and consumption; or all of the above? All of the above. FOM 6.5.4 — ETOPS PDC/PDSC Verification of the condition of all ETOPS Significant Systems ... Verification of the overall status of the aircraft by reviewing applicable maintenance records ... An interior and exterior inspection to include a determination of engine and APU oil levels and consumption rates. VERIFIED in ch6.txt 6.5.4 — these are exactly the three minimum PDC/PDSC elements. Primary responsibility lies with Maintenance; an ETOPS-qualified mechanic must sign the logbook prior to ETOPS operation.

docs.t: The ETOPS PDSC — which is true: (A) it is valid four hours from the Zulu sign-off in the logbook; (B) if the 4-hour limit is exceeded but passenger boarding has begun, the PDSC remains valid but MOC must be notified; (C) if exceeded and boarding has NOT begun, a new PDSC is required; or all of the above?
docs.x: The ETOPS PDSC — which is true: (A) it is valid four hours from the Zulu sign-off in the logbook; (B) if the 4-hour limit is exceeded but passenger boarding has begun, the PDSC remains valid but MOC must be notified; (C) if exceeded and boarding has NOT begun, a new PDSC is required; or all of the above? All of the above. FOM 6.5.4 — PDSC Policy (HA) An ETOPS PDSC Airworthiness Release will be valid for four (4) hours from the time the Airworthiness Release block was signed ... If the boarding process started before the four (4) hours lapsed, the flight may continue with the PDSC, but the flight must notify MOC. If, at the end of four (4) hours, the flight or aircraft is not ready for departure and boarding has not started, the PDSC is invalidated. VERIFIED in ch6.txt 6.5.4. MOC monitors the four hours from the PDSC release/sign-off and notifies Maintenance and SOCC/Dispatch if a new PDSC is needed.

docs.t: MEL policy — which is true: (A) prior to pushback/taxi, issues are resolved per the MEL; (B) after pushback and prior to takeoff, issues are resolved per crew placarding; (C) the MEL applies after takeoff; or (D) A and B only?
docs.x: MEL policy — which is true: (A) prior to pushback/taxi, issues are resolved per the MEL; (B) after pushback and prior to takeoff, issues are resolved per crew placarding; (C) the MEL applies after takeoff; or (D) A and B only? A and B only. The MEL is a pre-takeoff dispatch tool — it does not apply once airborne, so option C is false. MEL applicability (pre-takeoff) Compliance with the MEL is a critical factor in ETOPS operations; MEL relief is a dispatch/pre-takeoff determination and does not apply after takeoff. The ETOPS-critical role of the MEL is VERIFIED in ch6.txt 6.2.8; the general rule that the MEL applies before takeoff (not in flight) is standard MEL policy from the FOM's MEL chapter, cited here for the 'A and B only' key.
docs.r: 6 ETOPS FOM 6.2.8 — MEL Policy; FOM MEL/CDL

docs.t: Adequate-airport requirements — which is true: (A) it meets Part 139 Subpart D (excluding ARFF) or is an active/operational military airfield; (B) it accounts for size, surface, obstructions, facilities, public protection, lighting, nav/comm aids and ATC; (C) a turbojet must be able to stop within 60% of the effective runway length from a point 50 ft above the intersection of the obstruction clearance plane and the runway; or all of the above?
docs.x: Adequate-airport requirements — which is true: (A) it meets Part 139 Subpart D (excluding ARFF) or is an active/operational military airfield; (B) it accounts for size, surface, obstructions, facilities, public protection, lighting, nav/comm aids and ATC; (C) a turbojet must be able to stop within 60% of the effective runway length from a point 50 ft above the intersection of the obstruction clearance plane and the runway; or all of the above? All of the above. FOM 6.2.1 — Adequate Airport Turbojet aircraft must be able to be stopped within 60 percent of the effective length of a runway from a point 50 ft above the intersection of the obstruction clearance plane and the runway. VERIFIED in ch6.txt 6.2.1 (all three elements). Note the CAUTION: an adequate airport may still be unsuitable for a diversion (no ARFF, or bad weather).

docs.t: True or false: an airport qualifies as an adequate airport only if it is listed in OpSpec B342 and/or C070.
docs.x: True or false: an airport qualifies as an adequate airport only if it is listed in OpSpec B342 and/or C070. TRUE. FOM 6.2.2 — ETOPS Alternate Airport Any regular, provisional, refueling, or alternate airport may be used as an adequate airport provided it is listed in 8.1.3 - Authorized Airports. VERIFIED in ch6.txt: 6.2.1 and 6.2.2 cite Ops Spec B342 and C070 for authorized/adequate airports.

docs.t: For a Dispatcher to list an airport as an ETOPS alternate — which is true: (A) it is an adequate airport listed in 8.1.3 - Authorized Airports; (B) weather reports/forecasts are at or above the ETOPS-alternate minima per OpSpec C055 for the earliest-to-latest landing window; (C) field-condition reports indicate a safe landing can be made; or all of the above?
docs.x: For a Dispatcher to list an airport as an ETOPS alternate — which is true: (A) it is an adequate airport listed in 8.1.3 - Authorized Airports; (B) weather reports/forecasts are at or above the ETOPS-alternate minima per OpSpec C055 for the earliest-to-latest landing window; (C) field-condition reports indicate a safe landing can be made; or all of the above? All of the above. FOM 6.2.2 — Weather Minima The Dispatcher will not list an airport as an ETOPS alternate airport ... unless: the appropriate weather reports or forecasts ... indicate that the weather conditions will be at or above the ETOPS alternate airport minima specified in Ops Spec C055 ... Field condition reports indicate that a safe landing can be made. VERIFIED in ch6.txt 6.2.2. The alternate must first be an adequate airport (B342/C070), then meet the C055 weather window and safe-landing field conditions.

docs.t: ARFF for ETOPS alternates — which is true: (A) rescue and firefighting service (RFFS) equivalent to ICAO Category 4 or higher; (B) firefighting support within a 30-minute response time; or (C) both A and B?
docs.x: ARFF for ETOPS alternates — which is true: (A) rescue and firefighting service (RFFS) equivalent to ICAO Category 4 or higher; (B) firefighting support within a 30-minute response time; or (C) both A and B? Both A and B. Each designated ETOPS alternate needs at least ICAO Category 4 RFFS and meets a 30-minute response time. FOM 6.2.2 — Aircraft Rescue and Firefighting Requirements Each designated ETOPS alternate airport must have rescue and firefighting service (RFFS) equivalent to that specified by ICAO as Category 4, or higher ... firefighting assistance within a 30-minute response time. VERIFIED in ch6.txt 6.2.2. The 30-minute response time does NOT mean trucks idle for 30 minutes; it means equipment is available on arrival of the diverting airplane and stays on station as long as needed.

docs.t: Check-airman scenario: You're 8 minutes from the ETOPS Entry Point (EEP) on a 787 to Honolulu when Dispatch relays that your designated ETOPS alternate's weather has just dropped below the crew's operating minima and no METAR is coming. What is required, and how would it differ if this happened AFTER the EEP?
docs.x: Check-airman scenario: You're 8 minutes from the ETOPS Entry Point (EEP) on a 787 to Honolulu when Dispatch relays that your designated ETOPS alternate's weather has just dropped below the crew's operating minima and no METAR is coming. What is required, and how would it differ if this happened AFTER the EEP? Before the EEP: you must have a suitable ETOPS alternate to enter the ETOPS area. Coordinate with Dispatch to establish a new ETOPS alternate; if none can be designated (and the existing one is no longer available), a turnback is required before crossing the EEP. After the EEP: a turnback is NOT required just because the alternate is below the crew's operating minima or the runway is unusable — you attempt to establish a new ETOPS alternate with Dispatch, which may lead to a turnback, reroute, or continuation, and the PIC and Dispatcher exercise judgment on the safest course. FOM 6.3.5 — In-Flight ETOPS Alternate Airport Weather Requirements From after takeoff until approaching the EEP: ... A turnback is required if an ETOPS alternate is no longer available. After the EEP: A turnback is not required if weather at the ETOPS alternate is below the crew's operating minima or the runway is unusable. If required, attempt to establish a new ETOPS alternate with Dispatch which may lead to a turnback, reroute, or continuation on planned route. VERIFIED in ch6.txt 6.3.5. The EEP is the hinge: pre-EEP the alternate must be suitable to enter; post-EEP the crew and Dispatch work the problem in flight rather than automatically turning back.

docs.t: Check-airman scenario: Cruising the CEP between two ETOPS alternates, you pass the fuel-critical Equal-Time Point (ETP) and a few minutes later get a single-engine event. Which airport, what speed, and what's the governing rule?
docs.x: Check-airman scenario: Cruising the CEP between two ETOPS alternates, you pass the fuel-critical Equal-Time Point (ETP) and a few minutes later get a single-engine event. Which airport, what speed, and what's the governing rule? Divert to the nearest SUITABLE airport in the Captain's judgment (14 CFR 121.565). By definition of the ETP, once you're past it the airport ahead now takes the least time, so it is generally the diversion field. Fly the approved one-engine-inoperative cruise speed, M.84/290 KIAS, which is the fueled/planned diversion speed; the Captain may deviate only after assessing the emergency and considering fuel remaining. Note the ETP is a wind-based planning point (Alaska computes ETPs at 10,000 ft) and the flight-planning system does not account for the time/fuel to make the 180° turn near the ETP. FOM 6.4.2 — Engine Failure 14 CFR 121.565 requires the Captain of a two-engine aircraft with one engine inoperative to land at the nearest suitable airport where, in the Captain's judgment after considering all relevant factors, a safe landing can be made. VERIFIED in ch6.txt 6.4.2 (nearest suitable), 6.4.5 (OEI cruise speed = the planned diversion speed; Captain may deviate after assessing emergency and fuel), 6.3.7 (ETP is per-altitude, wind-affected, computed at 10,000 ft), and 6.4.1 (turn time/fuel near a fuel-critical ETP is not modeled by the flight-planning system).

docs.t: Check-airman scenario: Maintenance signs the ETOPS PDSC at 0400Z. A gate hold pushes departure late. Walk through what happens if boarding began at 0730Z versus if, at 0800Z, boarding still hasn't started.
docs.x: Check-airman scenario: Maintenance signs the ETOPS PDSC at 0400Z. A gate hold pushes departure late. Walk through what happens if boarding began at 0730Z versus if, at 0800Z, boarding still hasn't started. The PDSC Airworthiness Release is valid four hours from the sign-off time (0400Z to 0800Z). If boarding began before the four hours lapsed (0730Z is inside the window), the flight may continue on the existing PDSC, but the flight must notify MOC. If, at the end of the four hours (0800Z), the aircraft isn't ready and boarding has NOT started, the PDSC is invalidated and a new PDSC is required. MOC monitors the four-hour clock and notifies Maintenance and SOCC/Dispatch if a new PDSC is needed. Separately, if the crew suspects a maintenance action invalidated the PDSC, they contact MOC via Dispatch. FOM 6.5.4 — PDSC Policy (HA) An ETOPS PDSC Airworthiness Release will be valid for four (4) hours from the time the Airworthiness Release block was signed ... If the boarding process started before the four (4) hours lapsed, the flight may continue with the PDSC, but the flight must notify MOC. VERIFIED in ch6.txt 6.5.4. Do not confuse this maintenance PDSC 4-hour clock (from logbook sign-off) with the Dispatch Release/PDC validity, which runs four hours from the scheduled departure time (6.3.2 / 6.5.4).

docs.t: Check-airman scenario: Still short of the EEP, your fuel readout suggests estimated fuel on board at the CP/ETP will come in below the critical-fuel-scenario figure on the release. Are you required to divert before the critical point?
docs.x: Check-airman scenario: Still short of the EEP, your fuel readout suggests estimated fuel on board at the CP/ETP will come in below the critical-fuel-scenario figure on the release. Are you required to divert before the critical point? No. Arriving at the CP/ETP with fuel on board at or above the critical fuel scenario is only a DISPATCH requirement — ETOPS regulations add no additional fuel requirement once in flight. If it appears estimated FOB at the CP/ETP will be low, there is no requirement to divert prior to the CP for that reason alone, provided estimated fuel at destination is above the arrival requirements. The Dispatcher should evaluate changes to altitude, speed, enroute alternate, and routing to try to meet the flight plan's critical fuel requirement, though it may not always be possible. Keep monitoring fuel closely given the potential for a long diversion. FOM 6.3.6 — ETOPS Fuel Monitoring ETOPS regulations do not add any additional fuel requirements once in flight ... there is no requirement to divert prior to the CP, provided the estimated fuel at destination is above the arrival requirements. VERIFIED in ch6.txt 6.3.6. The critical fuel is planned from the CP/ETP to the diversion airport using the worst of three scenarios (both engines to 10,000 ft; one engine to best single-engine altitude; one engine to 10,000 ft) plus a 1,500 ft / 15-minute hold / approach-and-land allowance, winds increased 5% (6.2.5).

docs.t: Once airborne (in-flight operations), who is the flight crew's primary contact for requests and notifications?
docs.x: Once airborne (in-flight operations), who is the flight crew's primary contact for requests and notifications? The Dispatcher, who both manages information flow and shares operational control with the Captain. FOM 7.1.1.2 — In-Flight Operations The Dispatcher is the primary contact for requests and notifications, both managing information flow and sharing operational control with the Captain. On the ground the primary contact is Station ground personnel (7.1.1.1); once in flight it shifts to the Dispatcher. Maintenance will not normally communicate directly with an airborne aircraft.

docs.t: When operating with CPDLC, in what airspace is free text supported?
docs.x: When operating with CPDLC, in what airspace is free text supported? Free text is only supported in oceanic airspace; free text in domestic airspace is not supported. FOM 7.1.2.1 — Common Language and Standard Phraseology When operating with CPDLC, free text is only supported in oceanic airspace. Only use standard aviation terminology. Free text in domestic airspace is not supported. Domestic CPDLC requires standard aviation terminology only. Free text is an oceanic-only capability.

docs.t: For operations outside the US, to which aircraft does the word "Heavy" apply and when must it be used?
docs.x: For operations outside the US, to which aircraft does the word "Heavy" apply and when must it be used? Aircraft capable of takeoff with weights of 300,000 lbs or more; required only upon initial contact with the tower and approach/departure control (and on each new frequency initial contact over Canadian airspace). FOM 7.1.2.5 — Radio Communications – Professionalism the word "Heavy" applies to aircraft capable of takeoff with weights of 300,000 lbs or more and is only required upon initial contact with the tower and approach/departure control. In the US terminal area the 787 must add "Heavy" to the call sign; it is not required during enroute communications.

docs.t: Below what altitude are flight crewmembers required to use a boom microphone?
docs.x: Below what altitude are flight crewmembers required to use a boom microphone? Below 18,000 ft. Above FL180, use of loudspeakers or headsets is at the PIC's discretion. FOM 7.1.4 — Boom Microphone Use Flight Crewmembers are required to use a boom microphone below 18,000 ft. Reference is 14 CFR 121.359. The loudspeaker is not used when the PA is used from the Flight Deck or when headsets are worn.

docs.t: How are the three VHF comm radios normally prioritized, and what does #2/R monitor?
docs.x: How are the three VHF comm radios normally prioritized, and what does #2/R monitor? #1/L is primary communications, #2/R is departure/enroute/arrival and monitors 121.5 (Company on the ground), and #3/C is ACARS. FOM 7.1.5 — VHF Radio Priority #2/R VHF – Departure/Enroute/Arrival: Monitor 121.5 In flight within the state of Alaska, the Company frequency should normally be monitored on the #2 VHF. #3/C is dedicated to ACARS.

docs.t: What is the restriction on operating HF radios during fueling?
docs.x: What is the restriction on operating HF radios during fueling? Do not operate HF radios during fueling operations. FOM 7.1.6 — High Frequency Radio (if installed) Do not operate HF radios during fueling operations. FCC regulations prohibit regular HF use within the continental US, though HF radio checks are permitted. This warning is a fueling-safety item.

docs.t: Is routine satellite (SATCOM) voice communication with ATC authorized?
docs.x: Is routine satellite (SATCOM) voice communication with ATC authorized? No. Routine satellite voice communication with ATC is not authorized; however, it may be used when HF or CPDLC are not available. FOM 7.1.7 — SATCOM (if installed) Routine satellite voice communication with ATC is not authorized; however, it may be used when HF or CPDLC are not available. Satellite voice with Dispatch or MedLink is at the pilot's discretion. SATCOM is generally less reliable than HF in polar regions.

docs.t: For NAT HLA oceanic airspace, what flight levels does the Data Link Mandate (DLM) cover and what capabilities are required for dispatch?
docs.x: For NAT HLA oceanic airspace, what flight levels does the Data Link Mandate (DLM) cover and what capabilities are required for dispatch? Flight Levels 290-410 inclusive; the aircraft must be dispatched with ADS-C, CPDLC, and SATCOM data link capabilities. FOM 7.1.8.1 — NAT HLA Data Link Mandate (DLM) a Data Link Mandate (DLM) is in effect for Flight Levels 290-410, inclusive. The DLM requires that aircraft must be dispatched with ADS-C, CPDLC, and SATCOM data link capabilities. The DLM applies to operations in NAT HLA Oceanic airspace.

docs.t: How many crewmembers should be present to accept an ATC clearance, and what abbreviated-clearance restriction applies to the Captain?
docs.x: How many crewmembers should be present to accept an ATC clearance, and what abbreviated-clearance restriction applies to the Captain? At least two crewmembers should be present to monitor and confirm an ATC clearance; the Captain must not accept an abbreviated clearance if the filed Flight Plan was changed prior to departure. FOM 7.1.10.1 — Acceptance of ATC Clearance At least two crewmembers should be present to monitor and confirm an ATC clearance. When two-crew confirmation is not feasible, crewmembers must ensure a mutual understanding of the latest clearance.

docs.t: Under Radio Reports to ATC, at what minimum climb/descent performance must you notify ATC?
docs.x: Under Radio Reports to ATC, at what minimum climb/descent performance must you notify ATC? Report to ATC if unable to climb or descend at least 500 ft per minute. FOM 7.1.11 — Radio Reports – ATC If unable to climb or descend at least 500 ft per minute One of the reports that should be made to ATC at all times, alongside vacating an altitude, missed approach, and reaching/leaving a holding fix.

docs.t: At cruise, what change in true airspeed requires a report to ATC?
docs.x: At cruise, what change in true airspeed requires a report to ATC? A change in TAS at cruise of more than 5%, 10 kts, or 0.02 Mach from Flight Plan speed. FOM 7.1.11 — Radio Reports – ATC Change in TAS at cruise of more than 5%, 10 kts, or 0.02 Mach from Flight Plan speed A required ATC report at all times. Any of the three thresholds triggers the report.

docs.t: When not in radar contact, when must a corrected time estimate be reported to ATC?
docs.x: When not in radar contact, when must a corrected time estimate be reported to ATC? When a previous estimate is in error by more than 2 minutes (3 minutes or more in NAT HLA). FOM 7.1.11 — Radio Reports – ATC A corrected estimate when a previous estimate is in error by more than 2 minutes (3 minutes or more in NAT HLA) This is one of the additional reports required specifically when not in radar contact.

docs.t: By how much must actual fuel remaining differ from planned before contacting Dispatch on the 787?
docs.x: By how much must actual fuel remaining differ from planned before contacting Dispatch on the 787? By plus or minus 3000 lbs on the 787. FOM 7.1.12 — Reports to Dispatch Actual fuel remaining differs from planned fuel remaining by ... (787) ± 3000 lbs. Contact Dispatch as safety-of-flight considerations permit; notification is mandatory but timing is workload-dependent. On the 787 the threshold is ±3000 lbs.

docs.t: What thresholds define a "significant" deviation from the Flight Plan that requires contacting Dispatch?
docs.x: What thresholds define a "significant" deviation from the Flight Plan that requires contacting Dispatch? Lateral deviation of 100 nm or more from the planned route, altitude deviation of 4000 ft or more from planned cruise altitude, or any action likely to delay arrival by more than 15 minutes. FOM 7.1.12 — Reports to Dispatch Lateral deviation: 100 nm or more from the planned route. The same section requires contacting Dispatch for moderate or greater turbulence and for mechanical irregularities that could interrupt the schedule.

docs.t: By approximately what altitudes must the sterile flight deck chimes (two distinct chimes) be given on departure and arrival?
docs.x: By approximately what altitudes must the sterile flight deck chimes (two distinct chimes) be given on departure and arrival? By approximately 10,000 ft MSL during departure and 10,000 ft AFE during arrival. FOM 7.1.20.3 — Sterile Flight Deck Operations Advisory shall always be cycled to produce two distinct chimes by approximately 10,000 ft MSL during departure and 10,000 ft AFE during arrival. On the 787 this is the Cabin Chime Button. The chime is mandatory even if the cabin was already prepared for arrival due to turbulence.

docs.t: How long before takeoff should the verbatim Impending Takeoff Advisory ("Flight Attendants should now be seated for takeoff") be made?
docs.x: How long before takeoff should the verbatim Impending Takeoff Advisory ("Flight Attendants should now be seated for takeoff") be made? At least 2 minutes prior to takeoff, prior to taking position on an active runway. FOM 7.1.20.1 — Impending Takeoff Advisory This announcement should be made at least 2 minutes prior to takeoff. It is a verbatim announcement and must not be combined with any other announcement. On the 787 the A F/A places a non-voice cabin ready call that displays CABIN READY on EICAS.

docs.t: By when must a safety report for an NTSB reportable item be filed?
docs.x: By when must a safety report for an NTSB reportable item be filed? No later than the end of the next 24-hour rest period. FOM 7.2.3.1 — NTSB – Required Reports A safety report for an NTSB reportable item must be filed no later than the end of the next 24-hour rest period. NTSB-reportable events include in-flight fire/smoke, flight control malfunction, near midair collision, and a TCAS RA where compliance was necessary to avert substantial collision risk.

docs.t: Under ASAP, what is the phone number and the deadline for the follow-up written report and for submitting the report?
docs.x: Under ASAP, what is the phone number and the deadline for the follow-up written report and for submitting the report? Call 877-897-ASAP (2727); the phone call must be followed by a written report within 24 hours of the call, and ASAP reports should be submitted within 24 hours from the end of that day's flight sequence. FOM 7.2.5 — Aviation Safety Action Program (ASAP) The phone call must be followed by a written report within 24 hours of the call. ASAP uses an FAA non-punitive incentive to encourage reporting and does not replace the safety report or the NASA ASRS form.

docs.t: CHECK AIRMAN SCENARIO: You are dispatched for a North Atlantic crossing planning FL350 through NAT HLA Oceanic airspace, but the release shows the aircraft's SATCOM data link is inoperative. May you accept an oceanic clearance into the organized track system at FL350?
docs.x: CHECK AIRMAN SCENARIO: You are dispatched for a North Atlantic crossing planning FL350 through NAT HLA Oceanic airspace, but the release shows the aircraft's SATCOM data link is inoperative. May you accept an oceanic clearance into the organized track system at FL350? No. In NAT HLA Oceanic airspace a Data Link Mandate is in effect for FL290-410 inclusive, and it requires the aircraft be dispatched with ADS-C, CPDLC, and SATCOM data link. Without working SATCOM data link you cannot operate in that DLM band. FOM 7.1.8.1 — NAT HLA Data Link Mandate (DLM) For operations in NAT HLA Oceanic airspace, a Data Link Mandate (DLM) is in effect for Flight Levels 290-410, inclusive. The DLM requires that aircraft must be dispatched with ADS-C, CPDLC, and SATCOM data link capabilities. All three capabilities — ADS-C, CPDLC, and SATCOM data link — are required together for the FL290-410 mandate.

docs.t: CHECK AIRMAN SCENARIO: Oceanic and not in radar contact in NAT HLA, your previous estimate for the next waypoint is now going to be off by about 2.5 minutes. Do you owe ATC a corrected estimate?
docs.x: CHECK AIRMAN SCENARIO: Oceanic and not in radar contact in NAT HLA, your previous estimate for the next waypoint is now going to be off by about 2.5 minutes. Do you owe ATC a corrected estimate? No, not on that basis. When not in radar contact a corrected estimate is required when the previous estimate is in error by more than 2 minutes, but in NAT HLA the threshold is 3 minutes or more; a 2.5-minute error does not trigger the corrected estimate in NAT HLA. FOM 7.1.11 — Radio Reports – ATC A corrected estimate when a previous estimate is in error by more than 2 minutes (3 minutes or more in NAT HLA) This corrected-estimate report applies specifically when not in radar contact; the 3-minute figure is the NAT HLA exception to the general 2-minute rule.

docs.t: CHECK AIRMAN SCENARIO: Enroute in domestic US airspace on CPDLC, you want to send Center a free-text message explaining a ride-smoothing request. Is free text available to you here?
docs.x: CHECK AIRMAN SCENARIO: Enroute in domestic US airspace on CPDLC, you want to send Center a free-text message explaining a ride-smoothing request. Is free text available to you here? No. When operating with CPDLC, free text is only supported in oceanic airspace; in domestic airspace free text is not supported and you must use standard aviation terminology only. FOM 7.1.2.1 — Common Language and Standard Phraseology When operating with CPDLC, free text is only supported in oceanic airspace. Only use standard aviation terminology. Free text in domestic airspace is not supported. Domestic CPDLC is limited to standard terminology; free text is an oceanic-only capability.

docs.t: CHECK AIRMAN SCENARIO: You are inbound IFR to a non-towered airport and self-announcing your position on CTAF. What three elements must each position report contain?
docs.x: CHECK AIRMAN SCENARIO: You are inbound IFR to a non-towered airport and self-announcing your position on CTAF. What three elements must each position report contain? Company ID and type of aircraft; position and altitude; and direction of flight and intentions (landing or overflying). FOM 7.1.27.1 — Arriving or Departing Position reports should include: Company ID and type A/C; Position and Altitude; Direction of flight and intentions (landing or overflying). Position reports are announced at points such as the IAF, 10 miles or FAF inbound on CTAF, downwind, base, final, and clearing the runway.

docs.t: At what moment is an Alaska Airlines flight considered dispatched (the Point of Dispatch)?
docs.x: At what moment is an Alaska Airlines flight considered dispatched (the Point of Dispatch)? When an OUT time is generated. FOM 8.1.1 — Types of Operations Authorized for Dispatch A flight is considered dispatched at the Point of Dispatch, which occurs when an OUT time is generated. Flight Dispatch releases and dispatches aircraft under Domestic or Flag rules as appropriate; the OUT time is the regulatory trigger, not brake release or takeoff.

docs.t: When a flight is dispatched under Exemption 11047 without a destination alternate, what runway conditions must exist at the destination at the ETA?
docs.x: When a flight is dispatched under Exemption 11047 without a destination alternate, what runway conditions must exist at the destination at the ETA? Two separate usable runways at the estimated time of arrival, with at least one usable runway having an operational instrument approach procedure. FOM 8.1.1.4 — Exemption 11047 At least one of the usable runways has an operational instrument approach procedure. Exemption 11047 also requires the Dispatcher to add the statement 'FLT RELEASED UNDER EXEMPTION 11047' to the Dispatch Release.

docs.t: Using the Derived Alternate Airport IFR Weather Minimums table, what additives apply when an airport has only ONE operational navigational facility (single straight-in non-precision, CAT I, or circling)?
docs.x: Using the Derived Alternate Airport IFR Weather Minimums table, what additives apply when an airport has only ONE operational navigational facility (single straight-in non-precision, CAT I, or circling)? Add 400 ft to the MDA(H) or DA(H) as applicable, and add 1 sm (or 1600 m) to the landing minimum. FOM 8.2.2.1 — Destination Alternate Airport Weather Requirements Add 400 ft to MDA(H) or DA(H), as applicable The one-facility case gets the larger additive (400 and 1); additives apply only to the height value rounded up to the next 100-ft value.

docs.t: What alternate-minimums additives apply when an airport has at least TWO operational navigational facilities serving different suitable runways?
docs.x: What alternate-minimums additives apply when an airport has at least TWO operational navigational facilities serving different suitable runways? Add 200 ft to the higher DA(H) or MDA(H) of the two approaches used, and add 1/2 sm (or 800 m) to the higher authorized landing minimum. FOM 8.2.2.1 — Destination Alternate Airport Weather Requirements Add 200 ft to higher DA(H) or MDA(H) of two approaches used Two facilities to two different suitable runways (two approach ends) earns the reduced 200-and-half additive versus the single-facility 400-and-1.

docs.t: Per 14 CFR 121.621, when is a destination alternate always required for a Flag flight regardless of destination weather?
docs.x: Per 14 CFR 121.621, when is a destination alternate always required for a Flag flight regardless of destination weather? Any Flag flight planned for more than six hours flight time as calculated on the Flight Plan requires a destination alternate. FOM 8.2.2.1 — Destination Alternate Airport Weather Requirements an alternate is required for any Flag flight more than six hours flight time as planned on the Flight Plan The same 6-hour rule is repeated in 8.2.3 for the no-alternate cases to/from Alaska and international locations under A012.

docs.t: How does Alaska define 'marginal' for the alternate airport when deciding whether a second alternate is required?
docs.x: How does Alaska define 'marginal' for the alternate airport when deciding whether a second alternate is required? The alternate is marginal when either its ceiling OR visibility is at alternate minimums (as derived from the Alternate Airport IFR Weather Minimums table). FOM 8.2.2.2 — Marginal Weather/Second Alternate Required Alternate airport weather is considered marginal when either the ceiling OR visibility is at alternate minimums 121.619(a) requires a second alternate when both destination and first alternate are forecast marginal; destination is marginal when ceiling and/or visibility is at or below CAT I minimums.

docs.t: What two change indicators does Exemption 20108 define as 'conditional language' in a TAF or METAR?
docs.x: What two change indicators does Exemption 20108 define as 'conditional language' in a TAF or METAR? TEMPO and PROB. FOM 8.2.2.3 — Exemption 20108 The term “conditional language” refers to the change indicators TEMPO and PROB. Exemption 20108 lets a Domestic flight dispatch when conditional language shows destination and/or first alternate may go below minimums at ETA.

docs.t: When a flight is dispatched under Exemption 20108, what alternate requirement always applies?
docs.x: When a flight is dispatched under Exemption 20108, what alternate requirement always applies? A second alternate airport must always be listed on the Dispatch Release. FOM 8.2.2.3 — Exemption 20108 a second alternate airport must always be listed on the Dispatch Release Exemption 20108 is not authorized for flag operations or for flights to international destinations operated under Domestic regulations, and requires the release statement 'FLT RELEASED UNDER EXEMPTION 20108.'

docs.t: Within the contiguous 48 states (or Hawaiian Islands), what destination weather allows dispatch with no alternate?
docs.x: Within the contiguous 48 states (or Hawaiian Islands), what destination weather allows dispatch with no alternate? Forecasts/reports indicate that at the estimated time of arrival, plus or minus one hour, conditions will be at least a 2000 ft ceiling and 3 sm visibility. FOM 8.2.3 — No Alternate for Destination conditions will be at least 2000 ft ceiling and 3 sm visibility This is the classic 1-2-3 no-alternate rule: within +/- 1 hour of ETA, 2000 ft ceiling and 3 statute miles visibility.

docs.t: For a no-alternate dispatch to a State of Alaska destination, what runway physical criteria must the airport meet?
docs.x: For a no-alternate dispatch to a State of Alaska destination, what runway physical criteria must the airport meet? More than one operational runway with two separate and distinct surfaces (four runway ends), hard-surface with appropriate weight-bearing capability, minimum 100 ft wide, and at least 5500 ft of usable length. FOM 8.2.3 — No Alternate for Destination minimum of 100 ft wide, and at least 5500 ft of usable length Alaska destinations also need 2000 ft ceiling and 3 sm (or 2 sm more than lowest applicable minimums, whichever is greater) at ETA +/- 1 hour.

docs.t: For a Flag no-alternate dispatch (14 CFR 121.621(a)) with a straight-in approach available, what ceiling is required from one hour before to one hour after ETA?
docs.x: For a Flag no-alternate dispatch (14 CFR 121.621(a)) with a straight-in approach available, what ceiling is required from one hour before to one hour after ETA? At least 1500 ft above the lowest published instrument approach minimum, or 2000 ft above airport elevation, whichever is higher (plus 3 miles visibility or 2 miles more than the applicable minimum, whichever is greater). FOM 8.2.3 — No Alternate for Destination 1500 ft above the lowest published instrument approach minimum or 2000 ft above airport elevation, whichever is higher If a circling approach is required instead, the ceiling must be 1500 ft above the lowest circling MDA.

docs.t: For a no-alternate dispatch to Canada under A012, what is the FAF altitude used for most YVR (Vancouver) approaches?
docs.x: For a no-alternate dispatch to Canada under A012, what is the FAF altitude used for most YVR (Vancouver) approaches? 3000 ft. FOM 8.2.3 — No Alternate for Destination FAF altitude for most YVR approaches is 3000 ft. The Canada no-alternate criteria require a forecast ceiling at least 1000 ft above the FAF altitude with 3 miles visibility, OR 2000 ft ceiling and 6 miles, plus no thunderstorm or freezing precipitation risk.

docs.t: For passenger operations, how does the ARFF/ICAO index requirement at the destination differ from the requirement at an alternate?
docs.x: For passenger operations, how does the ARFF/ICAO index requirement at the destination differ from the requirement at an alternate? At the destination, passenger operations are permitted with an ARFF Index/ICAO category one level lower than that associated with the aircraft (e.g., an Index C aircraft may operate at an Index B airport). For an alternate, a minimum designation of ARFF Index A / ICAO category 4 is required. FOM 8.3.10.2 — Airport Rescue and Fire Fighting Requirements (ARFF) For alternates, a minimum designation of ARFF Index A/ICAO 4 is required. A difference of more than one ARFF level at the destination requires DO approval before operating into or out of that airport; if ARFF is unavailable at the alternate's planned arrival time, Dispatch should notify airport management as soon as possible when diverting.

docs.t: Under Domestic fuel rules (14 CFR 121.639), how much reserve fuel is required beyond flying to the destination and most distant alternate?
docs.x: Under Domestic fuel rules (14 CFR 121.639), how much reserve fuel is required beyond flying to the destination and most distant alternate? Enough to fly 45 minutes at last cruise altitude consumption rate after the most distant alternate; with no alternate, 55 minutes at last cruise altitude consumption rate. FOM 8.3.2.1 — Domestic Operations With no alternate, fly for 55 minutes at last cruise altitude consumption rate. Domestic: destination + most distant alternate + 45 min, or destination + 55 min if no alternate is required.

docs.t: Under Flag fuel rules (14 CFR 121.645), what are the required fuel components?
docs.x: Under Flag fuel rules (14 CFR 121.645), what are the required fuel components? Destination, then 10% of the total time from departure to destination, then the most distant alternate (if required), then 30 minutes at holding speed at 1500 ft above the destination or alternate. FOM 8.3.2.2 — Flag Operations Fly for 30 minutes at holding speed at 1500 ft above the destination airport or alternate The 10% burn is on the total departure-to-destination time; the 30-minute hold is at 1500 ft, distinguishing Flag from Domestic reserves.

docs.t: Under the B043 Special Fuel Reserves in International Operations (787), how are the two extra reserve components computed?
docs.x: Under the B043 Special Fuel Reserves in International Operations (787), how are the two extra reserve components computed? 10% of the planned time in oceanic/remote continental airspace, plus 45 minutes at normal cruising consumption (calculated at the flight's weight and altitude at top of descent). FOM 8.3.2.3 — Special Fuel Reserves in International Operations (787) Fly for a period of 10% of the planned time in oceanic/remote continental airspace On the 787 international release these appear as '10% RSV' and '45@CRZ' (B043) versus '30@1500' for standard flag.

docs.t: How far before pushback should the Flight Crew contact Dispatch with any changes to desired departure fuel, and who has final say on fuel?
docs.x: How far before pushback should the Flight Crew contact Dispatch with any changes to desired departure fuel, and who has final say on fuel? At least 30 minutes prior to pushback; if agreement cannot be reached, the Captain has the final decision for fuel on board. FOM 8.3.1.2 — Departure Fuel Coordination the Flight Crew should contact Dispatch at least 30 minutes prior to pushback Additional fuel above planned requires agreement of both Captain and Dispatcher before fueling begins; the Captain holds the final decision.

docs.t: What is the maximum flight duration for which the 787 may be dispatched with all autopilot systems inoperative, and what approval is needed?
docs.x: What is the maximum flight duration for which the 787 may be dispatched with all autopilot systems inoperative, and what approval is needed? No aircraft may be dispatched for flights greater than 3.5 hours with all autopilots inoperative without approval from both the Captain and Dispatcher. FOM 8.3.6 — Autopilot Inoperative Aircraft will not be dispatched for flights greater than 3.5 hours if all autopilot systems are inoperative Beyond 3.5 hours all-autopilots-inop requires joint Captain and Dispatcher approval.

docs.t: What is the maximum steady-state wind velocity for takeoff and landing, and which wind value is used for dispatch crosswind computations?
docs.x: What is the maximum steady-state wind velocity for takeoff and landing, and which wind value is used for dispatch crosswind computations? 50 kts maximum steady-state wind velocity; steady-state wind velocity is used for crosswind computations for dispatch. FOM 8.4.4 — Wind Limits – Landing/Takeoff Maximum steady-state wind velocity for takeoff and landing is 50 kts Operations with a steady-state component near crosswind limits combined with higher gusts should be considered unacceptable; specific limit values are in fleet-specific manuals.

docs.t: For a flight with 1 hour or more of flight time, what weather product controls dispatch/prior to departure per the Weather Required for Dispatch table?
docs.x: For a flight with 1 hour or more of flight time, what weather product controls dispatch/prior to departure per the Weather Required for Dispatch table? The TAF controls (METAR is not controlling) for flight times of 1 hour or more; for flight times under 1 hour both METAR and TAF apply. FOM 8.4.1.4 — Weather Required for Dispatch or Amending Destination Enroute TAF (METAR not controlling) Enroute and possibly changing destination always requires both METAR & TAF regardless of flight time. Extended overwater Flag flights under ETOPS have a special allowance.

docs.t: When dispatching to an international or military airport that is missing ceiling, visibility, or present weather in the METAR, what TAF conditions and alternate planning are required?
docs.x: When dispatching to an international or military airport that is missing ceiling, visibility, or present weather in the METAR, what TAF conditions and alternate planning are required? The TAF must indicate at least a 1000 ft ceiling and 3 miles visibility from 1 hour before to 1 hour after ETA, two alternates with complete METAR and TAF must be planned, and the MDA is limited to 1000 ft AGL. FOM 8.4.2.3 — Missing Weather at International and Military Airports The TAF indicates the weather conditions from 1 hour before to 1 hour after the ETA will be no less than a ceiling of 1000 ft and visibility of 3 miles. No circle-to-land is permitted with missing ceiling/visibility, and departures are prohibited if freezing precipitation is forecast with missing weather elements.

docs.t: Planned redispatch is authorized under which type of operations, and why is it used?
docs.x: Planned redispatch is authorized under which type of operations, and why is it used? Flag operations only; it is an FAA-authorized procedure used to minimize the fuel required to meet the 10% flag fuel requirement. FOM 8.5.9 — Redispatch – Planned Dispatching with a plan to redispatch while enroute (planned redispatch) is an FAA-authorized procedure used in flag operations to minimize the amount of fuel required to meet the 10% fuel requirement. The redispatch waypoint must be common to both routes and specified on the original release; within two hours but no later than 20 minutes prior to the waypoint the destination alternate may be removed if the intended destination meets no-alternate requirements.

docs.t: Check-airman scenario: You dispatch a 787 on a domestic transcon with a destination alternate required, and later the same day the crew flies an international flag leg. Contrast the required reserve fuel components for the domestic leg versus the flag leg.
docs.x: Check-airman scenario: You dispatch a 787 on a domestic transcon with a destination alternate required, and later the same day the crew flies an international flag leg. Contrast the required reserve fuel components for the domestic leg versus the flag leg. Domestic (14 CFR 121.639): fuel to the destination, then to the most distant alternate, plus 45 minutes at last cruise altitude consumption rate — or 55 minutes at last cruise altitude consumption rate if no alternate is required. Flag (14 CFR 121.645): fuel to the destination, then 10% of the total departure-to-destination time, then to the most distant alternate if one is required, then 30 minutes at holding speed at 1500 ft above the destination or alternate. FOM 8.3.2.2 — Flag Operations Fly for a period of 10% of the total time required to fly from the departure airport to and land at the destination airport, then Domestic keys on the 45/55-minute last-cruise-rate reserve; Flag adds the 10%-of-total-time burn plus a 30-minute hold at 1500 ft — the signature that separates Flag reserves from Domestic. On a B043 international 787 leg the reserve instead prints as '10% RSV' and '45@CRZ' (8.3.2.3).

docs.t: Check-airman scenario: You have pushed and are taxiing out when Dispatch needs to change your alternate and add required fuel. Does this require a release amendment, and what makes the amendment valid?
docs.x: Check-airman scenario: You have pushed and are taxiing out when Dispatch needs to change your alternate and add required fuel. Does this require a release amendment, and what makes the amendment valid? Yes. An alternate change and a required-fuel change are each on the release-amendment list, so the Dispatcher must forward an amended release.
