The Captain acknowledges acceptance by verbally accepting via Company communications, by acknowledging an ACARS message containing the amended information, or by leaving a signed copy at stations that require paper. At the time of amendment all dispatch rules (14 CFR 121.593 through 121.661 and 121.173) must be met. FOM 8.5.1.3 — Dispatch Release – Amendments If it becomes necessary for the PIC or Dispatcher to change the conditions of the release, the Dispatcher shall forward an amended release. Alternate change and Required Fuel change both appear on the (AS) release-amendment list (8.5.1.4). Any airborne change to destination or alternate also requires a recalculated Flight Plan/Dispatch Release with associated weather and NOTAM information.

docs.t: Check-airman scenario: You are planning a 787 from LAX to SEA, both in the contiguous 48. The SEA forecast at ETA +/- 1 hour is 2500 ft ceiling and 4 sm. May you dispatch with no destination alternate, and what is the governing rule?
docs.x: Check-airman scenario: You are planning a 787 from LAX to SEA, both in the contiguous 48. The SEA forecast at ETA +/- 1 hour is 2500 ft ceiling and 4 sm. May you dispatch with no destination alternate, and what is the governing rule? Yes. Within the contiguous 48 states (or the Hawaiian Islands), no alternate is required if forecasts or reports indicate that at ETA +/- one hour conditions will be at least a 2000 ft ceiling and 3 sm visibility. 2500 and 4 clears the 1-2-3 threshold. An alternate is still required for any Flag flight planned more than 6 hours, and one must be listed if thunderstorms or volcanic ash are forecast in the TAF at the ETA. FOM 8.2.3 — No Alternate for Destination conditions will be at least 2000 ft ceiling and 3 sm visibility. The 1-2-3 rule: within +/- 1 hour of ETA, 2000 ft ceiling and 3 sm. Thunderstorms or volcanic ash forecast in the TAF at the ETA still force an alternate onto the release.

docs.t: Check-airman scenario: A 787 is dispatched SEA-LIH under planned redispatch, with the redispatch waypoint set late in the overwater leg. How late may Dispatch remove the destination alternate, and what condition must the intended destination meet?
docs.x: Check-airman scenario: A 787 is dispatched SEA-LIH under planned redispatch, with the redispatch waypoint set late in the overwater leg. How late may Dispatch remove the destination alternate, and what condition must the intended destination meet? Within two hours of arrival at the redispatch point, but no later than 20 minutes prior to the redispatch waypoint, the destination alternate may be removed from the redispatch Flight Plan, provided the intended destination meets the no-alternate requirements. Planned redispatch is authorized in flag operations only, and the redispatch waypoint must be specified on the original release and common to both routes. FOM 8.5.9 — Redispatch – Planned Within two hours, but no later than 20 minutes prior to the redispatch waypoint, the destination alternate may be removed from the redispatch Flight Plan, provided the intended destination meets the no alternate requirements. Redispatch exists to minimize the 10% flag fuel. Planned-redispatch flights to/from Hawaii must depart with an alternate for the intended destination (8.2.3). If routing is modified to bypass the redispatch point, redispatch stays valid without further planning within 100 nm of the planned route (8.5.9.1).

docs.t: Rev 125: how far before scheduled departure is the Dispatch Release and ATS Flight Plan made available, and which 787 flying is the exception?
docs.x: Rev 125: how far before scheduled departure is the Dispatch Release and ATS Flight Plan made available, and which 787 flying is the exception? 90 minutes as standard. Exceptions: Interisland Hawaii 70 minutes; South Korea departures 180 minutes; Amazon Cargo 180 minutes; and, new in Rev 125, (787/A330) Europe departures 180 minutes. FOM 8.5.2.1 - Dispatch Release - Preparation A Dispatch Release and ATS Flight Plan will be generated and made available to the Flight Crew 90 minutes prior to the scheduled flight departure time except as noted below: Interisland Hawaii: 70 minutes; South Korea Departures: 180 minutes; Amazon Cargo: 180 minutes; (787/A330) Europe Departures: 180 minutes. The 787/A330 Europe line is NEW in Rev 125, and it drives a D-180 Operational Control Window per FOM 2.2.2.1.

docs.t: Per the (AS) definition, when is a runway classified as a Wet Runway?
docs.x: Per the (AS) definition, when is a runway classified as a Wet Runway? When more than 25% of the runway area being used is visibly damp or covered by no more than 1/8 inch (3 mm) of water, slush, dry snow, or wet snow. FOM 9.1.1.1 — Runway Conditions More than 25% of the runway area (length and width) being used is visibly damp or covered by no more than 1/8 inch (3 mm) of water, slush, dry snow, or wet snow. The 25% coverage plus 1/8 inch (3 mm) threshold is the dividing line; beyond 1/8 inch of loose contaminant the runway becomes Contaminated.

docs.t: In the absence of a descriptor, at what temperatures are snow considered dry versus wet?
docs.x: In the absence of a descriptor, at what temperatures are snow considered dry versus wet? Snow is considered dry at temperatures -3 degrees C or colder, and wet at temperatures -2 degrees C or warmer. FOM 9.1.1.2 — Contaminants snow is considered dry at temperatures -3°C or colder Dry snow can be blown if loose or will not stick together to form a snowball; wet snow makes a well-compacted snowball but water will not squeeze out.

docs.t: What does a Slippery When Wet NOTAM tell the crew about the runway condition code?
docs.x: What does a Slippery When Wet NOTAM tell the crew about the runway condition code? It is a continuous alert that if the runway were to become wet, it would immediately degrade to 3/3/3 instead of 5/5/5. FOM 9.1.1.4 — Runway Definitions it would immediately degrade to 3/3/3 instead of 5/5/5 Usually caused by rubber deposits; the reduced braking applies when the runway is in fact wet, and the NOTAM remains visible even when the runway is dry.

docs.t: May a braking action PIREP be used to upgrade the expected braking action from the RCAM or FICON?
docs.x: May a braking action PIREP be used to upgrade the expected braking action from the RCAM or FICON? No. A PIREP may only downgrade expected braking action; it must not be used to upgrade it, and airport personnel cannot issue braking action reports. FOM 9.1.2 — Braking Action Report A PIREP must not be used to upgrade the expected braking action. A PIREP from a similar size aircraft may be used when no FICON is available or to downgrade expected braking action.

docs.t: Is reduced thrust using assumed temperature (AT or FLEX) authorized on a contaminated runway?
docs.x: Is reduced thrust using assumed temperature (AT or FLEX) authorized on a contaminated runway? No. Reduced thrust using assumed temperature, labeled AT or FLEX, is not authorized on a contaminated runway. FOM 9.1.8 — Takeoff Operations on a Wet/Contaminated Runway Reduced thrust using assumed temperature, labeled AT or FLEX, is not authorized on a contaminated runway. Takeoff data selection depends on whether the contaminant is hard-packed (accelerate-stop concern) or loose (also a drag concern after engine failure).

docs.t: When landing on a smooth runway in moderate or heavy rain, what RWYCC must the crew plan with, and when may RWYCC 5 be used?
docs.x: When landing on a smooth runway in moderate or heavy rain, what RWYCC must the crew plan with, and when may RWYCC 5 be used? Consider the surface contaminated with standing water and use data associated with a RWYCC of 2. RWYCC 5 may be used with light rain (-RA) on any runway, or on a SK-R runway with moderate rain (RA). FOM 9.1.9 — Landing Precipitation must use landing performance data associated with a RWYCC of 2 when planning to land on The RWYCC 2 requirement applies to a smooth runway under moderate (RA) or heavy rain (+RA), or a SK-R runway under +RA.

docs.t: How is the Latest Touchdown Point (LTP) calculated, and when must it be briefed?
docs.x: How is the Latest Touchdown Point (LTP) calculated, and when must it be briefed? Subtract landing distance from LDA and add 1000 ft for air-run. Brief LTP when LDA is less than 7000 ft or BA is less than GOOD. FOM 9.1.12.1 — Latest Touchdown Point (LTP) Subtract landing distance from LDA and add 1000 ft for air-run. LTP calculations are not applicable for HGS AIII/Autoland.

docs.t: May WET landing data be used when the Landing Distance Available is less than 7000 ft?
docs.x: May WET landing data be used when the Landing Distance Available is less than 7000 ft? No. For LDA less than 7000 ft, do not use WET data. FOM 9.1.12.3 — Wet vs. Contaminated Data For LDA less than 7000 ft, do not use WET data. For LDA less than 7000 ft with BA less than GOOD, the maximum selectable autobrake setting must be used if available.

docs.t: For the 787, what minimum prepared surface width must contaminated runway preparation leave for takeoffs and landings to be allowed?
docs.x: For the 787, what minimum prepared surface width must contaminated runway preparation leave for takeoffs and landings to be allowed? No less than 45 m (148 ft). FOM 9.2.1 — Takeoff and Landing Prohibited 787 45 m 148 ft Takeoffs and landings are prohibited if contaminated runway preparation leaves an available prepared surface width less than the 787 figure of 45 m (148 ft).

docs.t: At what contaminant depths, and at what contaminated-runway tailwind, are takeoffs prohibited?
docs.x: At what contaminant depths, and at what contaminated-runway tailwind, are takeoffs prohibited? When contaminant depth is greater than 1/2 inch for wet snow, slush, or water, or greater than 4 inches for dry snow; and when the steady-state tailwind component exceeds 10 kts on a contaminated runway. FOM 9.2.1 — Takeoff and Landing Prohibited Contaminant depth is greater than 1/2 inch for wet snow, slush, or water or greater than 4 inches for dry snow. A steady-state tailwind component exceeding 10 kts on a contaminated runway also prohibits takeoff.

docs.t: At what steady-state wind velocity are takeoffs and landings prohibited?
docs.x: At what steady-state wind velocity are takeoffs and landings prohibited? When steady-state wind velocity is greater than 50 kts. FOM 9.2.1 — Takeoff and Landing Prohibited Steady-state wind velocity is greater than 50 kts. Takeoffs and landings are also prohibited when braking action is NIL or the RWYCC is 0 on any portion of the runway, and with moderate or greater freezing rain.

docs.t: In heavy snow, what anti-ice fluid and timing are required for takeoff?
docs.x: In heavy snow, what anti-ice fluid and timing are required for takeoff? The aircraft must be anti-iced with undiluted Type IV fluid and a successful Contamination Check completed within 5 minutes of takeoff. FOM 9.2.2 — Heavy Snow successful Contamination Check has been completed within 5 minutes of takeoff Type IV is preferred; if not available, Type II may be used.

docs.t: When barometric pressure exceeds 31.00 inches of Hg, what altimeter setting is used for enroute operations below 18,000 ft MSL?
docs.x: When barometric pressure exceeds 31.00 inches of Hg, what altimeter setting is used for enroute operations below 18,000 ft MSL? Set 31.00 and maintain it until beyond the affected area or reaching the final approach segment; on departure/missed approach set 31.00 prior to a mandatory/crossing altitude or 1500 ft AGL, whichever is lower. FOM 9.2.3 — High Barometric Pressure Set 31.00 for enroute operations below 18,000 ft MSL. Airports unable to accurately measure pressures above 31.00 inHg report 'in excess of 31.00 inches of Hg,' and operations there are limited to VFR weather conditions.

docs.t: How is Moderate airframe icing described, and what action does it require?
docs.x: How is Moderate airframe icing described, and what action does it require? The rate of accumulation is such that even short encounters become potentially hazardous; use of deicing/anti-icing equipment or flight diversion is necessary. FOM 9.3.2.2 — Airframe Icing Intensity even short encounters become potentially hazardous With Severe icing, deicing/anti-icing fails to control the hazard and immediate flight diversion is necessary. Trace and Light become a concern chiefly over 1 hour.

docs.t: How fast does fuel temperature typically move toward TAT, and how fast in extreme conditions?
docs.x: How fast does fuel temperature typically move toward TAT, and how fast in extreme conditions? Approximately 3 degrees C per hour typically, but as high as 12 degrees C per hour in extreme conditions. FOM 9.3.2.3 — Fuel Freeze Considerations at a rate of approximately 3°C per hour but can be as high as 12°C per hour in extreme conditions To warm fuel, a 4000 ft descent below the tropopause yields about a 7 C TAT increase, and an increase of M 0.01 produces about a 0.7 C TAT increase; in severe cases descent as low as 25,000 ft may be needed.

docs.t: When temperature is colder than ISA, how does true altitude compare to indicated altitude?
docs.x: When temperature is colder than ISA, how does true altitude compare to indicated altitude? True altitude is lower than indicated altitude. FOM 9.3.3.1 — Cold Temperature Altimeter Corrections true altitude is lower than indicated altitude This effect becomes extremely important with very cold temperatures and minimum terrain separation; US charts note in the briefing strip when cold temperature corrections apply.

docs.t: What is the policy on intentionally operating through validated severe or extreme turbulence?
docs.x: What is the policy on intentionally operating through validated severe or extreme turbulence? Under no circumstances will a flight be operated intentionally through areas of validated severe or extreme turbulence. FOM 9.4.1 — Turbulence Avoidance Policy Under no circumstances, will a flight be operated intentionally through areas of validated severe or extreme turbulence. Avoidance of departure/arrival routings is not required for moderate clear air turbulence at climb/descent altitudes; it is safer to transit those altitudes as rapidly as practical with cabin precautions.

docs.t: By how much must a thunderstorm identified as severe or giving an intense radar echo be avoided, and how must cloud tops be cleared?
docs.x: By how much must a thunderstorm identified as severe or giving an intense radar echo be avoided, and how must cloud tops be cleared? Avoid by at least 20 miles. When in the clear on top, clear cloud tops by 5000 ft; if clearing by less than 5000 ft, avoid the thunderstorm by 20 nm. FOM 9.5.5 — Thunderstorm Avoidance Avoid by at least 20 miles any thunderstorm identified as severe or giving an intense radar echo. Also avoid flying under a cumulonimbus overhang; if unavoidable, use antenna up tilt to locate and avoid hail.

docs.t: What restriction applies below 1000 ft AGL when ATC has reported a Microburst Alert, and how long do windshear/microburst advisories remain in effect?
docs.x: What restriction applies below 1000 ft AGL when ATC has reported a Microburst Alert, and how long do windshear/microburst advisories remain in effect? Do not take off or continue an approach below 1000 ft AGL to that runway. Windshear and microburst advisories remain in effect for 20 minutes after the alert is issued. FOM 9.5.6 — Windshear Do not take off or continue approach below 1000 ft AGL to a runway where ATC has reported a Microburst Alert. Takeoffs and landings are permitted with windshear or microburst advisories in effect, but the crew should exercise caution.

docs.t: How close may a flight operate to a volcano where an eruption is imminent or underway, and above what latitude are flights not dispatched with solar radiation S3 or higher?
docs.x: How close may a flight operate to a volcano where an eruption is imminent or underway, and above what latitude are flights not dispatched with solar radiation S3 or higher? Not within 10 nm of a volcano with an imminent or underway eruption when significant ash emission is likely; and Alaska will not dispatch flights at latitudes above 78 degrees N with solar radiation S3 or higher. FOM 9.6.1 — Operational Policies Flights will not operate within 10 nm of a volcano where an eruption is imminent or underway Per 9.7.5, radiation is a significant concern at high latitudes; the 78°N / S3 dispatch limit is a hard cutoff. A significant space weather event is R3, S3, or G4 or greater.

docs.t: Check-airman scenario: You're departing on a runway with a FICON of 3/3/3, packed snow — a hard-packed contaminant. The FMC still offers an assumed-temperature (FLEX) takeoff and your FO reaches for it. What thrust setting is legal here, and why does contaminant type drive your data selection?
docs.x: Check-airman scenario: You're departing on a runway with a FICON of 3/3/3, packed snow — a hard-packed contaminant. The FMC still offers an assumed-temperature (FLEX) takeoff and your FO reaches for it. What thrust setting is legal here, and why does contaminant type drive your data selection? Reduced thrust using assumed temperature (AT/FLEX) is NOT authorized on a contaminated runway — stop your FO before they select it. Takeoff data selection is based on contaminant type: hard-packed is an accelerate-and-stop concern, while loose contaminant also requires concern for drag when continuing takeoff after an engine failure. Use the appropriate contaminated-runway data at full/rated thrust. FOM 9.1.8 — Takeoff Operations on a Wet/Contaminated Runway Reduced thrust using assumed temperature, labeled AT or FLEX, is not authorized on a contaminated runway. Takeoff data selection is based on the type of contaminant — hard-packed or loose. Hard-packed contaminant is an accelerate-and-stop concern, while loose contaminant also requires concern for drag when continuing takeoff after an engine failure.

docs.t: Check-airman scenario: Night approach into a mountainous field at -40°C, and the chart briefing strip flags cold-temperature corrections. A new FO on IOE asks whether the jet is really where the altimeter reads. What do you tell them about true versus indicated altitude, and when does the error bite hardest?
docs.x: Check-airman scenario: Night approach into a mountainous field at -40°C, and the chart briefing strip flags cold-temperature corrections. A new FO on IOE asks whether the jet is really where the altimeter reads. What do you tell them about true versus indicated altitude, and when does the error bite hardest? When temperature is colder than ISA, true altitude is LOWER than indicated altitude — the airplane is physically lower than the altimeter shows. The effect becomes extremely important with very cold temperatures and minimum terrain separation, which is exactly why US instrument approach charts flag the correction in the briefing strip. Apply the published cold-temperature altitude corrections. FOM 9.3.3.1 — Cold Temperature Altimeter Corrections When the temperature is lower than International Standard Atmosphere (ISA), true altitude is lower than indicated altitude. This temperature effect on indicated altitude becomes extremely important with very cold temperatures and minimum terrain separation; within the US, instrument approach charts contain a note in the briefing strip when cold temperature corrections are to be applied.

docs.t: Check-airman scenario: Cruising at night you paint a cell giving an intense radar echo about 15 miles off the nose. You're tempted to press on and overfly it in the clear on top. What lateral and vertical clearances does the FOM require, and is 15 miles enough?
docs.x: Check-airman scenario: Cruising at night you paint a cell giving an intense radar echo about 15 miles off the nose. You're tempted to press on and overfly it in the clear on top. What lateral and vertical clearances does the FOM require, and is 15 miles enough? Avoid by at least 20 miles any thunderstorm identified as severe or giving an intense radar echo — 15 miles is inside the limit, so deviate. When 'in the clear' on top, cloud tops should be cleared by 5000 ft; if you can only clear the tops by less than 5000 ft, you must avoid the storm by 20 nm. Also avoid flying under a cumulonimbus overhang. FOM 9.5.5 — Thunderstorm Avoidance Avoid by at least 20 miles any thunderstorm identified as severe or giving an intense radar echo. When 'in the clear' on top, cloud tops should be cleared by 5000 ft. If clearing the cloud tops by less than 5000 ft, avoid the thunderstorm by 20 nm.

docs.t: Check-airman scenario: On short final at 900 ft AGL, the tower calls a Microburst Alert for your landing runway; the alert was issued 8 minutes ago. May you continue the approach, and how long does that advisory bind you?
docs.x: Check-airman scenario: On short final at 900 ft AGL, the tower calls a Microburst Alert for your landing runway; the alert was issued 8 minutes ago. May you continue the approach, and how long does that advisory bind you? No — do not continue an approach below 1000 ft AGL to a runway where ATC has reported a Microburst Alert. At 900 ft AGL you are already below the gate, so go around. Windshear and microburst advisories remain in effect for 20 minutes after issuance, so an 8-minute-old alert is still active; hold, wait it out, or divert. FOM 9.5.6 — Windshear Do not take off or continue approach below 1000 ft AGL to a runway where ATC has reported a Microburst Alert. Windshear and microburst advisories remain in effect for 20 minutes after the alert has been issued. Takeoffs and landings are permitted with windshear or microburst advisories in effect; however, the Flight Crew should exercise caution.

docs.t: Where is CRM placed in Alaska Airlines' CRM/TEM model, and what does that placement signify?
docs.x: Where is CRM placed in Alaska Airlines' CRM/TEM model, and what does that placement signify? CRM is intentionally placed at the bottom of the model to signify that CRM is the foundation of TEM. FOM 10.1 — Alaska Airlines CRM and TEM CRM is intentionally placed at the bottom of the model to signify that CRM is the foundation of TEM The model is built with CRM underneath TEM. Effective TEM depends on the crew's underlying CRM skills.

docs.t: What are the four core CRM skills each Alaska Airlines pilot is expected to maintain and improve?
docs.x: What are the four core CRM skills each Alaska Airlines pilot is expected to maintain and improve? Communication, Workload Management, Leadership, and Flight Discipline. FOM 10.1 — Alaska Airlines CRM and TEM a set of core skills (Communication, Workload Management, Leadership, and Flight Discipline) These four core skills, plus supportive behaviors, are the framework every pilot is expected to refine over their career.

docs.t: Within the assertiveness ladder (Ask, Say, Command, Assume Control), when should a pilot Assume Control of the aircraft?
docs.x: Within the assertiveness ladder (Ask, Say, Command, Assume Control), when should a pilot Assume Control of the aircraft? As a last resort, when safety is at imminent risk due to PF confusion, incapacitation, or inaction. FOM 10.1.1.1 — Communication As a last resort, take control of the aircraft when safety is at imminent risk due to PF confusion, incapacitation, or inaction. Assume Control is the top rung of the Ask/Say/Command/Assume Control assertiveness ladder and is reserved for imminent risk.

docs.t: What should crew briefings include regarding threats?
docs.x: What should crew briefings include regarding threats? A review of relevant threats and management strategies to reduce the risk of those threats to the operation. FOM 10.1.1.1 — Communication Briefings should include a review of relevant threats and management strategies to reduce the risk of those threats to the operation. Briefings should also include specific PM duties when appropriate, and are conducted to the level of detail appropriate to the circumstances.

docs.t: Under Prioritize Tasks in Workload Management, what is the first priority?
docs.x: Under Prioritize Tasks in Workload Management, what is the first priority? Fly the aircraft first; when the aircraft is stable and safe, navigate while properly analyzing the situation. FOM 10.1.1.2 — Workload Management Fly the aircraft first. Operational tasks are prioritized by risk/criticality to safety of flight, with high-priority tasks accomplished first.

docs.t: How does the FOM direct use of the autopilot in areas of high-density traffic?
docs.x: How does the FOM direct use of the autopilot in areas of high-density traffic? Use the autopilot as much as practical during operations in areas of high-density traffic. FOM 10.1.1.2 — Workload Management Use the autopilot as much as practical during operations in areas of high-density traffic. Automation should be used to prevent excessive workload, and disengaged when it excessively increases workload or reduces situational awareness.

docs.t: Under Address Conflicts, what three forms may a resolution take?
docs.x: Under Address Conflicts, what three forms may a resolution take? Command ("my way"), collaborate ("our way"), or accommodate ("your way"). FOM 10.1.1.3 — Leadership Command Resolutions may consist of command ("my way"), collaborate ("our way"), or accommodate ("your way") Crews should focus on what is right, not who is right; operational conflicts are resolved as they arise while interpersonal conflicts are resolved as time permits.

docs.t: Under Flight Discipline, what verbal tool does the PM use to restore degraded situational awareness or safety margins?
docs.x: Under Flight Discipline, what verbal tool does the PM use to restore degraded situational awareness or safety margins? "Ask, Say, Command" as applicable. FOM 10.1.1.4 — Flight Discipline Uses "Ask, Say, Command" as applicable to restore degraded situational awareness and/or safety margins. The PM is primarily responsible for monitoring the aircraft's flight path and assessing/communicating threats within a shared mental model.

docs.t: Into what two categories are threats divided in Alaska's TEM model, and what are examples of each?
docs.x: Into what two categories are threats divided in Alaska's TEM model, and what are examples of each? Environmental threats (outside the airline's direct control, such as weather, ATC, and Terrain) and airline threats (originating within flight operations, such as system malfunctions, scheduling, and ground problems). FOM 10.1.2.1 — Definitions environmental threats, which are outside the airline's direct control, such as weather, ATC, and Terrain, and airline threats Threats are events, errors, or circumstances that increase operational complexity and require crew attention if safety margins are to be maintained.

docs.t: Into what three types can Flight Crew errors be divided?
docs.x: Into what three types can Flight Crew errors be divided? Aircraft handling, procedural, and communication errors. FOM 10.1.2.1 — Definitions Flight Crew errors can be divided into three types: aircraft handling, procedural, and communication errors. Errors are crew actions or inactions that deviate from intentions/expectations and reduce safety margins; they may be a slip/lapse or induced by a threat.

docs.t: How is an Undesired Aircraft State (UAS) defined?
docs.x: How is an Undesired Aircraft State (UAS) defined? A position, speed, attitude, or configuration of an aircraft that clearly reduces safety margins resulting from Flight Crew error, actions, or inaction. FOM 10.1.2.1 — Definitions a position, speed, attitude, or configuration of an aircraft that clearly reduces safety margins A UAS is a safety-compromising state resulting from ineffective error management; examples include unstable approaches and improper configuration.

docs.t: In the Prevent/Trap/Mitigate framework, what is described as the best resource for preventing threats from becoming errors?
docs.x: In the Prevent/Trap/Mitigate framework, what is described as the best resource for preventing threats from becoming errors? A threat-based briefing/TPC. FOM 10.1.2.1 — Definitions A threat-based briefing/TPC is the best resource for preventing threats from becoming errors. Trapping uses resources like checklists and SOPs; mitigating uses timely resources such as a PM with assertive communication skills once a UAS exists.

docs.t: What three concepts sit at the top of the TEM model and yield successful threat and error management?
docs.x: What three concepts sit at the top of the TEM model and yield successful threat and error management? Anticipate, Recognize, and Recover. FOM 10.1.2.2 — Threat and Error Management Philosophy three concepts that yield successful threat and error management: Anticipate, Recognize, and Recover These are crewmember habits and skills that must be employed to effectively manage threats and errors.

docs.t: Anticipation is described as a two-step process. What are the two steps?
docs.x: Anticipation is described as a two-step process. What are the two steps? (1) Identify relevant threats, and (2) develop management strategies for each using various resources. FOM 10.1.2.3 — Anticipate/Recognize/Recover It is essentially a two-step process: (1) identify relevant threats and (2) develop management strategies for each The PF develops, communicates, and executes the plan; the PM aids by identifying/managing threats and maintaining a shared mental model.

docs.t: In the Recognize phase, what should the PM do if they observe a new threat or error the PF does not respond to?
docs.x: In the Recognize phase, what should the PM do if they observe a new threat or error the PF does not respond to? Communicate in a clear, concise, and effective manner what they observed — the "See it, Say it" principle (e.g., PM: "You're 10 knots fast" or "SPEED;" PF: "Correcting"). FOM 10.1.2.3 — Anticipate/Recognize/Recover communicate in a clear, concise, and effective manner what they have observed (i.e., "See it, Say it") Communicating this way obligates the PF to respond, improving situational awareness and regaining an adequate margin of safety.

docs.t: SCENARIO — TEM in action: You are briefing an approach into a station where LLWS (low-level windshear) advisories are in effect. Per the Prevent stage of the TEM model, what is your single best resource, and what should the briefing cover?
docs.x: SCENARIO — TEM in action: You are briefing an approach into a station where LLWS (low-level windshear) advisories are in effect. Per the Prevent stage of the TEM model, what is your single best resource, and what should the briefing cover? A threat-based briefing/TPC is the best resource for preventing threats from becoming errors. With LLWS advisories active, the briefing should review the resources that will keep that threat from progressing into an error or UAS — for example, delay, change runways, adjust speeds, monitor radar, and review windshear procedures. FOM 10.1.2.1 — Definitions (Prevent) A threat-based briefing/TPC is the best resource for preventing threats from becoming errors. For example, if LLWS advisories are in effect, the briefing should review resources that will be used to prevent that threat from progressing into an error or UAS (e.g., delay, change runways, adjust speeds, monitor radar, review windshear procedures). Prevent is the first stage of the Prevent/Trap/Mitigate progression: applying appropriate resources to relevant threats is the most effective way to keep a threat from progressing through the model.

docs.t: SCENARIO — Assertive callout to a senior captain: You are the PM flying with a check airman on the glideslope. The approach is deteriorating and you feel yourself wanting to soften the call because of the captain's seniority. What does the FOM require of your speech in this high-risk moment?
docs.x: SCENARIO — Assertive callout to a senior captain: You are the PM flying with a check airman on the glideslope. The approach is deteriorating and you feel yourself wanting to soften the call because of the captain's seniority. What does the FOM require of your speech in this high-risk moment? Do not mitigate your speech. It is imperative that pilots do not lessen or downplay the importance of a callout in high-risk situations — say it clearly and with the urgency the situation demands, regardless of the other pilot's seniority. FOM 10.1.2.3 — Anticipate/Recognize/Recover (CAUTION) It is imperative that pilots do not mitigate their speech (lessen or downplay the importance) in high-risk situations. This CAUTION reinforces the assertiveness ladder and the "See it, Say it" principle; seniority does not reduce the PM's obligation to speak up assertively.

docs.t: SCENARIO — Recover, last resort: On approach the aircraft reaches full-scale glideslope deflection. You command "Go around" and the PF does not react. What is the FOM's last-resort action, and what is the exact control-transfer exchange?
docs.x: SCENARIO — Recover, last resort: On approach the aircraft reaches full-scale glideslope deflection. You command "Go around" and the PF does not react. What is the FOM's last-resort action, and what is the exact control-transfer exchange? As a last resort, the PM must assume aircraft control to restore safety margins. The exchange is PM: "I have control, going around." PF: "You have control." FOM 10.1.2.3 — Anticipate/Recognize/Recover (Recovery) As a last resort, the PM must assume aircraft control to restore safety margins. (e.g., PM: "I have control, going around." PF: "You have control.") This is the top rung of the assertiveness ladder (Assume Control) meeting the top of the TEM model (Recover); it follows an unheeded one- or two-word corrective command.

docs.t: On a two-way radio failure, what transponder code do you select?
docs.x: On a two-way radio failure, what transponder code do you select? Change the transponder to code 7600. FOM 11.1.4 — Lost Communications – Two-Way Radio Failure If two-way radio failure occurs, change transponder code to 7600. If the failure is in or later meets VFR conditions, continue VFR and land as soon as practicable; if in IFR, fly the Route/Altitude/Leave-Clearance-Limit rules of 14 CFR 91.185.

docs.t: If you lose two-way radio and must enter the US ADIZ, what do you do and what code do you squawk?
docs.x: If you lose two-way radio and must enter the US ADIZ, what do you do and what code do you squawk? Use emergency authority and enter the ADIZ as close to the Flight Plan crossing position and time as possible, squawking 7700; then follow standard comm-failure procedures. FOM 11.1.4.1 — Entering ADIZ without Radio Contact use emergency authority and enter the ADIZ as close to the Flight Plan crossing position and time as possible with transponder code 7700 Note the distinction: 7600 for the comm failure itself, but 7700 specifically to enter the ADIZ under emergency authority.

docs.t: What temperature threshold makes an ill traveler a reportable communicable-disease case?
docs.x: What temperature threshold makes an ill traveler a reportable communicable-disease case? A temperature of 100 degrees F (38 degrees C) or greater that has persisted more than 48 hours (or fever with certain other symptoms, or diarrhea). FOM 11.1.8.2 — Communicable Diseases has a temperature of 100°F (38°C) or greater which has persisted more than 48 hours Contact MedLink and ensure Dispatch is notified; if the CDC quarantines the aircraft they may direct you to one of the 20 stations on the listed map.

docs.t: Post-decompression, if oxygen needs exceed available masks or quantity, what descent target relieves adverse physiological reactions?
docs.x: Post-decompression, if oxygen needs exceed available masks or quantity, what descent target relieves adverse physiological reactions? After terrain and fuel considerations, a descent to 8000 ft cabin altitude should eliminate adverse physiological reactions. FOM 11.1.8.4 — Portable Oxygen Bottles (POB) a descent to 8000 ft cabin altitude, after terrain and fuel considerations are addressed, should eliminate any adverse physiological reactions Enroute use or depletion of a POB imposes no restriction on flight operations and requires no pilot action.

docs.t: What is the MedLink Inflight Medical Assistance phone number?
docs.x: What is the MedLink Inflight Medical Assistance phone number? (602) 282-4910. Ground Medical Assistance is (602) 282-6613 or (800) 961-4847. FOM 11.1.9.3 — Responsibility for Contacting MedLink MedLink Inflight Medical Assistance may be reached at (602) 282-4910 On the 787, when the Flight Crew calls MedLink they conference in the F/As with the cabin headset.

docs.t: After extinguishing a lithium battery fire, why must you cool the device and how long can it take?
docs.x: After extinguishing a lithium battery fire, why must you cool the device and how long can it take? HALON extinguishes the fire but the device must then be cooled, preferably with water; it may take 15 or more minutes to fully cool. Avoid ice, which insulates and can let remaining cells reignite. FOM 11.1.10 — Lithium Battery Fire It may take 15 or more minutes to completely cool the device. AVOID USING ICE to cool the device; ice acts as an insulator, and an insulated but not-yet-cooled device can reignite.

docs.t: Can water be used on a lithium battery fire?
docs.x: Can water be used on a lithium battery fire? Water may be used to fight a lithium ion battery fire, but should not be used on a lithium metal battery fire. Cool with water preferably, or any non-alcoholic liquid if water is not available. FOM 11.1.10 — Lithium Battery Fire Water may be used to fight a lithium ion battery fire, but should not be used on a lithium metal battery fire. FIGHT THE FIRE with a HALON extinguisher, then COOL THE DEVICE; non-alcoholic liquids such as milk, fruit juice, or POG are acceptable coolants.

docs.t: What does emergency authority allow the Captain to do in a situation requiring immediate decision and action?
docs.x: What does emergency authority allow the Captain to do in a situation requiring immediate decision and action? Take any action considered necessary, including deviating from prescribed procedures, methods, weather minimums, and regulations to the extent required in the interest of safety. FOM 11.2.1 — Emergency Authority the Captain may take any action considered necessary, including deviating from prescribed procedures, methods, weather minimums, and regulations to the extent required in the interest of safety Emergency authority is granted to both the Captain and the Dispatcher; FOM 11.2.1 cites 14 CFR 91.3, 121.557, 121.559, 121.627, and Ops Spec A008.

docs.t: Must you declare an emergency with ATC to use emergency authority?
docs.x: Must you declare an emergency with ATC to use emergency authority? No. The Captain may use emergency authority without declaring an emergency if traffic or handling priority is not needed, but should still advise ATC of intentions as soon as possible. FOM 11.2.1 — Emergency Authority The Captain may use emergency authority without declaring an emergency with ATC if traffic or handling priority is not needed. The FOM adds: do not hesitate to declare an emergency if the situation warrants it.

docs.t: Name situations the FOM says pilots will consider an emergency.
docs.x: Name situations the FOM says pilots will consider an emergency. Fire or smoke endangering the aircraft; inability to definitely establish position; failure of a component jeopardizing safety of flight; an in-flight medical condition requiring a diversion; and a high probability of an emergency evacuation. FOM 11.2.2 — Declaring an Emergency An in-flight medical condition that requires a diversion Immediately advise ATC and Dispatch; if workload is high or time short, ask ATC to notify the Company.

docs.t: When should MAYDAY be used versus PAN-PAN?
docs.x: When should MAYDAY be used versus PAN-PAN? MAYDAY (said three times) is the distress signal reserved for life-threatening situations; PAN-PAN (said three times) is the urgency signal for urgent situations that are not immediately life-threatening but require assistance. FOM 11.2.2.1 — Distress and Urgency Communication Signals Mayday should be reserved for life-threatening situations. Pan-Pan is for urgent situations that are not immediately life-threatening but require assistance from someone on the ground.

docs.t: What information belongs in an emergency message, and what is the Alaska HAZMAT emergency contact number?
docs.x: What information belongs in an emergency message, and what is the Alaska HAZMAT emergency contact number? Nature of emergency; number of passengers/crew and infants; passengers needing special assistance and their location; the HAZMAT emergency contact number if hazardous cargo is aboard (AS: 206-392-6465); and fuel remaining in minutes. FOM 11.2.2.3 — Emergency Message If there is hazardous cargo on board, relay the HAZMAT emergency contact number: The (AS) HAZMAT number is 206-392-6465; report fuel remaining in minutes.

docs.t: After exercising emergency authority that deviates from FARs or company procedures, by when must a Captain file the safety report?
docs.x: After exercising emergency authority that deviates from FARs or company procedures, by when must a Captain file the safety report? As soon as possible, but no later than the conclusion of the next mandatory 24-hour rest period. A Dispatcher who exercises emergency authority must report within 10 days. FOM 11.2.3 — Emergency Authority – Reporting no later than the conclusion of the next mandatory 24-hour rest period If the FAA later requests a written report and the crewmember fails to submit one, they may face punitive action including certificate action.

docs.t: Is a minimum fuel advisory an emergency, and when should it be declared?
docs.x: Is a minimum fuel advisory an emergency, and when should it be declared? No, minimum fuel is not an emergency and does not imply a need for traffic priority; it should only be declared once the flight has committed to land at a specific airport, not while a divert option still exists. FOM 11.2.5 — Minimum Fuel Minimum fuel is not an emergency situation, but merely indicates an emergency situation is possible should any undue delay occur. Coordinate any divert decision with Dispatch before declaring; avoid ending up at an alternate with less than 30 minutes of fuel.

docs.t: What must the PIC declare when landing will occur with less than a 30-minute fuel supply, and how is that 30 minutes defined?
docs.x: What must the PIC declare when landing will occur with less than a 30-minute fuel supply, and how is that 30 minutes defined? Declare MAYDAY, MAYDAY, MAYDAY, FUEL to ensure priority handling. The 30-minute supply is based on holding fuel flow or higher at 1500 ft above field elevation, and 30 minutes is a minimum the PIC may increase. FOM 11.2.6 — Emergency Fuel the PIC shall declare, “MAYDAY, MAYDAY, MAYDAY, FUEL” to ensure priority handling The PIC must take every precaution to avoid landing with less than a 30-minute supply, based on holding fuel flow at 1500 ft above field elevation.

docs.t: On a two-engine aircraft flying with one engine inoperative, what factors justify flying beyond the nearest suitable airport?
docs.x: On a two-engine aircraft flying with one engine inoperative, what factors justify flying beyond the nearest suitable airport? None. Sufficient fuel to fly farther, passenger accommodation other than safety, and availability of maintenance/repair are all specifically not sufficient justification to pass the nearest suitable airport. FOM 11.2.7.1 — Nearest Suitable Airport none of the following factors should be considered sufficient justification to fly beyond the nearest suitable airport After an in-flight engine shutdown, land at the nearest suitable airport based on time considerations where a safe landing can be made (FOM 11.2.7).

docs.t: How quickly are quick-don oxygen masks designed to be donned in an emergency descent?
docs.x: How quickly are quick-don oxygen masks designed to be donned in an emergency descent? With one hand within 5 seconds, because flight crews have very limited time of useful consciousness at altitude. FOM 11.2.8 — Emergency Descent Quick-don masks are designed to be donned with one hand within 5 seconds. An emergency descent may be driven by loss of pressurization or other events such as fire or a cabin security incident.

docs.t: For a 787 decompression over charted terrain polygons, how is the initial descent altitude determined?
docs.x: For a 787 decompression over charted terrain polygons, how is the initial descent altitude determined? From the polygon detail drawer in Jeppesen FD Pro. On the 787 the initial descent altitude is tied to the individual polygon, not to a region, and altitudes may vary between polygons because of the 787 passenger oxygen system design. (737/A330 is always 17,000 ft or FL170.) FOM 11.2.9 - Decompression Polygon Procedures (737/787/A330) (787) Refer to the detail drawer in Jeppesen FD Pro for the initial descent altitude(s) associated with each polygon. Rev 125.1 wording. Escape procedures come in three types (Exit Any Direction, Exit Toward Fix, To Fix then Route). Do not enter another polygon while navigating below the altitude in the detail drawer unless terrain clearance is assured.

docs.t: What is the NTSB flight attendant briefing format, and what drives whether it is a normal or emergency landing?
docs.x: What is the NTSB flight attendant briefing format, and what drives whether it is a normal or emergency landing? N - Nature of the emergency, T - Time to prepare, S - Special instructions, B - Brace signal. The type of landing is based on the likelihood of evacuation, not on what is declared with ATC. FOM 11.2.11 — Abnormal/Emergency Briefing of Flight Attendants – NTSB The type of landing should be based on the likelihood of evacuation and not what is declared with ATC. NORMAL LANDING means no evacuation prep required; EMERGENCY LANDING means evacuation is possible and the cabin should prepare.

docs.t: When may the Cabin Crew initiate an evacuation on their own, and what memory aid lists the triggers?
docs.x: When may the Cabin Crew initiate an evacuation on their own, and what memory aid lists the triggers? If life-threatening conditions require immediate evacuation and they cannot communicate with the Captain after trying all reasonable means. The FAST acronym lists triggers: Flight Deck incapacitated, Aircraft impacted/at a peculiar angle, Smoke and fire present, Threat of imminent danger. FOM 11.2.12.1 — Cabin Crew Initiated Evacuation Examples of Cabin Crew-initiated evacuation include (FAST acronym): Flight Attendants are separately authorized to initiate an evacuation without Captain orders in an obvious life-threatening situation (FOM 11.2.12).

docs.t: CHECK-AIRMAN SCENARIO: You've been holding for weather and it's now apparent you'll touch down with less than a 30-minute fuel supply. What exact call do you make, and how is that 30 minutes defined?
docs.x: CHECK-AIRMAN SCENARIO: You've been holding for weather and it's now apparent you'll touch down with less than a 30-minute fuel supply. What exact call do you make, and how is that 30 minutes defined? Declare "MAYDAY, MAYDAY, MAYDAY, FUEL" to ensure priority handling. The 30-minute supply is based on holding fuel flow or higher, as required by configuration, at 1500 ft above field elevation; 30 minutes is a minimum the PIC may increase for runway-availability and go-around contingencies. FOM 11.2.6 — Emergency Fuel When it becomes apparent that landing will occur with less than a 30-minute supply of fuel, the PIC shall declare, “MAYDAY, MAYDAY, MAYDAY, FUEL” to ensure priority handling. Do not confuse this with minimum fuel (11.2.5), which is not an emergency and grants no traffic priority.

docs.t: CHECK-AIRMAN SCENARIO: Rapid decompression at cruise over charted high-terrain polygons in your 787. Walk me through the masks, the descent target that relieves physiological reactions, and how you pick the initial descent altitude.
docs.x: CHECK-AIRMAN SCENARIO: Rapid decompression at cruise over charted high-terrain polygons in your 787. Walk me through the masks, the descent target that relieves physiological reactions, and how you pick the initial descent altitude. Don quick-don masks (one hand, within 5 seconds), execute the escape procedure for the polygon you are in, and descend to the initial descent altitude shown in that polygon's detail drawer in Jeppesen FD Pro. On the 787 that altitude varies by polygon. Do not enter another polygon below that altitude unless terrain clearance is assured. After terrain and fuel are addressed, a descent to 8000 ft cabin altitude should eliminate adverse physiological reactions. FOM 11.2.9 - Decompression Polygon Procedures (737/787/A330) Do not enter another polygon while navigating at less than the altitude indicated in the polygon detail drawer unless terrain clearance is assured. Rev 125.1. (787) altitudes vary by polygon per the FD Pro detail drawer. Quick-don masks are designed to be donned with one hand within 5 seconds (11.2.8).

docs.t: CHECK-AIRMAN SCENARIO: A passenger collapses two hours into an overwater leg. Who do you contact, who has final authority on whether to divert, and how does the 787 loop the flight attendants into the call?
docs.x: CHECK-AIRMAN SCENARIO: A passenger collapses two hours into an overwater leg. Who do you contact, who has final authority on whether to divert, and how does the 787 loop the flight attendants into the call? Contact MedLink Inflight Medical Assistance at (602) 282-4910; with MedLink's advice and Dispatch, the Captain determines whether a medical diversion is necessary and coordinates diversion-airport preferences. Company policy is to follow MedLink's recommendation, but the Captain retains final authority on any operational request. On the 787 the Flight Crew conferences in the F/As with the cabin headset. FOM 11.1.9.4 — Medical Diversion the Captain will determine whether a medical diversion is necessary and coordinate with Dispatch and MedLink for diversion airport preferences. MedLink Inflight Medical Assistance: (602) 282-4910. (787) The Flight Crew will conference in F/As with cabin headset (11.1.9.3).

docs.t: CHECK-AIRMAN SCENARIO: You shut an engine down in flight. A field 20 minutes closer has a shorter runway; your maintenance base is 90 minutes ahead with plenty of fuel to reach it. Where do you land, and does the extra fuel or the maintenance base justify pressing on?
docs.x: CHECK-AIRMAN SCENARIO: You shut an engine down in flight. A field 20 minutes closer has a shorter runway; your maintenance base is 90 minutes ahead with plenty of fuel to reach it. Where do you land, and does the extra fuel or the maintenance base justify pressing on? Land at the nearest suitable airport, based on time considerations, where a safe landing can be made. On a two-engine aircraft with one engine inoperative, neither sufficient fuel to fly farther, nor passenger accommodation other than safety, nor availability of maintenance/repair justifies flying beyond the nearest suitable airport. FOM 11.2.7 — Engine Shutdown in Flight If an engine fails or is shut down in flight, land the aircraft at the nearest suitable airport, based on time considerations, where a safe landing can be made. Per 11.2.7.1, none of these justify passing the nearest suitable airport: extra fuel, passenger accommodation other than safety, or maintenance/repair availability.

docs.t: Fueling with passengers boarding, on board, or deplaning at the gate is permitted only if certain cabin conditions are met. Name the required states of the Seat Belt Sign and the No Smoking Sign, and one other required condition.
docs.x: Fueling with passengers boarding, on board, or deplaning at the gate is permitted only if certain cabin conditions are met. Name the required states of the Seat Belt Sign and the No Smoking Sign, and one other required condition. The Seat Belt Sign is off and the No Smoking Sign is on. Other required conditions include: all engines shut down, aircraft chocked, a jetbridge/airstairs/boarding ramp at the door, the primary passenger entry door open, electrical power and lights on, and minimum Flight Attendants stationed near a continuously open floor-level exit. FOM 12.1.1.1 — At Gate Area Fueling/Defueling/Fuel transferring is permitted while passengers are boarding, remaining on board, or deplaning provided The full provided list also requires chocks, all engines shut down, a bridge/stairs/ramp at the door, primary door open, power and lights, Seat Belt Sign off, and No Smoking Sign on.

docs.t: During gate fueling with passengers on board, who is responsible for confirming fueling is complete, and at what point?
docs.x: During gate fueling with passengers on board, who is responsible for confirming fueling is complete, and at what point? The Captain verifies fueling is complete prior to door closure. FOM 12.1.1.1 — At Gate Area (Note) The Captain verifies fueling is complete prior to door closure. This is a Captain-specific verification captured in the Note under the at-gate fueling conditions.

docs.t: When fueling with passengers on board away from the gate area (no loading bridge or adequate stairs), what power source and door conditions are required?
docs.x: When fueling with passengers on board away from the gate area (no loading bridge or adequate stairs), what power source and door conditions are required? The APU or GPU must be available, all engines shut down, all doors armed, communications available with the fueler for the duration of fueling, and F/As stationed at their assigned exits keeping the slide deployment areas clear. FOM 12.1.1.2 — Away From Gate Area APU or GPU must be available. Communication with the fueler may be by radio, headset, or voice through the First Officer's window, and F/As must be notified when fueling begins and ends.

docs.t: Under what circumstance may an aircraft be fueled with one engine running, and what happens if fleet-specific procedures do not cover it?
docs.x: Under what circumstance may an aircraft be fueled with one engine running, and what happens if fleet-specific procedures do not cover it? Fueling with one engine running is only considered where a lack of APU, external power, or ground air would result in a stranded aircraft, per the FH/FCOM procedures. If procedures are not specified in fleet-specific manuals, fueling with one engine running is not authorized. FOM 12.1.1.3 — Fueling with One Engine Running If procedures are not specified in fleet-specific manuals, then fueling with one engine running is not authorized. Normally all engines are shut down during fueling; the single-engine-running case is an exception tied to avoiding a stranded aircraft.

docs.t: In a fuel spill with passengers on board, who decides whether to deplane, and on which side of the aircraft are passengers deplaned?
docs.x: In a fuel spill with passengers on board, who decides whether to deplane, and on which side of the aircraft are passengers deplaned? The Pilot-In-Command decides whether to deplane (if no pilot is on board, the 'A' Flight Attendant/FFA decides). If there is a choice of exits, passengers are deplaned on the side of the aircraft opposite the fuel spill. FOM 12.1.1.4 — Fuel Spills passengers will be deplaned on the side of the aircraft opposite the fuel spill. Any ground air conditioning unit should also be terminated to prevent pushing fumes into the aircraft and to remove an ignition source.

docs.t: If fueling is required from a non-Alaska Airlines approved fuel vendor, what must be done before fueling begins?
docs.x: If fueling is required from a non-Alaska Airlines approved fuel vendor, what must be done before fueling begins? Contact Maintenance Control before fueling begins; Maintenance Control provides the Captain with the required fuel acceptance procedures. FOM 12.1.2 — Fueling – Non-Approved Fuel Vendor contact Maintenance Control before fueling begins. The Captain does not self-clear a non-approved vendor; Maintenance Control supplies the acceptance procedures.

docs.t: Before operating the aircraft, what are the two acceptable states for every circuit breaker, and how is the 'normal position' identified visually?
docs.x: Before operating the aircraft, what are the two acceptable states for every circuit breaker, and how is the 'normal position' identified visually? Every circuit breaker shall be either in the normal position or properly pulled. In the normal position the CB is snapped into the closed position and the white stem is not visible. FOM 12.2.4 — Circuit Breaker (AS) The CB is snapped into the closed position. The white stem is not visible. Company-standard collars for pulled CBs are fluorescent yellow or red, though a different color collar does not affect airworthiness.

docs.t: During a maintenance engine run at the gate, what is the power limit and what flap configuration is required?
docs.x: During a maintenance engine run at the gate, what is the power limit and what flap configuration is required? Engines shall not be operated above idle power at a gate, and flaps shall remain retracted during the maintenance run. FOM 12.3.1 — Maintenance Engine Run at Gate (CAUTION) Engines shall not be operated above idle power at a gate. Flaps shall remain retracted during the maintenance run. Pilots are never authorized to conduct high power engine runs for maintenance, defined as any thrust setting above idle.

docs.t: May passengers be on board during a maintenance-run pressurization check, and is fueling permitted during engine runs with passengers aboard?
docs.x: May passengers be on board during a maintenance-run pressurization check, and is fueling permitted during engine runs with passengers aboard? No. Passengers shall not be on board during a pressurization check, and fueling operations during engine runs are prohibited with passengers on board, deplaning, or loading. FOM 12.3.1.1 — Passengers, F/As, and Doors – Passenger Aircraft (WARNING) Passengers shall not be on board during a pressurization check. Ramp activity should not be allowed behind an operating engine, and engine runs for an air contamination event or pressurization check are done without passengers/F/As on board.

docs.t: On the 787, what restriction applies to a #1 engine run relative to the boarding door and jetway?
docs.x: On the 787, what restriction applies to a #1 engine run relative to the boarding door and jetway? #1 engine runs are not permitted with the boarding door(s) open or the jetway extended to the boarding door(s). FOM 12.3.1.2 — Procedure and Safety Requirements – All aircraft #1 engine runs are not permitted with the boarding door(s) open or the jetway extended to the boarding door(s). On the 787, doors not used for boarding are also closed to minimize the FOD hazard, both pilots are at their stations, and the aircraft is chocked with the parking brake set.

docs.t: Are pilots ever authorized to conduct high power engine runs for maintenance, and how is 'high power' defined?
docs.x: Are pilots ever authorized to conduct high power engine runs for maintenance, and how is 'high power' defined? No. Pilots are not authorized to conduct high power engine runs for maintenance at any time. High power engine runs are defined as any engine thrust setting above idle. FOM 12.3.1.2 — Procedure and Safety Requirements – All aircraft (Note) High power engine runs are defined as any engine thrust setting above idle. At the completion of the maintenance idle engine run, the crew completes the Shutdown/Parking Checklist.

docs.t: With a yellow-side MSP-1 displayed on the power/thrust levers, may the aircraft be operated for flight, and what activities are still allowed?
docs.x: With a yellow-side MSP-1 displayed on the power/thrust levers, may the aircraft be operated for flight, and what activities are still allowed? No. With the yellow side displayed the aircraft may not be operated for the purpose of flight, but preflight may be performed (including normal Flight Deck flows and checklists, fueling, passenger boarding, etc.). Verbal permission from Maintenance in lieu of the logbook or yellow MSP-1 is not authorized. FOM 12.4.1.1 — Maintenance Status Placard (MSP-1) The aircraft may not be operated for the purpose of flight, but preflight may be performed The Flight Crew installs the MSP-1 yellow side out whenever there is an open discrepancy in the logbook.

docs.t: If the MSP-1 card is not installed and the logbook is not in the Flight Deck, how is the aircraft's status treated?
docs.x: If the MSP-1 card is not installed and the logbook is not in the Flight Deck, how is the aircraft's status treated? The aircraft status is treated as if the card were installed with the RED side up until the logbook is returned to the Flight Deck (i.e., systems/controls cannot be operated by non-Maintenance personnel). FOM 12.4.1.1 — Maintenance Status Placard (MSP-1) (Note) the aircraft status will be treated as if the card were installed with the RED side up until the logbook is returned to the Flight Deck. The red side warns that safety-sensitive maintenance is being performed and non-Maintenance personnel may not operate systems or controls.

docs.t: If an aircraft is designated Out of Service and the ACARS OTS message is received, what must occur before pushback even if the defect has been signed off?
docs.x: If an aircraft is designated Out of Service and the ACARS OTS message is received, what must occur before pushback even if the defect has been signed off? Dispatch must be contacted prior to pushback even if the defect resolution has been signed off and the aircraft has been released. FOM 12.4.3 — Aircraft Airworthiness If the ACARS OTS message is received, Dispatch must be contacted prior to pushback even if the defect resolution has been signed off and the aircraft has been released. The OTS designation auto-generates an ACARS message to the aircraft and Dispatch when the Load Closeout is sent.

docs.t: For the 787, a high-speed rejected takeoff requires a Maintenance Logbook entry above what speed, and what three items must be noted?
docs.x: For the 787, a high-speed rejected takeoff requires a Maintenance Logbook entry above what speed, and what three items must be noted? Above 80 kts. Note the gross weight, reject speed, and braking effort. FOM 12.4.6 — Maintenance Logbook – Required Entries (Boeing) 80 kts (note gross weight, reject speed, braking effort) This is one of many mandatory logbook entries, alongside limitation exceedances, hard/overweight landings, and returns for landing due to mechanical reasons.

docs.t: For an HA aircraft, on what time reference is the MEL valid period based, and may an aircraft depart with an MEL that will expire during the flight?
docs.x: For an HA aircraft, on what time reference is the MEL valid period based, and may an aircraft depart with an MEL that will expire during the flight? For HA, the MEL valid period is based on GMT, and an aircraft may not depart a station with an MEL whose time limit will expire during the planned duration of the flight. FOM 12.4.8.3 — MEL Expiration An aircraft may not depart a station with an MEL whose time limit will expire during the planned duration of the flight. By contrast, the AS valid period is based on Seattle local time and a flight may be dispatched if departure is within the valid period even if it ends outside it.

docs.t: For a non-ETOPS HA flight, how long is the Overnight Check valid in flight hours and in clock hours?
docs.x: For a non-ETOPS HA flight, how long is the Overnight Check valid in flight hours and in clock hours? The Overnight Check is valid for 25 flight hours in service and must not exceed 48 consecutive clock hours. A Post Flight Check does not reset the 48-hour Overnight Check requirement. FOM 12.4.12.2 — Airworthiness Release The Overnight Check is valid for 25 flight hours in service and must not exceed 48 consecutive clock hours. The PIC must verify the Airworthiness Release was signed off in the Aircraft Maintenance Logbook prior to each non-ETOPS flight or group of flights.

docs.t: May an aircraft depart with an open maintenance discrepancy in the logbook, and what entry must Maintenance make at major maintenance airports for open entries?
docs.x: May an aircraft depart with an open maintenance discrepancy in the logbook, and what entry must Maintenance make at major maintenance airports for open entries? No aircraft will be allowed to depart with an open maintenance discrepancy in the logbook. At major maintenance airports, Maintenance must make a balancing entry in the 'Action Taken' or 'Correction/Deferral' column for all open entries. FOM 12.4.12.6 — Maintenance Logbook Sign-Off No aircraft will be allowed to depart with an open maintenance discrepancy in the logbook. Under the Crew Placarding Procedure the MOC may direct the Flight Crew to complete the balancing entry to return the aircraft to service.

docs.t: CHECK-AIRMAN SCENARIO: You're the Captain at the gate, passengers boarding, fuel truck pumping. Your new First Officer, wanting to reduce cabin glare, reaches up and turns the No Smoking Sign OFF while leaving the Seat Belt Sign ON, and fueling continues. What is wrong, and what are the correct sign states plus the exit condition you must confirm?
docs.x: CHECK-AIRMAN SCENARIO: You're the Captain at the gate, passengers boarding, fuel truck pumping. Your new First Officer, wanting to reduce cabin glare, reaches up and turns the No Smoking Sign OFF while leaving the Seat Belt Sign ON, and fueling continues. What is wrong, and what are the correct sign states plus the exit condition you must confirm? The FO has both signs backwards. Fueling with passengers requires SONO: Seat Belt Sign OFF, No Smoking Sign ON. He must reverse both. You must also confirm chocks, all engines shut down, a bridge/stairs/ramp at the door, the primary door open, power and lights, and minimum Flight Attendants stationed near a floor-level exit that remains continuously open as the deplaning route. FOM 12.1.1.1 — At Gate Area Fueling/Defueling/Fuel transferring is permitted while passengers are boarding, remaining on board, or deplaning provided The provided list requires the Seat Belt Sign off and the No Smoking Sign on (SONO), plus chocks, all engines shut down, a bridge/stairs/ramp at the door, primary door open, power and lights, and an FA at a continuously open floor-level exit.

docs.t: CHECK-AIRMAN SCENARIO: Maintenance requests a #1 engine idle run at the gate to troubleshoot. The jetway is still extended to the forward boarding door, which is open with two agents aboard. May you start the #1 engine, and what must change first?
docs.x: CHECK-AIRMAN SCENARIO: Maintenance requests a #1 engine idle run at the gate to troubleshoot. The jetway is still extended to the forward boarding door, which is open with two agents aboard. May you start the #1 engine, and what must change first? No. On the 787, #1 engine runs are not permitted with the boarding door(s) open or the jetway extended to the boarding door(s). Retract the jetway and close that door first. Doors not used for boarding are closed to minimize FOD, both pilots must be at their stations, the aircraft chocked with parking brake set, and a dedicated Engine Safety Observer stationed at the side of the engine. FOM 12.3.1.2 — Procedure and Safety Requirements – All aircraft #1 engine runs are not permitted with the boarding door(s) open or the jetway extended to the boarding door(s). Doors not used for boarding are closed to minimize the FOD hazard; both pilots at their stations, aircraft chocked, parking brake set, dedicated Engine Safety Observer at the engine.

docs.t: CHECK-AIRMAN SCENARIO: At a remote station your APU is MEL'd inoperative, there is no ground power and no ground air, and you'll be stranded if you shut down. Ground crew asks if you can hot-fuel with the #2 engine running. Your 787 manuals publish no procedure for single-engine-running fueling. Are you authorized?
docs.x: CHECK-AIRMAN SCENARIO: At a remote station your APU is MEL'd inoperative, there is no ground power and no ground air, and you'll be stranded if you shut down. Ground crew asks if you can hot-fuel with the #2 engine running. Your 787 manuals publish no procedure for single-engine-running fueling. Are you authorized? No. Fueling with one engine running is only considered where a lack of APU, external power, or ground air would strand the aircraft, and only per the FH/FCOM procedure. Because your 787 fleet-specific manuals do not specify a procedure, fueling with one engine running is not authorized regardless of the stranding risk. FOM 12.1.1.3 — Fueling with One Engine Running If procedures are not specified in fleet-specific manuals, then fueling with one engine running is not authorized. Fueling with one engine running is only considered where a lack of APU, external power, or ground air will result in a stranded aircraft, per the FH/FCOM.

docs.t: CHECK-AIRMAN SCENARIO: After block-in at an outstation with no HA maintenance, you write up a discrepancy. Maintenance Control says the item is deferrable and directs you via ACARS to make a balancing entry to return the aircraft to service. The outbound Captain sees an open write-up with nothing in the 'Action Taken/Correction/Deferral' column. May the aircraft depart as-is, and who may direct the balancing entry?
docs.x: CHECK-AIRMAN SCENARIO: After block-in at an outstation with no HA maintenance, you write up a discrepancy. Maintenance Control says the item is deferrable and directs you via ACARS to make a balancing entry to return the aircraft to service. The outbound Captain sees an open write-up with nothing in the 'Action Taken/Correction/Deferral' column. May the aircraft depart as-is, and who may direct the balancing entry? No aircraft may depart with an open maintenance discrepancy in the logbook. At major maintenance airports Maintenance makes the balancing entry in the 'Action Taken' or 'Correction/Deferral' column for all open entries. When authorized under the Crew Placarding Procedure, the MOC may direct the Flight Crew to complete that column to return the aircraft to service. FOM 12.4.12.6 — Maintenance Logbook Sign-Off No aircraft will be allowed to depart with an open maintenance discrepancy in the logbook. At major maintenance airports Maintenance makes a balancing entry in the Action Taken or Correction/Deferral column; under the Crew Placarding Procedure the MOC may direct the Flight Crew to complete it.

docs.t: When must Flight Attendants verify the suitability of exit seat customers?
docs.x: When must Flight Attendants verify the suitability of exit seat customers? Prior to each door closure, to ensure each customer meets exit seat criteria. FOM 13.1 — Emergency Exit Row Seating must verify suitability of exit seat customers prior to each door closure Verification is repeated before every door closure, not just at initial boarding, so re-boarded or reseated passengers are re-checked.

docs.t: Who has final authority in determining suitability of exit seat occupants?
docs.x: Who has final authority in determining suitability of exit seat occupants? The Flight Attendants, in accordance with FAA regulations. FOM 13.1 — Emergency Exit Row Seating Flight Attendants have final authority in determining suitability criteria of exit seat occupants on board the aircraft A CRO may be consulted for an exit seat disability concern, but the FA retains final say on exit-seat suitability.

docs.t: If a CRO does not deny boarding, can the PIC still override that decision?
docs.x: If a CRO does not deny boarding, can the PIC still override that decision? Yes. The PIC has authority to override the CRO's decision based on a safety-of-flight concern. FOM 13.2.1 — Complaint Resolution Official (CRO) If a CRO does not deny boarding, the PIC has the authority to override the decision based on a safety-of-flight concern. The CRO manages ACAA compliance, but safety of flight keeps the PIC as the final decision-maker on carriage.

docs.t: When ACAA compliance conflicts with an FAA regulation, which takes precedence?
docs.x: When ACAA compliance conflicts with an FAA regulation, which takes precedence? FAA regulations take precedence. FOM 13.2.1 — Complaint Resolution Official (CRO) if ACAA compliance conflicts with FAA regulation, FAA regulations take precedence A CRO may waive Company policy to mitigate a disability, but cannot waive an FAA regulation.

docs.t: How does the FOM define a service animal?
docs.x: How does the FOM define a service animal? A dog, regardless of breed or type, that is individually trained to do work or perform tasks for the benefit of a qualified individual with a disability. FOM 13.3 — Unacceptable Service Animal Behavior A service animal is defined as a dog, regardless of breed or type, that is individually trained to do work or perform tasks The disability covered may be physical, sensory, psychiatric, intellectual, or other mental disability.

docs.t: After an in-flight unacceptable service animal incident, what should the Flight Crew relay?
docs.x: After an in-flight unacceptable service animal incident, what should the Flight Crew relay? Seat number, passenger name, a brief description of the incident, and a request that a CRO meet the aircraft. FOM 13.3.2 — After Departure Request that a CRO meet the aircraft At the gate the FAs instead consult a CRO before departure per 13.3.1; the four-item relay applies after departure.

docs.t: May spare lithium batteries be placed in checked baggage?
docs.x: May spare lithium batteries be placed in checked baggage? No. Spare lithium batteries may not be placed in checked baggage due to the potential fire hazard; they must go in carry-on baggage. FOM 13.4.1 — Lithium Batteries in PEDs Spare lithium batteries of any type, including external battery chargers containing a lithium-ion battery, may not be placed in checked baggage because of the potential fire hazard Checked baggage may only contain lithium batteries installed in a device; spares must be carried on with terminals covered/insulated.

docs.t: When may passengers use cell phone transmit (talk/text) features during a ground delay?
docs.x: When may passengers use cell phone transmit (talk/text) features during a ground delay? During a ground delay of 15 minutes or longer, with the Captain's permission. FOM 13.5 — Cell Phones – Passengers during a ground delay of 15 minutes or longer with the Captain's permission Transmit features are also allowed until door closure and while taxiing to the gate on arrival; the Captain may suspend use at any time if interference is suspected.

docs.t: Which mobility-device batteries may be carried and stowed in the passenger cabin?
docs.x: Which mobility-device batteries may be carried and stowed in the passenger cabin? Only lithium-ion batteries used to power mobility devices; all other mobility device batteries must be stowed in the cargo compartment. FOM 13.6 — Wheelchair/Mobility Device – Battery Powered Only lithium-ion batteries used to power mobility devices can be carried and stowed in the passenger cabin. A NOTOC is not required for these batteries; wet-cell (spillable) and gel/dry-cell batteries go in the cargo compartment.

docs.t: What will the Flight Deck Report state when a lithium-ion wheelchair battery is carried in the cabin?
docs.x: What will the Flight Deck Report state when a lithium-ion wheelchair battery is carried in the cabin? The Flight Deck Report will state "Lithium Battery Wheelchair," and the "A" FA/FFA notifies the Captain of the battery's location. FOM 13.6.1 — Lithium-Ion Battery the Flight Deck Report will state “Lithium Battery Wheelchair.” Wheelchairs with lithium-ion batteries that cannot be easily removed will not be transported; the removed battery rides in the cabin.

docs.t: Are Portable Oxygen Concentrators (POCs) considered HAZMAT?
docs.x: Are Portable Oxygen Concentrators (POCs) considered HAZMAT? No. Authorized POCs are not considered HAZMAT and may be carried in the cabin and used by passengers. FOM 13.7 — Portable Oxygen Concentrator (POC) POCs are not considered HAZMAT An authorized POC is on the FAA-approved list or bears a red-lettered label stating it meets FAA-acceptance criteria.

docs.t: How must filled oxygen bottles be transported, and what documents are required?
docs.x: How must filled oxygen bottles be transported, and what documents are required? In an approved container (superbox), shipped as HAZMAT; a NOTOC and the Emergency Response Guide (ERG) are required. FOM 13.8.1 — Oxygen Bottle Transportation filled oxygen bottles must be transported in an approved container (superbox) and are shipped as HAZMAT; therefore, a NOTOC and the Emergency Response Guide (ERG) are required Empty oxygen bottles are not HAZMAT and require no superbox or NOTOC; a DOT Special Permit allows filled bottles without a superbox within Alaska to remote communities.

docs.t: How does the crew handle a DNR request to withhold resuscitation on board?
docs.x: How does the crew handle a DNR request to withhold resuscitation on board? Cabin crews are obligated to perform resuscitation attempts; any request to withhold must be denied unless otherwise instructed by MedLink. FOM 13.9 — Do Not Resuscitate (DNR) Customers any request to withhold resuscitation attempts must be denied unless otherwise instructed by MedLink Alaska cannot validate a DNR order in flight, but will not refuse travel to a DNR customer if escort/other requirements are met.

docs.t: In an apparent death on board, until when is the individual presumed alive?
docs.x: In an apparent death on board, until when is the individual presumed alive? The individual is presumed alive until MedLink or a physician has determined that death has occurred. FOM 13.10 — Apparent Death on Board The individual is presumed to be alive until MedLink or a physician has determined that death has occurred. MedLink assumes liability for stopping CPR; radio communication to indicate a death occurred on board is inappropriate.

docs.t: Under the Fallen Soldier Program, how are the family and military escort boarded and deplaned?
docs.x: Under the Fallen Soldier Program, how are the family and military escort boarded and deplaned? "Last On" during boarding and "First Off" during deplaning; the military escort is seated in first class if available. FOM 13.14.2 — Boarding The family and military escort should be “Last On” during boarding and “First Off” during deplaning. The remains normally load into an aft pit; keep the Seat Belt Sign illuminated until after the escort and family have deplaned (13.14.3.2).

docs.t: SCENARIO: On a 787, a customer seated in the emergency exit row raises a disability concern moments before door closure. The gate agent already checked him in and a CRO, called to consult, believes the seat is fine. The lead Flight Attendant judges the customer cannot perform the exit functions. Who has the final say on whether he keeps that exit seat, and on what basis?
docs.x: SCENARIO: On a 787, a customer seated in the emergency exit row raises a disability concern moments before door closure. The gate agent already checked him in and a CRO, called to consult, believes the seat is fine. The lead Flight Attendant judges the customer cannot perform the exit functions. Who has the final say on whether he keeps that exit seat, and on what basis? The Flight Attendant.
