Per FOM 13.1, Flight Attendants have final authority in determining suitability of exit seat occupants on board the aircraft, in accordance with FAA regulations. A CRO may be called to consult on an exit-seat disability concern, but the FA decides the exit seat and must verify suitability prior to each door closure. FOM 13.1 — Emergency Exit Row Seating If an exit seat “disability concern” is expressed by a customer, a CRO may be called to consult with Flight Attendants on how to address the situation in accordance with the Air Carrier Access Act. Flight Attendants have final authority in determining suitability criteria of exit seat occupants on board the aircraft in accordance with FAA regulations. Verification is required prior to each door closure. If the customer is reseated after door closure and is continuing past the next stop on the same aircraft, the FAs must inform the pilots to notify the station.

docs.t: SCENARIO: Your 787 is airborne. A passenger's service animal — a dog — growls and lunges at other customers in the cabin, meeting the unacceptable-behavior criteria. There is no CRO on board. As Flight Crew, what four items should you relay so the situation is handled on arrival?
docs.x: SCENARIO: Your 787 is airborne. A passenger's service animal — a dog — growls and lunges at other customers in the cabin, meeting the unacceptable-behavior criteria. There is no CRO on board. As Flight Crew, what four items should you relay so the situation is handled on arrival? Relay the seat number, the passenger name, a brief description of the incident, and a request that a CRO meet the aircraft (FOM 13.3.2, After Departure). At the gate before departure the FAs instead consult a CRO per 13.3.1; the four-item relay is the after-departure procedure. FOM 13.3.2 — After Departure After an incident involving unacceptable service animal behavior, the Flight Crew should relay the following: Seat number; Passenger name; Brief description of the incident; Request that a CRO meet the aircraft. A service animal is defined in 13.3 as a dog, regardless of breed or type, individually trained to do work or perform tasks for a qualified individual with a disability.

docs.t: SCENARIO: Two oxygen items show up for the same 787 flight. A passenger wants to bring an authorized Portable Oxygen Concentrator (POC) into the cabin and use it in cruise; separately, Cargo presents a filled oxygen bottle for the hold. How is each handled, and what paperwork does the filled bottle require?
docs.x: SCENARIO: Two oxygen items show up for the same 787 flight. A passenger wants to bring an authorized Portable Oxygen Concentrator (POC) into the cabin and use it in cruise; separately, Cargo presents a filled oxygen bottle for the hold. How is each handled, and what paperwork does the filled bottle require? The authorized POC may be carried in the cabin and used by the passenger, and is NOT considered HAZMAT (FOM 13.7). The filled oxygen bottle must be transported in an approved container (superbox) and is shipped as HAZMAT, so a NOTOC and the Emergency Response Guide (ERG) are required (FOM 13.8.1). Empty bottles are not HAZMAT and need no superbox or NOTOC. FOM 13.7 — Portable Oxygen Concentrator (POC); 13.8.1 — Oxygen Bottle Transportation Authorized POCs may be carried in the cabin and used by passengers. ... POCs are not considered HAZMAT. ... filled oxygen bottles must be transported in an approved container (superbox) and are shipped as HAZMAT; therefore, a NOTOC and the Emergency Response Guide (ERG) are required. An authorized POC is on the FAA-approved list or bears a red-lettered label stating it meets FAA-acceptance criteria. A DOT Special Permit allows filled bottles without a superbox within Alaska to remote communities where ground or vessel transportation is unavailable.

docs.t: May hazardous materials be carried in the flight deck of an Alaska aircraft?
docs.x: May hazardous materials be carried in the flight deck of an Alaska aircraft? No. No hazardous materials may be carried in the flight deck of any aircraft, except excepted items required for operation (e.g., an installed fire extinguisher) or personal HAZMAT allowances. FOM 14.1.1 — Regulatory Compliance No hazardous materials may be carried in the Flight Deck of any aircraft. This does not apply to excepted items required for operation (e.g., installed fire extinguisher) or personal HAZMAT allowances. The prohibition is on the flight deck specifically; installed equipment and personal allowances are carved out.

docs.t: Under what FAA Ops Spec is Alaska Airlines authorized to carry hazardous materials?
docs.x: Under what FAA Ops Spec is Alaska Airlines authorized to carry hazardous materials? Ops Spec A055, Carriage of Hazardous Materials (HAZMAT), which certifies the company is authorized by the FAA to accept, handle, and carry HAZMAT. FOM 14.1.1 — Regulatory Compliance Alaska Airlines is issued FAA Ops Spec A055, Carriage of Hazardous Materials (HAZMAT). A055 is the operations specification underpinning all DG carriage; DG are handled per IATA DGR and 49 CFR.

docs.t: Does the PIC handle dangerous goods or carry civil/criminal liability for them?
docs.x: Does the PIC handle dangerous goods or carry civil/criminal liability for them? No. The PIC does not handle DG and does not have civil or criminal liability for DG. Acceptance is done by the DG Acceptance Agent via a thorough acceptance checklist. FOM 14.1.2 — Dangerous Goods – Acceptance, General Information, and Responsibilities The PIC does not handle DG and does not have civil or criminal liability for DG. The Acceptance Agent and a computerized database perform acceptance; the PIC's role is notification and awareness via the NOTOC.

docs.t: What does NOTOC stand for?
docs.x: What does NOTOC stand for? Notification to Captain. It is the form that prints the DG information the PIC needs to deal with any emergency. FOM 14.1.2 — Dangerous Goods – Acceptance, General Information, and Responsibilities printed on a form called a “NOTOC” which stands for Notification to Captain. DG regulations require the PIC receive a NOTOC so they have the information needed for emergencies; the Dispatcher also has access to a copy.

docs.t: How many NOTOC copies are printed for an AS flight, and what does the PIC do with them?
docs.x: How many NOTOC copies are printed for an AS flight, and what does the PIC do with them? Two copies are printed, one for Ops and one for the Captain. The Ramp Agent signs both; the PIC signs both, returns one to the RSA/Ramp Lead, and retains the other for the duration of the flight. FOM 14.1.3 — NOTOC Package (AS) Two copies of the NOTOC are printed, one for Ops and one for the Captain. The Ramp Agent must verify no damaged or leaking packages and sign before presenting the copies to the PIC.

docs.t: On HA, when is the eNOTOC sent to the flight crew relative to departure?
docs.x: On HA, when is the eNOTOC sent to the flight crew relative to departure? Departure time minus 30 minutes for trans-Pacific and international flights, and departure time minus 15 minutes for inter-island flights. FOM 14.1.4 — eNOTOC (HA) sent to the Flight Crew at departure time minus 30 minutes for trans-Pacific and international flights and at departure time minus 15 minutes for inter-island flights. The eNOTOC also prints automatically on all aircraft.

docs.t: When may the AS Captain sign the hard-copy NOTOC?
docs.x: When may the AS Captain sign the hard-copy NOTOC? Only after the Ramp Agent has signed it. The PIC signs both hard copies to acknowledge awareness of the DG listed. FOM 14.1.5 — Captain Responsibilities (AS) Signing both hard copies of the NOTOC (only after the Ramp Agent has signed it) to acknowledge awareness of the DG listed on the NOTOC. The Captain reviews the NOTOC for correct departure airport, flight number, and tail number; hand edits to tail number and DG location are allowed by the Ramp Lead.

docs.t: How does the HA Captain acknowledge the eNOTOC, and are hand edits allowed?
docs.x: How does the HA Captain acknowledge the eNOTOC, and are hand edits allowed? By selecting either ACCEPT* on the MCDU or ACKNOWLEDGE NOTOC on the Comm page, depending on fleet type. Hand edits are not permissible on HA. FOM 14.1.6 — Captain Responsibilities (HA) Acknowledging the eNOTOC by selecting either “ACCEPT*” on the MCDU or “ACKNOWLEDGE NOTOC” on the Comm page (depending on fleet type). Contrast with AS, where the Ramp Lead may hand-edit the tail number and DG location; on HA hand edits are not permissible.

docs.t: When is a hand-generated (written) NOTOC used on AS?
docs.x: When is a hand-generated (written) NOTOC used on AS? Only when any computer-generated NOTOC is not available, and only for time-critical DG shipments such as medical supplies or AOG parts. FOM 14.1.7 — NOTOC – Acceptable Versions (AS) used when any computer-generated NOTOC is not available and only for time-critical DG shipments such as medical supplies or AOG parts. The normal version is the FOGS NOTOC; the cargo management system NOTOC (hash-marked) is the computer-generated backup.

docs.t: For how many flights is a NOTOC valid on AS?
docs.x: For how many flights is a NOTOC valid on AS? One flight only. A new NOTOC is required for each flight segment, and also whenever a new DG shipment is added after the NOTOC package arrives at the aircraft. FOM 14.1.9 — New NOTOC Required (AS) Each flight segment (NOTOC valid for one flight only) Any new DG added after the package arrives also triggers a new NOTOC.

docs.t: What is the dry ice limit that does not require a NOTOC entry for a passenger, and does it change internationally?
docs.x: What is the dry ice limit that does not require a NOTOC entry for a passenger, and does it change internationally? Dry ice may not exceed 2.5 kg (5.5 pounds) per person on domestic flights only. International flights require a NOTOC. FOM 14.1.11 — NOTOC Entry Not Required Dry ice (carbon dioxide, solid) may not exceed 2.5 kg (5.5 pounds) per person (domestic flights only, international flights require a NOTOC) For cargo, the same 2.5 kg (5.5 lb) applies per package under UN1845, domestic only.

docs.t: Which UN numbers cover lithium-ion/lithium metal cells or batteries that (as small Section II batteries) do not require a NOTOC entry?
docs.x: Which UN numbers cover lithium-ion/lithium metal cells or batteries that (as small Section II batteries) do not require a NOTOC entry? UN3480/UN3481/UN3090/UN3091, lithium-ion or lithium metal cells or batteries meeting the provisions of Section II (small batteries and cells), coded ELI/ELM. FOM 14.1.11 — NOTOC Entry Not Required UN3480/UN3481/UN3090/UN3091, lithium-ion or lithium metal cells or batteries meeting the provisions of Section II (small batteries and cells) (ELI/ELM) These are the small-battery exceptions; larger lithium shipments still require a NOTOC.

docs.t: What crosscheck does the ACARS Load Closeout provide against the NOTOC on AS?
docs.x: What crosscheck does the ACARS Load Closeout provide against the NOTOC on AS? The number of items on the ACARS Load Closeout must equal the number of shipments listed on the NOTOC. It is a discrepancy crosscheck only; if none, the message reads 'No HAZMAT.' FOM 14.1.14 — Load Closeout Message (AS) The number of items on the ACARS Load Closeout must be equal to the number of shipments listed on the NOTOC The Load Closeout HAZMAT message is informational and not required for dispatch; contact Station Operations for any discrepancy.

docs.t: Whom does the AS PIC contact with concerns about a DG shipment, and when may the PIC reject it?
docs.x: Whom does the AS PIC contact with concerns about a DG shipment, and when may the PIC reject it? Contact Cargo Network Support at 1-877-815-8254, staffed 24/7. The PIC may reject if the shipment arrives too late to review and sign the NOTOC, or if concerns cannot be resolved with the RSA/Ramp Lead or Air Cargo personnel. FOM 14.1.16 — Dangerous Goods – Rejected Shipments (AS) contact Cargo Network Support at 1-877-815-8254. Cargo Network Support is staffed 24/7. Notify Operations with the reason for rejecting any DG, and time permitting notify the RSA/Ramp Lead.

docs.t: How often is the DOT ERG updated, and which Guide is used when nothing else is available?
docs.x: How often is the DOT ERG updated, and which Guide is used when nothing else is available? The DOT ERG is updated every four years. If no UN/ID number, Proper Shipping Name, or placard lookup is available, search Guide 111 and use that guidance until qualified help arrives. FOM 14.1.19 — DOT Emergency Response Guide (ERG) (AS) search “Guide 111” and use that Emergency Response Guide information until qualified help arrives on scene. The DOT ERG is updated every four years and lives on the EFB; the DOT ERG also carries first-aid info the ICAO ERG decode tables do not.

docs.t: What do the packing groups PG I, PG II, and PG III indicate?
docs.x: What do the packing groups PG I, PG II, and PG III indicate? Relative risk of a substance: PG I High, PG II Medium, PG III Low. FOM 14.1.21 — Dangerous Goods – Notifications and Required Items (AS) Relative risk (PG I High; PG II Medium; PG III Low) of a particular substance. Packing Group is one of the NOTOC data fields alongside Class/Division and Sub-Risk.

docs.t: On the NOTOC, when is Gross Weight (weight including packaging) used?
docs.x: On the NOTOC, when is Gross Weight (weight including packaging) used? Gross Weight is only used for Class 9 DG shipments. Otherwise the Quantity field shows Net Weight, excluding packaging. FOM 14.1.21 — Dangerous Goods – Notifications and Required Items (AS) Gross Weight— The total weight or quantity, in metric, of the DG product including packaging. Only used for Class 9 DG shipments. Net Weight excludes packaging; Transportation Index (TI) applies to Class 7 Radioactive instead of weight.

docs.t: How are the lower-compartment pit numbers arranged, and are they accessible in flight?
docs.x: How are the lower-compartment pit numbers arranged, and are they accessible in flight? Pits 1, 2, 3 are forward and 4, 5, 6 are aft. All DG shipments in the lower compartments on all aircraft are inaccessible in flight. FOM 14.1.21 — Dangerous Goods – Notifications and Required Items (AS) Pits 1, 2, 3 are fwd and 4, 5, 6 are aft. The NOTOC also notes all lower-compartment DG is inaccessible in flight; on the 787 eNOTOC, POS 11-23 = FWD and POS 32-53 = AFT.

docs.t: What HAZMAT emergency contact numbers may be given to ATC when declaring an emergency with HAZMAT on board?
docs.x: What HAZMAT emergency contact numbers may be given to ATC when declaring an emergency with HAZMAT on board? AS: Chief Dispatcher 888-526-4392 or 206-392-6465. HA: Dispatch 1-808-838-5566. Dispatch is responsible for notifying down-line ARFF. FOM 14.1.24 — HAZMAT Emergency Contact Number (AS) Chief Dispatcher 888-526-4392 or 206-392-6465 These numbers expedite HAZMAT information on type, location, and quantity to ATC and down-line ARFF.

docs.t: For a gate-checked wheelchair/mobility device battery, what PIC notification is required?
docs.x: For a gate-checked wheelchair/mobility device battery, what PIC notification is required? No NOTOC is required, but PIC verbal or SSR notification is required. There is no quantity or weight limit, and the battery is processed by the Gate/Ramp Agent. FOM 14.1.25 — Dangerous Goods – Exceptions and Variations No NOTOC required. PIC verbal or SSR notification required. Spillable batteries are removed and stored in a battery box; lithium-ion may be carried in the cabin if removable per 13.6.

docs.t: During an airborne DG spill/leak producing toxic fumes or smoke, what should the crew consider for protection?
docs.x: During an airborne DG spill/leak producing toxic fumes or smoke, what should the crew consider for protection? Consider supplemental oxygen or PBE use for all crewmembers, notify ATC and Dispatch, relay the HAZMAT emergency number (AS 206-392-6465 / HA 808-838-5566), and consider declaring an in-flight emergency. FOM 14.1.26 — Dangerous Goods – Damaged or Leaking (Airborne) consider supplemental oxygen or PBE use for all crewmembers. If the spill involves infectious substances, immediately notify the local public health authority.

docs.t: CHECK-AIRMAN SCENARIO: You are Captain on a 787. Your eNOTOC lists three DG shipments, but the ACARS Load Closeout shows four HAZMAT lines. What is this crosscheck telling you and what do you do?
docs.x: CHECK-AIRMAN SCENARIO: You are Captain on a 787. Your eNOTOC lists three DG shipments, but the ACARS Load Closeout shows four HAZMAT lines. What is this crosscheck telling you and what do you do? On AS the number of items on the ACARS Load Closeout must equal the number of shipments listed on the NOTOC. This is a discrepancy crosscheck only; a mismatch means you contact Station Operations to reconcile the load closeout HAZMAT section against the actual HAZMAT status before you rely on the NOTOC. Note the HAZMAT Load Closeout message is informational and not required for dispatch. FOM 14.1.14 — Load Closeout Message (AS) The number of items on the ACARS Load Closeout must be equal to the number of shipments listed on the NOTOC. This is a discrepancy crosscheck only. If no HAZMAT is on the flight the Load Closeout reads 'No HAZMAT'; contact Station Operations for any discrepancy.

docs.t: CHECK-AIRMAN SCENARIO: At the gate, a passenger's lithium-ion powered wheelchair is being checked at the jet bridge and no NOTOC prints. Does 'no NOTOC' mean nothing is required of you as PIC?
docs.x: CHECK-AIRMAN SCENARIO: At the gate, a passenger's lithium-ion powered wheelchair is being checked at the jet bridge and no NOTOC prints. Does 'no NOTOC' mean nothing is required of you as PIC? No. Gate-checked wheelchair/mobility device batteries require No NOTOC, but PIC verbal or SSR notification is still required. There is no quantity or weight limit and the device is processed by the Gate/Ramp Agent; a lithium-ion battery may be carried in the cabin if it can be removed and the 13.6 requirements are met. Do not let 'no NOTOC' become 'no notification.' FOM 14.1.25 — Dangerous Goods – Exceptions and Variations No NOTOC required. PIC verbal or SSR notification required. Spillable batteries are removed and stored in a battery box; non-spillable power is disabled and the battery removed if not securely attached.

docs.t: CHECK-AIRMAN SCENARIO: A passenger boards your 787 with dry ice packing a cooler of fresh fish. On a domestic segment no NOTOC is needed within limits, but when does that dry ice become a NOTOC item?
docs.x: CHECK-AIRMAN SCENARIO: A passenger boards your 787 with dry ice packing a cooler of fresh fish. On a domestic segment no NOTOC is needed within limits, but when does that dry ice become a NOTOC item? For passenger items, dry ice (carbon dioxide, solid) may not exceed 2.5 kg (5.5 pounds) per person, and that no-NOTOC allowance is domestic flights only; any international flight requires a NOTOC. For cargo, the same 2.5 kg (5.5 lb) limit applies per package under UN1845, domestic shipments only, international requires a NOTOC. FOM 14.1.11 — NOTOC Entry Not Required Dry ice (carbon dioxide, solid) may not exceed 2.5 kg (5.5 pounds) per person (domestic flights only, international flights require a NOTOC) Exceeding the per-person limit, or crossing a border, moves the shipment onto the NOTOC.

docs.t: CHECK-AIRMAN SCENARIO: Cargo hands you paperwork for a shipment of lithium-ion batteries coded ELI, declared as meeting Section II. Should this appear as a NOTOC entry, and what would change your answer?
docs.x: CHECK-AIRMAN SCENARIO: Cargo hands you paperwork for a shipment of lithium-ion batteries coded ELI, declared as meeting Section II. Should this appear as a NOTOC entry, and what would change your answer? No. UN3480/UN3481/UN3090/UN3091 lithium-ion or lithium metal cells or batteries meeting the provisions of Section II (small batteries and cells), coded ELI/ELM, do not require a NOTOC entry. What changes the answer is size: larger lithium shipments that do not meet Section II still require a NOTOC. FOM 14.1.11 — NOTOC Entry Not Required UN3480/UN3481/UN3090/UN3091, lithium-ion or lithium metal cells or batteries meeting the provisions of Section II (small batteries and cells) (ELI/ELM) Section II small-battery exception only; ELI is lithium-ion, ELM is lithium metal.

docs.t: Who is designated as the In-Flight Security Coordinator (ISC) for each flight?
docs.x: Who is designated as the In-Flight Security Coordinator (ISC) for each flight? The Pilot-in-Command (PIC) is designated as the ISC for each flight, responsible for the safety and security of the aircraft, guests, and crewmembers. FOM 15.1.8 — In-Flight Security Coordinator (ISC) The Pilot-in-Command (PIC) is designated as the ISC for each flight. The ISC performs required duties per the applicable security program for the type of flight operated.

docs.t: At what point is security responsibility transferred to the ISC?
docs.x: At what point is security responsibility transferred to the ISC? Once an aircraft door closes, security responsibility is transferred to the ISC. FOM 15.1.8 — In-Flight Security Coordinator (ISC) Once an aircraft door closes, security responsibility is transferred to the ISC. The ISC must review pertinent security information with the GSC for each flight segment before the transfer.

docs.t: During what period must the Flight Deck Door be closed and locked under the Secure Flight Deck procedure?
docs.x: During what period must the Flight Deck Door be closed and locked under the Secure Flight Deck procedure? From pushback (or from engine start if pushback is not required) until the aircraft has been brought to a stop at its final position on the ramp and the engines are shut down. FOM 15.2.6.1 — Secure Flight Deck The Flight Deck Door shall be closed and locked from pushback (or engine start, if pushback is not required) until the time the aircraft has been brought to a stop at its final position on the ramp and the engines are shut down. Secure Flight Deck procedures are not required during Part 91 operations.

docs.t: During the Secure Flight Deck period, for what four circumstances may the Flight Deck Door be opened?
docs.x: During the Secure Flight Deck period, for what four circumstances may the Flight Deck Door be opened? To conduct a contamination check or perform MEL inspection; to allow a crewmember to attend to physiological needs; to deliver or remove meal service items; and with the Captain's specific approval. FOM 15.2.6.1 — Secure Flight Deck To conduct a contamination check or perform MEL inspection The time the door is open shall be kept to a minimum, and all door opening and exiting procedures shall be followed.

docs.t: Who is authorized access to the Flight Deck during Secure Flight Deck time?
docs.x: Who is authorized access to the Flight Deck during Secure Flight Deck time? Access is limited to Alaska Airlines crewmembers, Federal Inspectors, Secret Service, Federal Air Marshals, and those with specific authorization. FOM 15.2.6.1 — Secure Flight Deck Access to the Flight Deck during Secure Flight Deck time is limited to Alaska Airlines crewmembers, Federal Inspectors, Secret Service, Federal Air Marshals, and those with specific authorization Specific authorization references Flight Deck Jumpseat Access procedures.

docs.t: To how long should crewmembers strive to limit the time the Flight Deck Door is open?
docs.x: To how long should crewmembers strive to limit the time the Flight Deck Door is open? Three seconds or less, because the Flight Deck is most vulnerable when the door is open. FOM 15.2.6.1 — Secure Flight Deck crewmembers should strive to limit the time the door is open to three seconds or less If any threat is perceived while the door is open, any crewmember must loudly shout, “Door, Door, Door” to alert others to immediately close it.

docs.t: What must any crewmember shout if a threat is perceived while the Flight Deck Door is open?
docs.x: What must any crewmember shout if a threat is perceived while the Flight Deck Door is open? "Door, Door, Door" to alert other crewmembers to immediately close the Flight Deck Door. FOM 15.2.6.1 - Secure Flight Deck If any threat is perceived while the Flight Deck Door is open, any crewmember must loudly shout, “Door, Door, Door” to alert other crewmembers to immediately close the Flight Deck Door Flight Deck Lockdown Procedures (15.3.13) are then followed if necessary.

docs.t: If the Flight Crew receives a keypad activation warning signal, what must they assume?
docs.x: If the Flight Crew receives a keypad activation warning signal, what must they assume? Without any other information from the Flight Attendants, they must assume that a Level 4 Hijack or Attempted Hijack is in progress in the passenger cabin. FOM 15.2.6.3 — Keypad Control they must assume, without any other information from the Flight Attendants, that a Level 4 Hijack or Attempted Hijack, is in progress in the passenger cabin The keypad control device shall not be used for normal entry; entry attempts using the keypad shall be denied by the Flight Crew.

docs.t: What is the minimum number of people that must be in the Flight Deck when the door is closed after a crewmember exits?
docs.x: What is the minimum number of people that must be in the Flight Deck when the door is closed after a crewmember exits? A minimum of two people must be in the Flight Deck when the door is closed. FOM 15.2.6.7 — Flight Deck Door Operations With IPSB A minimum of two people must be in the Flight Deck when the door is closed If a pilot and a jumpseater both need to leave, the “A” Flight Attendant/FFA (or designee) must enter the Flight Deck.

docs.t: May medical personnel be given access to the Flight Deck?
docs.x: May medical personnel be given access to the Flight Deck? No. Medical personnel shall not be given access to the Flight Deck. FOM 15.2.6.12 — MedLink/Medical Personnel Medical personnel shall not be given access to the Flight Deck. This applies even when MedLink or onboard medical personnel are assisting with a passenger.

docs.t: May a KCM/CMAP participant whose boarding pass shows SSSS use a KCM/CMAP access point?
docs.x: May a KCM/CMAP participant whose boarding pass shows SSSS use a KCM/CMAP access point? No. KCM/CMAP participants with a boarding pass showing SSSS are not permitted to use KCM/CMAP access points and must proceed to a standard passenger screening checkpoint. FOM 15.1.13.2 - Known Crewmember (KCM)/Crewmember Access Point (CMAP) KCM/CMAP participants with a boarding pass showing SSSS are not permitted to use KCM/CMAP access points. KCM participants also cannot bring other individuals, pets, or others' personal property through KCM access points.

docs.t: Are uniformed crewmembers subject to the one carry-on plus one personal item limit, and what inspection are all their bags subject to?
docs.x: Are uniformed crewmembers subject to the one carry-on plus one personal item limit, and what inspection are all their bags subject to? Uniformed crewmembers, whether assigned to a flight or not, are not subject to the one carry-on bag plus one personal item limitation. All bags are subject to random Explosive Trace Detection (ETD) inspection. FOM 15.1.13.3 — Flight Crew Uniformed crewmembers, whether assigned to a flight or not, are not subject to the limitation of one carry-on bag plus one personal item. Crewmember baggage is not subject to random hand searches after clearing the x-ray unless an illegal or unexplained item is detected.

docs.t: Who is permitted to carry a firearm on duty, and what personal protection devices are Flight Crew prohibited from carrying?
docs.x: Who is permitted to carry a firearm on duty, and what personal protection devices are Flight Crew prohibited from carrying? Only a Flight Crewmember authorized as a Federal Flight Deck Officer (FFDO) may carry firearms; otherwise the carriage of firearms or other weapons on duty or on Company property is prohibited. Flight Crew are also prohibited from carrying chemical irritating agents such as pepper spray (Mace). FOM 15.1.14 — Firearms and Weapons the carriage of firearms or other weapons while on duty or while on Company property is prohibited The only exception is a Flight Crewmember authorized as an FFDO.

docs.t: Whose ID does the CSA verify for a Federal Air Marshal team, and must the Flight Crew check FAM ID?
docs.x: Whose ID does the CSA verify for a Federal Air Marshal team, and must the Flight Crew check FAM ID? The FAM Team Lead provides ID to the CSA and advises of additional team members; the CSA only needs to verify the Team Lead's ID. The Flight Crew need not check ID, but if there is doubt as to identity, contact Dispatch via telephone, not the aircraft radio. FOM 15.2.9.1 — Overview/General Procedures The CSA only needs to verify the Team Lead's ID. The Flight Crew need not check ID Do not transmit any communication regarding the FAM program via the radio.

docs.t: What is the standing rule about taking off with a known passenger disturbance?
docs.x: What is the standing rule about taking off with a known passenger disturbance? NEVER take off with a KNOWN passenger disturbance. FOM 15.3.5 — Passenger Removal Procedures NEVER take off with a KNOWN passenger disturbance. If the situation escalates, consider contacting the local airport police for assistance.

docs.t: How many high risk prisoners are allowed per flight and how many armed LEOs must accompany each?
docs.x: How many high risk prisoners are allowed per flight and how many armed LEOs must accompany each? Only one high risk prisoner is allowed per flight unless specifically approved in advance by TSA, and each prisoner must be accompanied by two or more armed LEOs who may not be responsible for any other prisoners. FOM 15.3.6.2 — Prisoners Only one high risk prisoner is allowed per flight, unless specifically approved in advance by TSA. For low risk, one LEO may control two low risk prisoners on flights up to four hours; two LEOs are required for up to two low risk prisoners on flights over four hours.

docs.t: Once the Flight Deck Door has been locked down in response to a Level 3 or Level 4 threat, may it be reopened?
docs.x: Once the Flight Deck Door has been locked down in response to a Level 3 or Level 4 threat, may it be reopened? No. The door shall not be reopened under any circumstances; declare an emergency and land at the nearest suitable airport. During Levels 3 and 4 the Flight Attendants will also lockdown the cabin. FOM 15.3.13 — Flight Deck Lockdown Procedures the door shall not be reopened under any circumstances—declare an emergency, and land at the nearest suitable airport For a Level 1 or Level 2 event, do not terminate lockdown restrictions until the F/As communicate the threat is resolved.

docs.t: Which transponder code is used for hijacking, and may code 7700 be used during a hijacking?
docs.x: Which transponder code is used for hijacking, and may code 7700 be used during a hijacking? Code 7500 is the unique code used for hijacking. Code 7700 shall not be used during a hijacking; that procedure has been eliminated from the common strategy. FOM 15.3.15.2 — Code 7500 Code 7500 is the unique code used for hijacking. Per 15.3.15.1, do not use code 7700 during a hijacking; ATC will normally ask for confirmation of a 7500 squawk only once due to concern over possible duress.

docs.t: How many distinct passenger threat levels does Common Strategy identify, and what does each describe?
docs.x: How many distinct passenger threat levels does Common Strategy identify, and what does each describe? Four passenger threat levels: Level One is disruptive behavior, suspicious or threatening; Level Two is physically abusive behavior; Level Three is life-threatening behavior; and Level Four is attempted breach of the Flight Deck or actual breach. FOM 15.3.18 — Passenger Threat Levels There are four passenger threat levels, developed by government and industry experts They help identify the seriousness of suspicious or threatening activity occurring on board an aircraft.

docs.t: After deplaning at a remote location for a credible bomb threat during taxiing, how far must the PIC move passengers and crew?
docs.x: After deplaning at a remote location for a credible bomb threat during taxiing, how far must the PIC move passengers and crew? The PIC will direct passengers and crew to move at least 100 yards upwind of the aircraft and initiate a passenger and crew count; the GSC ensures ground personnel are at least 100 yards from the aircraft. FOM 15.2.19.2 — Credible IED/Bomb Threat – During Taxiing The PIC will direct the passengers and crew to move at least 100 yards upwind of the aircraft An aircraft with a credible bomb threat may never be taxied to the gate until the NOC/SOCC deems the threat terminated.

docs.t: SCENARIO (Flight Deck Door discipline): In cruise, the First Officer opens the Flight Deck Door to step out per the exit procedure. As the door swings open, a passenger near the forward galley suddenly lunges toward the aisle. What is the required immediate action, and what is the door-open time target?
docs.x: SCENARIO (Flight Deck Door discipline): In cruise, the First Officer opens the Flight Deck Door to step out per the exit procedure. As the door swings open, a passenger near the forward galley suddenly lunges toward the aisle. What is the required immediate action, and what is the door-open time target? Any crewmember who perceives the threat must loudly shout "Door, Door, Door" to alert other crewmembers to immediately close the Flight Deck Door, then follow Flight Deck Lockdown Procedures (15.3.13) if necessary. Crewmembers strive to keep the door open three seconds or less because the Flight Deck is most vulnerable when the door is open. FOM 15.2.6.1 - Secure Flight Deck If any threat is perceived while the Flight Deck Door is open, any crewmember must loudly shout, “Door, Door, Door” to alert other crewmembers to immediately close the Flight Deck Door. The Flight Deck is most vulnerable when the door is open, so crewmembers should strive to limit the time the door is open to three seconds or less.

docs.t: SCENARIO (jumpseat / two-person rule): You are the Captain. Your First Officer and the flight-deck jumpseater both need to leave the Flight Deck at the same time. What must occur before both can step out?
docs.x: SCENARIO (jumpseat / two-person rule): You are the Captain. Your First Officer and the flight-deck jumpseater both need to leave the Flight Deck at the same time. What must occur before both can step out? A minimum of two people must be in the Flight Deck when the door is closed. Because a pilot and the jumpseater both need to leave, the "A" Flight Attendant/FFA (or designee) must enter the Flight Deck to hold the number at two. The second person closes and secures the door and follows Flight Deck Reentry Procedures when the crewmember returns. FOM 15.2.6.7 - Flight Deck Door Operations With IPSB If a pilot and the jumpseater both need to leave, the “A” Flight Attendant/FFA (or designee) must enter the Flight Deck. A minimum of two people must be in the Flight Deck when the door is closed; if a jumpseater remains, the F/A does not need to enter.

docs.t: SCENARIO (threat level response): In cruise you receive a keypad activation warning signal, with no other communication from the Flight Attendants. What must the Flight Crew assume, and once locked down at that level, may the door be reopened?
docs.x: SCENARIO (threat level response): In cruise you receive a keypad activation warning signal, with no other communication from the Flight Attendants. What must the Flight Crew assume, and once locked down at that level, may the door be reopened? Without any other information from the Flight Attendants, the Flight Crew must assume a Level 4 Hijack or Attempted Hijack is in progress in the passenger cabin. Once locked down in response to a Level 3 or Level 4 threat, the door shall not be reopened under any circumstances; declare an emergency and land at the nearest suitable airport. FOM 15.2.6.3 — Keypad Control If the Flight Crew receives a keypad activation warning signal they must assume, without any other information from the Flight Attendants, that a Level 4 Hijack or Attempted Hijack, is in progress in the passenger cabin. Per 15.3.13, once locked down for a Level 3 or 4 threat the door shall not be reopened under any circumstances—declare an emergency and land at the nearest suitable airport.

docs.t: SCENARIO (armed LEO notification): Armed Individuals are already continuing through on your aircraft, and additional Armed Individuals are joining for the next segment. What must be completed before the aircraft door(s) can be closed?
docs.x: SCENARIO (armed LEO notification): Armed Individuals are already continuing through on your aircraft, and additional Armed Individuals are joining for the next segment. What must be completed before the aircraft door(s) can be closed? All notifications must be made to the assigned crew and all Armed Individuals before the door(s) can be closed. The gate agent must inform each AI of the location of the others who are armed, including FAMs, and communications between Flight Crew, Flight Attendants, and AIs should be as discreet as possible. FOM 15.2.8 — Armed Individuals (other than FAM and FFDO) If AIs are joining a flight where AIs are continuing through, all notifications must be made to the assigned crew and all AIs before the door(s) can be closed. The gate agent must inform the AI of the location of others who are armed, including FAMs; communications should be as discrete as possible.

docs.t: Rev 125: on an aircraft with the IPSB installed, what must happen before the Flight Deck Door is opened during the Secure Flight Deck period?
docs.x: Rev 125: on an aircraft with the IPSB installed, what must happen before the Flight Deck Door is opened during the Secure Flight Deck period? The IPSB must be deployed before the Flight Deck Door is opened. A Secure Flight Deck is the combination of a locked door and, where equipped, the Installed Physical Secondary Barrier. FOM 15.2.6.1 - Secure Flight Deck A Secure Flight Deck is achieved by using a combination of a locked Flight Deck Door and, for aircraft so equipped, an Installed Physical Secondary Barrier (IPSB) between the cabin and the Flight Deck for use when the Flight Deck Door must be opened. Any time the Flight Deck Door is opened during the Secure Flight Deck period for aircraft with the IPSB installed, the IPSB shall be deployed before the Flight Deck Door is opened. NEW in Rev 125. 15.2.6.6 is now 'Flight Deck Operations Without IPSB' and 15.2.6.7 is 'Flight Deck Door Operations With IPSB'.

docs.t: Rev 125: on the 787, which galley cart arrangement options remain when the Flight Deck Door is opened without an IPSB?
docs.x: Rev 125: on the 787, which galley cart arrangement options remain when the Flight Deck Door is opened without an IPSB? Options 1 or 2 only. Rev 125 deleted Option 3 for the 787/A330. FOM 15.2.6.6 - Flight Deck Operations Without IPSB (787/A330) Arrange carts and Cabin Crew in accordance with Options 1 or 2. Through 124.2 this read 'Options 1, 2, or 3'. Option 3 no longer exists for the 787.

docs.t: How many types of NRFO operations does the FOM define, and what are they?
docs.x: How many types of NRFO operations does the FOM define, and what are they? Three: (1) Flights that must be operated under Part 121, (2) Flights that may be operated under Part 91, and (3) Flights operated under Part 121 Cargo Only. FOM 16.1.1 — Non-Routine Flight Operations (NRFOS) There are three types of NRFO operations NRFOs are all flight operations that are not on the published schedule. The type determines the governing rules and Flight Attendant requirements.

docs.t: What three conditions must be met to operate an NRFO under Part 121?
docs.x: What three conditions must be met to operate an NRFO under Part 121? The aircraft is on the Operations Specifications, the aircraft is equipped and maintained per the Alaska Airlines Maintenance Program, and the crew is fully qualified. FOM 16.1.1 — Non-Routine Flight Operations (NRFOS) Aircraft is on the Operations Specifications All three conditions must be satisfied before a Part 121 NRFO may be dispatched.

docs.t: Are Flight Attendants required on a cargo-only NRFO?
docs.x: Are Flight Attendants required on a cargo-only NRFO? No. Flight Attendants are not required on a cargo-only NRFO. FOM 16.1.1.3 — Part 121 Cargo-Only NRFO Flight Attendants are not required on a cargo-only NRFO. Non-essential passengers are also not allowed on flights dispatched as Part 121 – Cargo Only.

docs.t: On a Part 91 NRFO, at what passenger count is a Flight Attendant required to be on board?
docs.x: On a Part 91 NRFO, at what passenger count is a Flight Attendant required to be on board? A Flight Attendant must be on board if more than nineteen (19) passengers are carried. FOM 16.1.8.2 — Part 91 NRFO Flights a Flight Attendant must be on board if more than nineteen (19) passengers are carried Alaska policy is to use a full complement of Flight Attendants anytime one Flight Attendant is required (14 CFR 91.533).

docs.t: Who may be carried as passengers on a Part 91 flight operated without Flight Attendants?
docs.x: Who may be carried as passengers on a Part 91 flight operated without Flight Attendants? Passengers are restricted to Alaska Air Group employees, unless authorization for non-employees is received from the Director of Operations, FODO, or NRFO Management. FOM 16.1.8.2 — Part 91 NRFO Flights Passengers on Part 91 flights without Flight Attendants will be restricted to Alaska Air Group employees Non-employees require authorization from the DO, FODO, or NRFO Management.

docs.t: On a Part 91 non-revenue operation, how many Flight Attendants are required for more than 19 but less than 51 passengers?
docs.x: On a Part 91 non-revenue operation, how many Flight Attendants are required for more than 19 but less than 51 passengers? One (1) Flight Attendant. FOM 16.1.9.1 — Part 91 – Non-Revenue Operations more than 19 but less than 51 passengers – 1 The full scale: 19 or less – 0; 19 to under 51 – 1; more than 50 but less than 101 – 2; more than 100 – 2 (+1 for each unit of 50).

docs.t: On a Part 91 non-revenue operation, how many Flight Attendants are required with more than 100 passengers on board?
docs.x: On a Part 91 non-revenue operation, how many Flight Attendants are required with more than 100 passengers on board? Two (2), plus one additional for each unit of 50 passengers. FOM 16.1.9.1 — Part 91 – Non-Revenue Operations more than 100 passengers on board – 2 (+1 each unit of 50 passengers) This scaling applies to positioning and non-revenue misc operations on all-passenger aircraft.

docs.t: Besides crewmembers, name persons who may be carried on a Part 121 NRFO flight without Flight Attendants when approved.
docs.x: Besides crewmembers, name persons who may be carried on a Part 121 NRFO flight without Flight Attendants when approved. Essential Company employees, an FAA Air Carrier Inspector performing official duties, an NTSB official performing official duties, and persons handling or essential to cargo on NRFO cargo-only flights. FOM 16.1.8.1 — Part 121 NRFO Flights FAA Air Carrier Inspector performing official duties Requires approval by the Director of Operations or NRFO Management designee (14 CFR 121.583). Any other passenger triggers the full FA complement.

docs.t: What is a Positioning Flight?
docs.x: What is a Positioning Flight? A flight conducted with an airworthy aircraft flown from one destination to another under 14 CFR Part 91 with no revenue passengers or cargo; it can be for maintenance, charter, scheduling, etc. FOM 16.4.1 — Positioning Flight operated under 14 CFR Part 91 with no revenue passengers or cargo A positioning flight delivers the empty aircraft to where a charter begins or back into scheduled service after the charter is over.

docs.t: Which Ops Spec authorizes the Special Flight Permit Ferry, and what does it provide?
docs.x: Which Ops Spec authorizes the Special Flight Permit Ferry, and what does it provide? Maintenance Ops Spec D084 is the Special Flight Permit with Continuous Authorization to Conduct Ferry Flights. FOM 16.4.2 — Special Flight Permit Ferry Maintenance Ops Spec D084 is the Special Flight Permit with Continuous Authorization to Conduct Ferry Flights Section references 14 CFR 21.197 and GPM 05-00-05. The permit authorizes flying an aircraft that may not meet applicable airworthiness requirements.

docs.t: May passengers or cargo be carried on a Special Flight Permit Ferry?
docs.x: May passengers or cargo be carried on a Special Flight Permit Ferry? No. The flight shall not have passengers or cargo. FOM 16.4.2 — Special Flight Permit Ferry The flight shall not have passengers or cargo. If issued without limitations, the flight is limited to Flight Crew, Flight Attendants, and Maintenance Crew.

docs.t: Can MELs be applied to a flight on a Special Flight Permit, and is ETOPS PDC/PDSC required?
docs.x: Can MELs be applied to a flight on a Special Flight Permit, and is ETOPS PDC/PDSC required? Yes, MELs may be applied to flights on a Special Flight Permit. ETOPS PDC/PDSC is not required, but aircraft fluid levels will be inspected and serviced as required. FOM 16.4.2 — Special Flight Permit Ferry MELs may be applied to flights on a Special Flight Permit. Certain MEL Remarks/Exceptions and Operations Procedures may not apply, except for ER operations/ETOPS and flight level restrictions.

docs.t: Does a 787 require a Maintenance Check Flight after a double-engine change, and which group is it?
docs.x: Does a 787 require a Maintenance Check Flight after a double-engine change, and which group is it? Yes. A 787 flight after a double-engine change is a Group 2 Maintenance Check Flight, which must be flown by a qualified Functional Check Pilot. FOM 16.3.2.2 — Classification of Maintenance Check Flights flight after a double-engine change Group 2 checks major systems or components to determine airworthiness and may require emergency, abnormal, or special procedures in flight.

docs.t: What are Group 1 and Group 2 Maintenance Check Flights also called?
docs.x: What are Group 1 and Group 2 Maintenance Check Flights also called? A Group 1 Maintenance Check Flight is also referred to as an 'evaluation flight'; a Group 2 Maintenance Check Flight is also referred to as a 'test flight'. FOM 16.3.2.2 — Classification of Maintenance Check Flights also referred to as an “evaluation flight” Group 1 uses normal FCOM procedures; Group 2 involves specialized training and may use emergency, abnormal, or special procedures.

docs.t: Who may crew a Group 1 Maintenance Check Flight, and who is prohibited?
docs.x: Who may crew a Group 1 Maintenance Check Flight, and who is prohibited? It may be flown by a line Captain and a First Officer. A 'High-Minimums Captain' or 'Restricted First Officer' is prohibited from flying a Group 1 Maintenance Check Flight. FOM 16.3.2.2 — Classification of Maintenance Check Flights A “High-Minimums Captain” or “Restricted First Officer” is prohibited from flying a Group 1 Maintenance Check Flight. A Group 1 flight is not considered a 'test flight'; the crew is not trained or qualified as test pilots. Group 2 must be flown by a qualified Functional Check Pilot.

docs.t: What two DD Forms is Alaska Airlines issued for use of military airfields, and by whom?
docs.x: What two DD Forms is Alaska Airlines issued for use of military airfields, and by whom? DD Form 2401 (Civil Aircraft Landing Permit) and DD Form 2400 (Civil Aircraft Certificate of Insurance), issued by the US Air Force, the US Army, and the US Navy/Marine Corps. FOM 16.1.12 - Military Civil Aircraft Landing Permits and Certificate of Insurance Alaska Airlines is issued DD Form 2401, Civil Aircraft Landing Permit, and DD Form 2400, Civil Aircraft Certificate of Insurance by the US Air Force, the US Army, and the US Navy/Marine Corps. A second AF DD Form 2401 authorizes use of all US Air Force Aviation Facilities worldwide for government charters and contract flights (including AMC).

docs.t: Rev 125 change: where does the FOM now list the specific military bases Alaska Airlines may use?
docs.x: Rev 125 change: where does the FOM now list the specific military bases Alaska Airlines may use? It does not. Rev 125 deleted the per-service base lists (former 16.1.12.1, .2 and .3), including the Bucholz AAF exception. Use of US military installations is limited to those specifically authorized in the approved DD Form 2401. FOM 16.1.12 - Military Civil Aircraft Landing Permits and Certificate of Insurance Alaska Airlines is issued DD Form 2401, Civil Aircraft Landing Permit, and DD Form 2400, Civil Aircraft Certificate of Insurance by the US Air Force, the US Army, and the US Navy/Marine Corps. The Captain is responsible for knowledge of the limitations in the DD forms; they are located on the EFB in Comply365.

docs.t: How many Maintenance Logbook entries are required for a Special Flight Permit, and what does each describe?
docs.x: How many Maintenance Logbook entries are required for a Special Flight Permit, and what does each describe? Two: the first entry's Defect Description describes the mechanical defect and is resolved as a deferral referencing the Special Flight Permit to move the aircraft; the second entry states an inspection is required and resolves that the aircraft is safe for the intended flight and the Flight Crew has been briefed. FOM 16.4.2.1 — Maintenance Documentation two Maintenance Logbook entries are required for a Special Flight Permit The Maintenance Logbook with the 'aircraft released' statement and a copy of the ferry authorization, plus Ops Spec D084, must be carried on board.

docs.t: CHECK-AIRMAN SCENARIO: Maintenance has just completed a double-engine change on a 787 and requests a check flight. What group is this Maintenance Check Flight, who must be at the controls, and under what Part does it operate?
docs.x: CHECK-AIRMAN SCENARIO: Maintenance has just completed a double-engine change on a 787 and requests a check flight. What group is this Maintenance Check Flight, who must be at the controls, and under what Part does it operate? It is a Group 2 Maintenance Check Flight (a 'test flight'). It must be flown by a qualified Functional Check Pilot. Like all Maintenance Check Flights, it operates under 14 CFR Part 91, flown for the express purpose of verifying airworthiness. FOM 16.3.2.2 — Classification of Maintenance Check Flights Group 2 Maintenance Check Flights must be flown by a qualified Functional Check Pilot. A 787 flight after a double-engine change is a listed Group 2 example. Group 2 involves specialized training and may require emergency, abnormal, or special procedures in flight. Final group categorization is approved by the Director of Operations or the Standards/Part 119 Chief Pilot (16.3.2.1).

docs.t: CHECK-AIRMAN SCENARIO: A 787 has a mechanical defect that is being deferred, and it must be flown empty to a maintenance base on a Special Flight Permit Ferry under Ops Spec D084. Can you carry passengers or cargo, may MELs be applied, and how many Maintenance Logbook entries are required?
docs.x: CHECK-AIRMAN SCENARIO: A 787 has a mechanical defect that is being deferred, and it must be flown empty to a maintenance base on a Special Flight Permit Ferry under Ops Spec D084. Can you carry passengers or cargo, may MELs be applied, and how many Maintenance Logbook entries are required? No passengers or cargo may be carried. MELs may be applied to flights on a Special Flight Permit. Two Maintenance Logbook entries are required — one deferring the defect by referencing the Special Flight Permit, and one stating the aircraft is safe for the intended flight and the Flight Crew has been briefed. The Flight Crew shall not perform any troubleshooting or non-standard activities. FOM 16.4.2 — Special Flight Permit Ferry The flight shall not have passengers or cargo. Ops Spec D084 authorizes flying an aircraft that may not meet applicable airworthiness requirements (14 CFR 21.197). ETOPS PDC/PDSC is not required, but aircraft fluid levels are inspected and serviced. Two Maintenance Logbook entries are required per 16.4.2.1.

docs.t: CHECK-AIRMAN SCENARIO: You are positioning a 787 under Part 91 with no Flight Attendants on board, and a non-employee observer asks to ride along. Is that allowed, and whose authorization would it take?
docs.x: CHECK-AIRMAN SCENARIO: You are positioning a 787 under Part 91 with no Flight Attendants on board, and a non-employee observer asks to ride along. Is that allowed, and whose authorization would it take? By default, no. Passengers on Part 91 flights without Flight Attendants are restricted to Alaska Air Group employees. Carrying a non-employee requires authorization from the Director of Operations, FODO, or NRFO Management. FOM 16.1.8.2 — Part 91 NRFO Flights Passengers on Part 91 flights without Flight Attendants will be restricted to Alaska Air Group employees Authorization for non-employees comes from the DO, FODO, or NRFO Management (14 CFR 91.533). If a Flight Attendant is required, Alaska policy is to use a full complement.

docs.t: What proof of citizenship must a US citizen crewmember carry on international operations, and is a photocopy acceptable?
docs.x: What proof of citizenship must a US citizen crewmember carry on international operations, and is a photocopy acceptable? Each US citizen crewmember must carry a valid US Passport; photocopies are not a valid substitute. FOM 18.1.1 — Crewmember Proof of Citizenship Each US Citizen crewmember must carry a valid US Passport (photocopies are not a valid substitute). Alien crewmembers must instead carry their Alien Registration Card (green card) and Passport. Passports must be carried on all flights, domestic and international, so reroutes do not remove a crewmember from a flight.

docs.t: Under the CBP Biometric Air Exit program, can crewmembers opt out, and what happens if they do?
docs.x: Under the CBP Biometric Air Exit program, can crewmembers opt out, and what happens if they do? Yes. Crews may opt out on an individual basis; if a crewmember opts out, the CSA manually verifies that the crewmember's passport name matches the name on the Gen Dec. FOM 18.1.2 — Biometric Air Exit crews may opt out on an individual basis Biometric Air Exit uses facial recognition to validate the identity of individuals leaving the United States. Air carrier use of biometric boarding is mandated, but the opt-out is per-individual.

docs.t: When operating within a foreign country, whose air traffic and airport rules do you follow, and what is the exception?
docs.x: When operating within a foreign country, whose air traffic and airport rules do you follow, and what is the exception? Comply with the air traffic and local airport rules of the country concerned, except where any FAR rule is more restrictive and may be followed without violating that country's rules. FOM 18.1.4 — International Operation comply with the air traffic and local airport rules of the country concerned, except where any rule of the FARs is more restrictive Governed by 14 CFR § 91.703 and 14 CFR § 121.11. See the Jeppesen FD Pro application for further guidance.

docs.t: For international altimeter settings, what is set above the Transition Level, including the standard pressure value?
docs.x: For international altimeter settings, what is set above the Transition Level, including the standard pressure value? STD is set above the Transition Level: 1013.25 hPa / 29.92 in Hg. The appropriate QNH value is set below the Transition Altitude. FOM 18.1.6 — International Altimeter Settings – QNH or QNE STD (1013.25 hPa/29.92 in Hg) above the Transition Level Where QFE is given by ATC, the Flight Crew shall request QNH and set it normally. See Jeppesen FD Pro for region-specific guidance.

docs.t: How long does residual disinsection spraying remain active, and when is it applied?
docs.x: How long does residual disinsection spraying remain active, and when is it applied? Residual spraying remains active for up to eight weeks (56 days), applied during an overnight parking at a remote parking location. FOM 18.1.10.1 — Residual Spraying aircraft undergo treatment that remains active for up to eight weeks (56 days) Once complete, a Certificate of Disinsection is placed in the Comply365 app under Flying > Regulatory & Operating Docs > International Documents > Europe.

docs.t: During pre-departure disinsection spraying, what must the 787 crew do if on board while the cabin is sprayed?
docs.x: During pre-departure disinsection spraying, what must the 787 crew do if on board while the cabin is sprayed? On the 787, ensure the entire aircraft is powered down, including disconnected from ground power. Crews are not required to remain on board once the aircraft has been configured. FOM 18.1.10.2 — Pre-Departure Spraying (787) ensure the entire aircraft is powered down including disconnected from ground power A short three-second spray is directed at the floor of the cockpit just prior to the spray team exiting. Crews need not remain on board once the aircraft is configured.

docs.t: During disinsection spraying, how long is the saturation period during which lavatory or cargo smoke warnings should be treated as spurious?
docs.x: During disinsection spraying, how long is the saturation period during which lavatory or cargo smoke warnings should be treated as spurious? A 5-minute saturation time is observed; smoke warnings from the start of spraying through completion (including the 5-minute saturation) are treated as spurious, but warnings outside those times follow the associated procedure. FOM 18.1.10.3 — Post-Arrival Spraying A period of 5 minutes must be observed to allow the saturation of insecticide before any doors or vents can be opened Smoke detectors in cargo compartments, lavatories, and avionics may detect aerosol particulate and cause spurious smoke or fire alerts during spraying.

docs.t: At which post-arrival disinsection destinations may a passenger with a serious aerosol-aggravated medical condition disembark before disinsection?
docs.x: At which post-arrival disinsection destinations may a passenger with a serious aerosol-aggravated medical condition disembark before disinsection? New Zealand and Tahiti allow passengers who have identified themselves as having a serious medical condition aggravated by an aerosol to disembark before disinsection. FOM 18.1.10.3 — Post-Arrival Spraying New Zealand/Tahiti allows passengers who have identified themselves as having a serious medical condition aggravated by an aerosol to be permitted to disembark before disinsection Keep the seat belt sign ON until spraying is complete; the air conditioning packs are turned off during the disinsection process.

docs.t: How does the US Public Health Service define an 'ill person' by temperature threshold?
docs.x: How does the US Public Health Service define an 'ill person' by temperature threshold? A person with a temperature of 100°F (38°C) or greater that has persisted more than 48 hours (among other listed criteria). FOM 18.1.15 — Death or Illness Reporting – International has a temperature of 100°F (38°C) or greater which has persisted more than 48 hours Other criteria include fever with rash, jaundice, persistent cough, difficulty breathing, or persistent diarrhea. Deaths or illness enroute to countries other than the US and Canada are entered on the General Declaration.

docs.t: For flights to Australia, how far in advance of landing must the Captain report an apparent death or ill person on board?
docs.x: For flights to Australia, how far in advance of landing must the Captain report an apparent death or ill person on board? At least 30 minutes before landing, the Captain must report the presence of any apparent death or ill person to the Australian authorities. FOM 18.1.15 — Death or Illness Reporting – International report to the Australian authorities the presence on board the aircraft of any apparent death or any ill person among passengers or crew at least 30 minutes before landing This is a country-specific requirement distinct from the General Declaration entry used for other foreign destinations.

docs.t: What separation do PBCS tracks (formerly RLatSM) provide laterally and longitudinally?
docs.x: What separation do PBCS tracks (formerly RLatSM) provide laterally and longitudinally? PBCS tracks are separated by half a degree laterally and utilize a longitudinal separation minima as small as 14 nm. FOM 18.1.23 — Performance-Based Communication And Surveillance (PBCS) Tracks fly tracks that are separated by half a degree and utilize a longitudinal separation minima as small as 14 nm PBCS tracks were formerly designated Reduced Lateral Separation Minimum (RLatSM) tracks and require authorized aircraft with the required equipment.

docs.t: What are the RCP240 time limits, and what is the primary means of meeting the standard?
docs.x: What are the RCP240 time limits, and what is the primary means of meeting the standard? RCP240 allows 240 seconds overall for a communication transaction for 99.9% of the time, with the transaction completed within 210 seconds for 95% of the time. SATCOM CPDLC is the primary means. FOM 18.1.23.1 — RCP and RSP Represents the overall time, 240 seconds, allowed for a communication transaction for 99.9% of the time. Additionally, the transaction time must be completed within 210 seconds for 95% of the time. SATCOM CPDLC is the primary means to meet the RCP240 standard. By contrast RCP400 allows 400 seconds for 99.9% and 350 seconds for 95%, met by SATCOM CPDLC and SATCOM voice.

docs.t: What are the RSP180 surveillance time limits, and what is the primary means of meeting them?
docs.x: What are the RSP180 surveillance time limits, and what is the primary means of meeting them? RSP180 allows 180 seconds overall for a surveillance data transaction for 99.9% of the time, completed within 90 seconds for 95% of the time. ADS-C is the primary means. FOM 18.1.23.1 — RCP and RSP Represents the overall time, 180 seconds, allowed for surveillance data transaction for 99.9% of the time. Additionally, the transaction time must be completed within 90 seconds for 95% of the time. ADS-C is the primary means to meet the RSP180 standard. RSP400 by contrast allows 400 seconds for 99.9% and 300 seconds for 95%, met by ADS-C and FMS waypoint position reporting.

docs.t: What equipment/approval items are required to use a PBCS filing code?
docs.x: What equipment/approval items are required to use a PBCS filing code? CPDLC/FANS 1/A+, RNP-4, RCP240, ADS-C, TCAS, and RSP180. FOM 18.1.23.2 — PBCS Requirements CPDLC/FANS 1/A+ RNP-4 RCP240 ADS-C TCAS RSP180 Aircraft on PBCS tracks must use CPDLC; if unable to log on, notify ATC immediately and expect a route or altitude change. Non-approved aircraft carry Company placard 1207 PBCS TRACKS NOT AUTHORIZED.

docs.t: In A-CDM, what is the Calculated Take-Off Time (CTOT) slot window?
docs.x: In A-CDM, what is the Calculated Take-Off Time (CTOT) slot window? The CTOT slot time is a 20-minute window (-5, +15) during which the aircraft must take off to avoid losing its place in the traffic flow. FOM 18.1.25 — Airport Collaborative Decision Making (A-CDM) This slot time is actually a 20-minute window (-5, +15) during which the aircraft must takeoff to avoid losing its place in the traffic flow CTOT is allocated by NMOC based on airspace congestion and ATS capacity. Related A-CDM times include TOBT (Target Off-Block Time), TSAT (Target Start-Up Approval Time), and TTOT (Target Take-Off Time).

docs.t: CHECK AIRMAN SCENARIO: You're planning a Pacific oceanic crossing and want to file a PBCS filing code for a PBCS track. Walk me through what equipment and approval items make you eligible, and then tell me what you do if, once established on the track, your CPDLC will not log on.
docs.x: CHECK AIRMAN SCENARIO: You're planning a Pacific oceanic crossing and want to file a PBCS filing code for a PBCS track. Walk me through what equipment and approval items make you eligible, and then tell me what you do if, once established on the track, your CPDLC will not log on. Eligibility to use a PBCS filing code requires six items: CPDLC/FANS 1/A+, RNP-4, RCP240, ADS-C, TCAS, and RSP180. Aircraft operating on PBCS tracks must use CPDLC — if unable to log on, notify ATC immediately and expect a route or altitude change to remain clear of the PBCS tracks. Aircraft not approved for PBCS operation carry Company placard 1207 PBCS TRACKS NOT AUTHORIZED. FOM 18.1.23.2 — PBCS Requirements Aircraft operating on PBCS tracks must use CPDLC. If unable to log on using CPDLC, notify ATC immediately and expect a route or altitude change to remain clear of PBCS tracks. Required items to use a PBCS filing code: CPDLC/FANS 1/A+, RNP-4, RCP240, ADS-C, TCAS, RSP180. Non-approved aircraft carry Company placard 1207 PBCS TRACKS NOT AUTHORIZED.

docs.t: CHECK AIRMAN SCENARIO: Departing a foreign field, ATC issues you QFE rather than QNH. Climbing out, what altimeter setting do you use below the Transition Altitude versus above the Transition Level, and how do you handle the QFE you were given?
docs.x: CHECK AIRMAN SCENARIO: Departing a foreign field, ATC issues you QFE rather than QNH. Climbing out, what altimeter setting do you use below the Transition Altitude versus above the Transition Level, and how do you handle the QFE you were given? Set the appropriate QNH value below the Transition Altitude and STD — 1013.25 hPa / 29.92 in Hg — above the Transition Level. Where QFE is given by ATC, request QNH and set it in the normal manner; procedural altitudes based on QFE are flown using the correction tables normally published on the relevant SID, STAR, and Instrument Approach charts. FOM 18.1.6 — International Altimeter Settings – QNH or QNE The aircraft shall be operated with the appropriate QNH value set below the Transition Altitude and STD (1013.25 hPa/29.92 in Hg) above the Transition Level. Where QFE is given by ATC, the Flight Crews shall request QNH and set in the normal manner. See Jeppesen FD Pro for region-specific guidance on altimeter settings.

docs.t: CHECK AIRMAN SCENARIO: On a post-arrival disinsection, a cargo smoke warning triggers three minutes into the 5-minute saturation period. Ten minutes after the crew is cleared to disembark, a lavatory smoke warning triggers. How do you treat each warning?
docs.x: CHECK AIRMAN SCENARIO: On a post-arrival disinsection, a cargo smoke warning triggers three minutes into the 5-minute saturation period. Ten minutes after the crew is cleared to disembark, a lavatory smoke warning triggers. How do you treat each warning? The warning during the saturation period is spurious: from the start of spraying until the clearance to disembark is given (including the 5-minute saturation time), lavatory or cargo smoke warnings are treated as spurious. The warning ten minutes after disembark clearance falls outside that window, so it is treated as real and the crew follows the associated procedure. FOM 18.1.10.3 — Post-Arrival Spraying From the start of spraying until the clearance to disembark is given (including 5-minute saturation time), any lavatory or cargo smoke warnings during this period should be treated as spurious. However, if any smoke warnings trigger outside those times, the crew should follow the associated procedure. Smoke detectors in cargo compartments, lavatory, and avionics may detect the aerosol particulate matter during spraying and cause spurious smoke or fire alerts. Keep the seat belt sign ON until spraying is complete.

docs.t: In the North America theater, into how many Area Control Centers (ACCs) is the United States divided, and what are Canada's three airspace regions?
docs.x: In the North America theater, into how many Area Control Centers (ACCs) is the United States divided, and what are Canada's three airspace regions? The United States is divided into 22 ACCs. Canada is divided into three airspace regions: the Southern Control Area (SCA), Northern Control Area (NCA), and Arctic Control Area (ACA). FOM 19.2 - Airspace (North America Theater) The United States is divided into 22 Area Control Centers (ACCs). Canada is divided into three airspace regions: the Southern Control Area (SCA), Northern Control Area (NCA), and Arctic Control Area (ACA). Ch 19 covers North America (US and Canada). The Canadian Domestic Airspace (CDA) is separately split into the Southern Domestic Airspace (SDA) and Northern Domestic Airspace (NDA).

docs.t: Under FOM 125.1, where do you find the initial descent altitude for a 787 decompression over the Canadian Rockies?
docs.x: Under FOM 125.1, where do you find the initial descent altitude for a 787 decompression over the Canadian Rockies? There is no longer a published Rockies floor. The regional decompression procedure was deleted from Ch 19 in Rev 125.1. Use the polygon detail drawer in Jeppesen FD Pro; on the 787 the initial descent altitude varies by polygon. FOM 11.2.9 - Decompression Polygon Procedures (737/787/A330) (787) Refer to the detail drawer in Jeppesen FD Pro for the initial descent altitude(s) associated with each polygon. Rev 125.1 removed the Decompression Procedure for the Canadian Rockies Mountain Range Region from 19.3 - Navigation. 19.3.1.1 is now Airspeed Restrictions Takeoff/Landing. The old 18,000 ft Rockies floor is no longer published anywhere in the FOM.

docs.t: What is the takeoff/landing airspeed restriction in Canada near a controlled airport?
docs.x: What is the takeoff/landing airspeed restriction in Canada near a controlled airport? Canada restricts speed to 200 kts (or minimum safe/clean maneuver speed, whichever is faster) below 3000 AFL within 10 miles of a controlled airport, unless assigned a higher speed by ATC clearance. FOM 19.3.1.2 - Airspeed Restrictions Takeoff/Landing Canada restricts speed to 200 kts or minimum safe speed (i.e., clean maneuver), whichever is faster, below 3000 AFL within 10 miles of a controlled airport Note the AFL (above field level) reference and the 10-mile radius, distinct from the US below-10,000 ft/250 kt convention.

docs.t: What defines the Juneau Taku wind hazard, and what system provides alerts for it?
docs.x: What defines the Juneau Taku wind hazard, and what system provides alerts for it? In the Gastineau Channel, mountainous terrain induces Taku winds with very strong gusts of 72 mph or greater, producing strong windshear, rotors, and turbulence. The Juneau Area Wind System (JAWS) provides wind information and alerts for moderate to severe turbulence. FOM 19.5.3 - Juneau Taku Winds Very strong wind gusts (72 mph or greater) can occur during these Taku wind events. See JNU 10-7 JAWS. This is a North America weather-hazard item alongside Anchorage Turnagain Arm turbulence and the LA Santa Ana rotor.

docs.t: On the NOPAC routes between FL340 and FL400, what is the lateral route separation and what performance capabilities are required?
docs.x: On the NOPAC routes between FL340 and FL400, what is the lateral route separation and what performance capabilities are required? Lateral route separation is 23 nm and requires aircraft to be capable of RCP240 (Required Communications Performance 240), RSP180 (Required Surveillance Performance 180), and RNP4. Between FL180-FL330, or FL410 and above, separation is 50 nm and allows RNP10. FOM 20.3.1 - North Pacific (NOPAC) between FL340-FL400, the lateral route separation is 23 nm and requires aircraft to be capable of Required Communications Performance 240 (RCP240), Required Surveillance Performance 180 (RSP180), and Required Navigation Performance 4 (RNP4) The 787 is RCP240, RSP180, and RNP4 capable unless an MEL reduces capability.

docs.t: How is the altimeter set within the Hawaiian Islands domestic area, and within the broader Oakland Oceanic FIR?
docs.x: How is the altimeter set within the Hawaiian Islands domestic area, and within the broader Oakland Oceanic FIR? Within the Hawaiian Islands domestic area: at FL180 and above set standard 29.92 (QNE); below 18,000 ft MSL set current altimeter (QNH). Within all areas of the Oakland FIR, at or above 5500 ft MSL, set standard 29.92 (QNE). FOM 20.7.1 - Altimeter Setting - Oakland Oceanic FIR/Hawaii at FL180 and above, to standard altimeter setting 29.92 (QNE). The Oakland FIR 5500 ft MSL transition to QNE is a lower crossover than the standard FL180, a common trap for Pacific/Hawaii altimetry questions.

docs.t: In the Pacific theater, what change in cruise Mach must be reported, and to whom?
docs.x: In the Pacific theater, what change in cruise Mach must be reported, and to whom? Oceanic control agencies require cruise Mach number be reported at FIR entry. All subsequent changes of cruise Mach of 0.02 or greater from any previously reported value must be communicated to ARINC. FOM 20.2.2 - Oceanic Cruise Mach - Reporting Requirement All subsequent changes of cruise Mach of 0.02 or greater from any previously reported value must be communicated to ARINC. FIR-entry Mach can be reported at check-in with ARINC (e.g., San Francisco Radio), via ADS-C, or free-text CPDLC. The 0.02 threshold mirrors the NAT/Atlantic Mach technique.

docs.t: In Pacific oceanic airspace with a total loss of communications, what transponder sequence is used?
docs.x: In Pacific oceanic airspace with a total loss of communications, what transponder sequence is used? Set transponder Code 7700 for a period of 1 (one) minute, then change to code 7600 and remain on 7600 for 15 minutes or the remainder of the flight, whichever occurs first; repeat the sequence as practicable. FOM 20.4.4 - Lost Communications in Oceanic Airspace adjust the transponder to Code 7700 for a period of 1 (one) minute. Then change to code 7600 and remain on 7600 for a period of 15 minutes or the remainder of the flight, whichever occurs first. Replying on 7700 first increases probability of early detection of the radio failure. In IMC, maintain last assigned speed and flight level for 20 minutes after failing to report over a compulsory point, then follow the filed flight plan.

docs.t: What are the maximum speed restrictions for operations in Mexico's National airspace?
docs.x: What are the maximum speed restrictions for operations in Mexico's National airspace? Maximum 250 KIAS at or below 10,000 ft within National airspace (and within 30 nm from any airport at or below 10,000 ft AGL of airport elevation). Maximum 200 KIAS within 10 nm of any airport below 3000 ft AGL above airport elevation. FOM 21.3.3.2 - Airspeed Restrictions (Mexico) Maximum Speed 200 KIAS within 10 nm of any airport below 3000 ft AGL above airport elevation. Certain Mexican airports restrict airspeed in National airspace at or below 18,000 ft, so check the applicable STARs.

docs.t: In the Central America portion of the Caribbean theater, what are the transition level and transition altitude?
docs.x: In the Central America portion of the Caribbean theater, what are the transition level and transition altitude? Transition Level is FL200 and Transition Altitude is 19,000 ft MSL, unless charted otherwise. FOM 21.3.4.2 - Transition Level/Altitude (Central America) Transition Level is FL200 and Transition Altitude is 19,000 ft MSL unless charted otherwise. Central America scheduled operations are Belize, Costa Rica, and Guatemala. 'Climb via'/'descend via' are NOT used in Central America (21.3.4.3).

docs.t: In Mexico, what is the rule regarding visual approaches relative to distance from the airport?
docs.x: In Mexico, what is the rule regarding visual approaches relative to distance from the airport? Mexico prohibits visual approaches outside of 10 nm. If you request the visual approach outside 10 nm from the airport, you will likely be advised to 'continue.' You must specifically request a 'visual descent' or a 'visual approach' since ATC does not respond to US colloquialisms. FOM 21.3.3.5 - Mexico Phraseology for Climbs and Descents Mexico prohibits visual approaches outside of 10 nm. A visual descent (remain on arrival routing, provide own terrain clearance) differs from a visual approach (routings/altitudes not restricted); the crew accepts responsibility for separation from traffic and terrain.

docs.t: How is the North Atlantic High Level Airspace (NAT HLA) defined by flight levels, and which oceanic control areas comprise it?
docs.x: How is the North Atlantic High Level Airspace (NAT HLA) defined by flight levels, and which oceanic control areas comprise it? NAT HLA is the airspace between flight levels 285 and 420 (inclusive) within the oceanic control areas of Bodo Oceanic (Norway), Gander Oceanic (Canada), New York Oceanic East (USA), Reykjavik (Iceland), Santa Maria (Portugal), and Shanwick (Ireland), excluding the Shannon and Brest Ocean Transition Areas. FOM 22.1.1 - North Atlantic Theater Defined defined as the volume of airspace between flight levels 285 and 420 (inclusive) Note NAT HLA spans FL285-FL420, which is wider than the FL290-FL410 RVSM/NAT DLM band. Source: NAT DOC 007, March 2025.

docs.t: For NAT HLA dispatch, what is the 787-specific inertial reference allowance?
docs.x: For NAT HLA dispatch, what is the 787-specific inertial reference allowance? The 787 can be dispatched with a single IRU, as long as at least one GPS is operational. (After departure, only a single HF radio and SATCOM data link are required.) FOM 22.1.10 - Required Equipment for NAT HLA Airspace The 787 can be dispatched with a single IRU, as long as at least one GPS is operational. Baseline NAT HLA required equipment includes dual IRS, dual long-range nav systems (2 MCDUs), dual NDs, one GPS receiver, ADS-C, CPDLC, SATCOM data link, and two HF radios or a single HF radio and SATVOICE.

docs.t: How is the North Atlantic Organized Track System (OTS) built and lettered, and what are its hours of validity at 30W?
docs.x: How is the North Atlantic Organized Track System (OTS) built and lettered, and what are its hours of validity at 30W? The OTS is published twice daily. Eastbound tracks (primarily night) are constructed by Gander Oceanic; westbound tracks (day) by Shanwick Oceanic. Tracks are lettered westbound from 'A' (most northerly) downward, and eastbound from 'Z' (most southerly) upward. Validity at 30W: Westbound 1130-1900 UTC; Eastbound 0100-0800 UTC. FOM 22.3.1 - North Atlantic Organized Track System (OTS) Eastbound tracks, primarily used at night, are constructed by Gander Oceanic, while westbound tracks, used during the day, are constructed by Shanwick Oceanic. OTS use is not mandatory; random routes are permitted. Times can be negotiated between Gander and Shanwick OACs, so check the NAT track message.

docs.t: What are the RCL (Request for Clearance) message timing intervals prior to the OEP for Gander, Shanwick, Santa Maria, and Bodo?
docs.x: What are the RCL (Request for Clearance) message timing intervals prior to the OEP for Gander, Shanwick, Santa Maria, and Bodo? Gander: 60-90 minutes (flights departing less than 45 min flying time from OEP send RCL 10 minutes prior to start-up). Shanwick: 30-90 minutes. Santa Maria: at least 40 minutes. Bodo: at least 20 minutes. FOM 22.7.4 - Timing for RCL Message Gander: 60-90 minutes. Except for Shanwick OCA, oceanic clearances are no longer issued in NAT OCAs; New York East does not require an RCL message at all. Shanwick still issues an oceanic clearance following the RCL.
