docs.t: How is the Northern Area of Magnetic Unreliability (AMU) defined, and how is navigation referenced within it?
docs.x: How is the Northern Area of Magnetic Unreliability (AMU) defined, and how is navigation referenced within it? The Northern AMU is the area within a 1000 nautical mile radius of the Northern Magnetic Pole (excluding airspace over Alaska and its territorial waters) and includes the Canadian Northern Domestic Airspace. Navigation relies on true headings rather than magnetic; runway headings, tracks, bearings, surface winds, and NAVAID tracks are all referenced to True North. FOM 22.2.3 - Northern Area of Magnetic Unreliability (AMU) navigation in the AMU relies on true headings rather than magnetic headings. If ATC issues a heading in the AMU, confirm whether it is magnetic or true. In the AMU the Heading Reference switch is moved from NORM to TRUE, and HDG SEL must be reselected after the switch change (NAT HLA training, FCOM SP.10.1).

docs.t: Under FOM 125.1, what is the published decompression floor for the Greenland Mountain Range region?
docs.x: Under FOM 125.1, what is the published decompression floor for the Greenland Mountain Range region? None. The Greenland regional decompression procedure was deleted from Ch 22 in Rev 125.1. Initial descent altitude comes from the polygon detail drawer in Jeppesen FD Pro and varies by polygon on the 787. Flights may not proceed through any charted No Ops Area. FOM 11.2.9 - Decompression Polygon Procedures (737/787/A330) Dispatchers and pilots will not permit flights to proceed through any areas charted as “No Ops Area.” Rev 125.1 removed the Decompression Procedure for Greenland Mountain Range Region from 22.5 - Weather. 22.6 is now Oceanic Procedures. The old 15,000 ft Greenland floor is no longer published. Greenland overflight limits are addressed via 11.2.9.

docs.t: What VHF channel spacing does Europe use, and how must 8.33 kHz frequencies be read back?
docs.x: What VHF channel spacing does Europe use, and how must 8.33 kHz frequencies be read back? Europe uses 8.33 kHz channel spacing across much of its airspace (three times as many channels as the 25 kHz US spacing). 8.33 kHz frequencies are shown with three decimal places and must be read back exactly, e.g., 132.015 MHz read back as 'WUN-TREE-TOO decimal ZE-RO-WUN-FIFE.' FOM 23.13 - Voice Procedures (Europe) Europe utilizes 8.33 kHz channel spacing across much of its airspace Capability is confirmed with 'CONFIRM EIGHT POINT THREE THREE' / 'AFFIRM EIGHT POINT THREE THREE' / 'NEGATIVE EIGHT POINT THREE THREE.'

docs.t: What lateral navigation accuracy does European RNAV 5 (formerly B-RNAV) require?
docs.x: What lateral navigation accuracy does European RNAV 5 (formerly B-RNAV) require? RNAV 5 requires aircraft to maintain a lateral navigation accuracy of plus/minus 5 nm for at least 95% of the flight time during the enroute phase. It is the standard for area navigation in ECAC enroute airspace, including SIDs and STARs into/out of terminal areas. The 787 is RNAV 5 compliant unless degraded. FOM 23.16.1 - Basic RNAV (B-RNAV) - RNAV 5 a lateral navigation accuracy of +/-5 nm for at least 95% of the flight time. For non-RNAV 5 compliant aircraft, notify ATC and Dispatch; Dispatch may obtain authorization to operate with the remaining nav equipment.

docs.t: In the Asia theater (Republic of Korea), what DMZ buffer must crews observe, and where is clear air turbulence a concern?
docs.x: In the Asia theater (Republic of Korea), what DMZ buffer must crews observe, and where is clear air turbulence a concern? Flight Crews must avoid overflying the Demilitarized Zone (DMZ); a buffer zone extends 5 nm south of the DMZ. With a strong jet stream present, be aware of the potential for clear air turbulence along the West Coast of Korea from FL300 to FL400. FOM 24.2 - Republic of Korea (and 24.2.1 Weather) a buffer zone extends 5 nm south of the DMZ. The Korea Office of Civil Aviation (KOCA) oversees all civil aviation activities; operations are under strict ATC control due to high traffic density and proximity to military-controlled zones.

docs.t: [NAT HLA] If you lose RNP4 capability (e.g., loss of GPS/GNSS), can you still enter the NAT HLA, and how long may you navigate on inertial position alone?
docs.x: [NAT HLA] If you lose RNP4 capability (e.g., loss of GPS/GNSS), can you still enter the NAT HLA, and how long may you navigate on inertial position alone? Yes. With loss of RNP4 the aircraft can still enter the NAT HLA under RNP10, though the clearance may be less optimal (e.g., altitude changes due to increased separation). Per OpSpec B036, navigation is unlimited with GPS updating and limited to 18 hours with inertial position updating. NAT HLA (training) - Reduction in Navigation Capability / NAT Doc 007 7.2 Loss of RNP 4, can you still enter the NAT? Aircraft can still enter the NAT HLA under RNP 10... OpSpec B036 - Unlimited with GPS updating. 18 hrs with inertial position updating. From the NAT HLA training deck (folds in RNP-degraded entry rules); cross-references NAT Doc 007 7.2 and OpSpec B036. Loss of RNP4 does not by itself bar NAT entry.

docs.t: [NAT HLA] If communications are lost AFTER entering the NAT, what should the pilot do?
docs.x: [NAT HLA] If communications are lost AFTER entering the NAT, what should the pilot do? Maintain the currently cleared route, flight level, and speed until reaching the Oceanic Exit Point. No route, flight level, or speed change should be made before the Oceanic Exit Point unless the pilot in command deems it necessary for the safety of the aircraft. NAT HLA (training) - Communications Failure / NAT Doc 007 5.6.10 The pilot shall maintain the currently cleared route, flight level and speed until reaching the Oceanic Exit Point. No route, flight level or speed change shall be made before the Oceanic Exit Point unless a change is deemed necessary by the pilot in command to ensure the safety of the aircraft. From the NAT HLA training deck. Contrast with comms lost PRIOR to the OEP, where you follow the RCF procedures of the adjacent (domestic) airspace and, if continuing, enter oceanic at the level/speed resulting from those procedures (FOM 7.8.8).

docs.t: [NAT HLA] After an engine failure/drift-down in NAT oceanic cruise with a diversion, how do you maneuver relative to the organized tracks, and how closely are PBCS tracks spaced?
docs.x: [NAT HLA] After an engine failure/drift-down in NAT oceanic cruise with a diversion, how do you maneuver relative to the organized tracks, and how closely are PBCS tracks spaced? Minimize your rate of descent until some distance from the track is established, then expedite descent to the feasible flight level. Unless the situation requires otherwise, continue to fly parallel to the tracks until below the lowest usable OTS flight level before turning toward the diversion point. PBCS tracks are only separated by 30 nm laterally, so paralleling the track first protects that spacing. NAT HLA (training) - Engine Failure and Drift Down / FOM 5.7.4 Unless the situation requires otherwise, continue to fly parallel to the tracks until below the lowest usable OTS flight level before turning to your diversion point... PBCS tracks are only separated by 30nm laterally. From the NAT HLA training deck (references FOM 5.7.4). Crews have forgotten to parallel the track due to task saturation - a called-out gotcha.

docs.t: SCENARIO (Pacific): On a Japan-to-North America leg the check airman assigns you a PACOTS track that then joins a NOPAC route. What navigation/performance approvals must the 787 hold for (a) the PACOTS track itself, and (b) the NOPAC segment?
docs.x: SCENARIO (Pacific): On a Japan-to-North America leg the check airman assigns you a PACOTS track that then joins a NOPAC route. What navigation/performance approvals must the 787 hold for (a) the PACOTS track itself, and (b) the NOPAC segment? For the PACOTS track: the aircraft must be RNP10/RNAV10 or RNP4 approved. When the PACOTS track ends on a NOPAC route, the NOPAC route requirements apply: RCP240, RSP180, and RNP4. PACOTS tracks are established at least 50 nm apart, and when operating on the ATS routes that may be assigned as PACOTS tracks (R220 east of NANAC, R580, A590 east of PUTER), NOPAC route system procedures should be applied. FOM 20.3.4 - Pacific Organized Track System (PACOTS) An aircraft on a PACOTS track must be RNP10/RNAV10 or RNP4 approved. If the PACOTS track ends on a NOPAC route, the route requirements of RCP240, RSP180, and RNP4 apply. Check-airman scenario. Related: the CEP (Central East Pacific, FOM 20.3.5) is the organized route system between Hawaii and California with seven charted ATS routes (R463, R464, R465, R576, R577, R578, R585) plus A331/A332 to the Pacific Northwest.

docs.t: SCENARIO (Atlantic): During NAT HLA prep the check airman fails one IRU at the gate, then asks whether you can still dispatch and what the minimum post-departure comms suite is. What do you tell him?
docs.x: SCENARIO (Atlantic): During NAT HLA prep the check airman fails one IRU at the gate, then asks whether you can still dispatch and what the minimum post-departure comms suite is. What do you tell him? Yes - the 787 can be dispatched with a single IRU as long as at least one GPS is operational. After departure, only a single HF radio and SATCOM data link are required. Baseline NAT HLA equipment is dual IRS, dual long-range nav systems (2 MCDUs), dual NDs, one GPS receiver, ADS-C, CPDLC, SATCOM data link, and two HF radios (or a single HF radio and SATVOICE). Separately, if you lose RNP4, you can still enter the NAT HLA under RNP10 (per the NAT HLA training material), though the clearance may be less optimal. FOM 22.1.10 - Required Equipment for NAT HLA Airspace After departure, only a single HF radio and SATCOM data link are required. The 787 can be dispatched with a single IRU, as long as at least one GPS is operational. Check-airman scenario. The RNP4->RNP10 entry allowance and the OpSpec B036 timing (unlimited with GPS updating, 18 hrs inertial) come from the NAT HLA (training) deck / NAT Doc 007 7.2, not this FOM section.

docs.t: SCENARIO (oceanic weather deviation): A cell is painting on the nose in Pacific oceanic cruise and you can't get an immediate clearance. How do you build the deviation, how do you prioritize the request, and how does SLOP factor in?
docs.x: SCENARIO (oceanic weather deviation): A cell is painting on the nose in Pacific oceanic cruise and you can't get an immediate clearance. How do you build the deviation, how do you prioritize the request, and how does SLOP factor in? Do NOT modify the FMC/FMS route - use the FMC/FMS Lateral Offset feature to build the weather-avoidance offset, then request that track deviation from Oceanic Control (the clearance is usually granted 'up to' the requested offset). When you call ATC/ARINC, state 'WEATHER DEVIATION REQUIRED' to get priority. Per the NAT HLA training material, if you cannot get a clearance: broadcast on 121.5/123.45, and use the weather-deviation logic - deviations less than 5 nm stay at altitude; deviations greater than 5 nm change altitude 300 ft using SAND (South Ascend, North Descend); once back within 5 nm return to assigned altitude and rejoin the centerline or SLOP offset. SLOP itself should be applied as a standard operating procedure for all oceanic crossings (entry point to exit point), but not within transition areas (NOTA, SOTA, BOTA, GOTA). FOM 20.5.1 - Weather Avoidance Lateral Offset Weather avoidance offsets must be accomplished utilizing the FMC/FMS Lateral Offset feature. Select a nm offset distance that will provide an adequate weather avoidance distance and request that track deviation from Oceanic Control; the clearance will generally be granted as 'up to' the requested offset distance... a more rapid response may be obtained by stating 'WEATHER DEVIATION REQUIRED' to indicate that priority is desired. Check-airman scenario. The SAND (South Ascend/North Descend), 300 ft, and 5NM thresholds, plus adjusting SLOP if turbulence is due to other aircraft, come from the NAT HLA (training) deck / NAT Doc 007 5.6.10. SLOP standard-use and transition-area exclusions are FOM 22.1.5.

docs.t: SCENARIO (altimetry): Descending into Hawaii through the Oakland Oceanic FIR, the check airman asks at exactly what point your altimeter should already be on 29.92, and how that differs from the Hawaiian Islands domestic transition. What's the trap?
docs.x: SCENARIO (altimetry): Descending into Hawaii through the Oakland Oceanic FIR, the check airman asks at exactly what point your altimeter should already be on 29.92, and how that differs from the Hawaiian Islands domestic transition. What's the trap? Within all areas of the Oakland FIR, at or above 5500 ft MSL the altimeter is set to standard 29.92 (QNE) - the trap is that this crossover is 5500 ft, not FL180. Within the Hawaiian Islands domestic area the normal split applies: at FL180 and above set standard 29.92 (QNE); below 18,000 ft MSL set current altimeter (QNH). So in the Oakland oceanic FIR you are on QNE far lower than the usual FL180 transition. FOM 20.7.1 - Altimeter Setting - Oakland Oceanic FIR/Hawaii Within all areas of the Oakland FIR, at or above 5500 ft MSL, the altimeter will be set to the standard 29.92 (QNE). Check-airman scenario. Contrast with the Atlantic/Europe convention (FOM 22.1.7 / 23.10) where settings are given in hectopascals (hPa) and transition altitudes are charted while transition levels come from the ATIS or approach controller.

docs.t: Rev 125: what is FOM 22.2.1 now called, and where did the Oceanic Entry Point definition go?
docs.x: Rev 125: what is FOM 22.2.1 now called, and where did the Oceanic Entry Point definition go? 22.2.1 is now 'Transition Areas'. The Oceanic Entry Point (OEP) definition moved to 22.2.2, and the Northern Area of Magnetic Unreliability moved to 22.2.3. Note the GOTA has OEPs in the middle of the airspace, which requires SLOP halfway through the transition area, and eastbound GOTA flights send an RCL to Gander Oceanic. FOM 22.2.1 - Transition Areas Note that exceptions to common rules may exist. For example, a unique feature of the GOTA is that it has OEPs in the middle of the airspace which requires SLOP procedures halfway through the transition area. Also, eastbound flights through the GOTA are to send an RCL message to Gander Oceanic. Chapter 22 renumbering is NEW in Rev 125: 22.2.1 Transition Areas, 22.2.2 OEP, 22.2.3 AMU, 22.2.4 West Atlantic.

docs.t: Rev 125: what is the jumpseat rule into and out of London Heathrow, and which brand new country chapter was added?
docs.x: Rev 125: what is the jumpseat rule into and out of London Heathrow, and which brand new country chapter was added? Per local regulations, jumpseaters are not authorized into or out of LHR unless operationally required. Rev 125 also added a new Italy chapter, 23.19, and retitled chapter 23.18 from London Heathrow to United Kingdom. FOM 23.18.1.13 - Jumpseat Per local regulations, jumpseaters are not authorized into/out of LHR unless operationally required. NEW section in Rev 125. LHR subsections renumbered under 23.18.1; 23.19 Italy is a new chapter.
